file: $550 MILLION CHINA LOAN IS APPROVED BY I.M.F.txt
text:
ï»¿
The International Monetary Fund today approved a $550 million loan to China, marking that country's largest borrowing from any financial institution.
The Washington-based I.M.F., which makes funds available to countries in balance-of-payments difficulties, said it had approved a so-called standby borrowing arrangement under which China would draw down 450 million special drawing rights (an internationally created reserve asset), equal to $550 million, over the next 12 months.
The fund said that China would also borrow an undisclosed amount from the institution's trust fund, a pool of money raised from the sale of gold. 
It is used to help countries particularly strapped financially. 
The advent of China as a significant borrower at a time when other poor countries are having increasing economic trouble because of higher oil prices could have major financial implications.
China gets $550 million loan approval from International Monetary Fund
Analysts noted that China's demands could reduce funds available for other prospective borrowers. 
China joined the monetary fund and World Bank last year as part of its efforts to draw closer into the world financial and trading network.
The World Bank, the official name of which is the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, chiefly makes development loans to build up the economies of poorer countries. 
It has not announced any loans to China, but a mission from the bank recently returned from a project study, and a lending program could be announced later this year.
In approving China's request for the $550 million, the monetary fund noted that China had started a necessary stabilization program to reduce inflationary pressures and whittle down a deficit in trade and services.
The fund makes loans conditioned upon a country's adoption of economic measures to strengthen its international accounts. 
An analysis by the fund of China's latest measures concluded that the Chinese authorities had embarked on the proper course.
Â 
Reluctant to Borrow Heavily
Although China's foreign exchange position is believed to be relatively healthy, the Chinese have so far been reluctant to borrow heavily in Western capital markets, especially while interest rates remain high.
Analysts noted, however, that China had already been borrowing more heavily in short-term financial markets, especially in Europe and Japan. 
Proceeds have been used mainly to finance energy developments.
The Chinese authorities began a program of rapid economic expansion four years ago. 
But when the steel mills and other heavy manufacturing operations began costing more than the planners contemplated, the program was sharply scaled back.
Â 
Main Objectives Listed
''The main objectives of the Government's economic program for this year,'' the fund said, ''are the elimination of inflationary pressures, the readjustment of the investment pattern to foster resumption of rapid economic growth and to maintain the current account (trade and services) deficit at a sustainable level.''
The fund noted that priority was now being given to investment in light industry, agriculture and energy. 
Last Saturday China's chief economic planner, Deputy Prime Minister Yao Yilin, announced a program of sharp spending cuts and said the Government intended to monitor supply more closely to improve the economic performance.

An 83- year-old Chinese man who abandoned his life as a clothing merchant to plant trees in the mountains has been honored by the Government, The China Daily newspaper reported today.
The official English-language daily said the man, Zhang Houla, working alone with a hoe, had planted more than a million trees on 50 acres in a remote valley in Shanxi Province in north-central China.
Chinese Government honors Zhang Houla, 83-year-old man who abandoned life as clothing merchant in '66 to plant trees in mountains of Shanxi Province (S)
Quoting from Outlook Magazine, the newspaper said Mr. Zhang was known as a ''forestry fanatic, madman and savage'' by local people.
In 1966, at the age of 66, he divorced his wife of more than 40 years and left his family to live in a mountain cave and plant trees. 
The report quoted Mr. Zhang's wife as telling neighbors, ''I can't stop him, nor can I stand him.''
He lived mostly on yams and wild herbs, bought no new clothes or shoes and used his own savings to buy seeds and nursery stock.
After Chinese leaders started a nationwide program to plant trees in 1981, Mr. Zhang's efforts finally gained respect. 
Local authorities decided to write his story in the county history book, award him $1,500 and appoint one of his sons as caretaker of the forest.

file: Business and the LawTamar Lewin Legal Claims Against China.txt
text:
ï»¿
ONE of the last acts of the imperial regime that ruled China in 1911 has come back to plague not only the modern Peoples Republic of China but America's State Department and Federal courts as well. 
Depending on how it is resolved, it could become a serious obstacle to trade between the United States and China.
The Qing dynasty, just before it collapsed, issued millions of dollars worth of bearer bonds for the construction of the railroad that runs from Canton to Peking. 
The 1951 maturity date on these Hukuang Railways Sinking Fund Gold Loan bonds came and went, but the bondholders never got paid. 
Many of them now hold the bonds more as curios than as financial paper.
But on Aug. 
21, 1981, Federal District Judge U. W. Clemon of Birmingham, Ala., entered a $41.3 million default judgment for the bondholders. 
China, as has been its custom whenever sued in United States courts, did not show up to defend itself. 
As the old Chinese proverb would have it: ''To enter a court of law is to enter a tiger's mouth.''
Since then, however, China has, for the first time, hired an American lawyer to conduct its defense: Eugene Theroux, of Washington's Baker & McKenzie.
Mr. Theroux, who has had long experience working with the Chinese, has asked Judge Clemon to set aside the default judgment and dismiss the bondholders' claims. 
''It is an odious debt forced on the Chinese by foreign bankers, on terms that were unfair,'' he said.
Mr. Theroux's request to overturn the default judgment is backed by the United States Government. 
Several months ago the State Department filed a statement of interest in which Secretary of State George P. Shultz said the case had become a major irritant in American-Chinese relations.
And in court papers filed last week, the Justice Department told Judge Clemon that allowing the default judgment to stand would exacerbate international tensions and could be ''expected to affect adversely our bilateral relations with China.''
The case is scheduled for argument Jan. 
17.
People familiar with the railway bond case and other pending American claims against China say the question of the default judgment is central to the future of relations between the two countries.
The Chinese maintain that China, as a sovereign government, has no obligation to appear in the courts of another nation.
''The United States has concluded that the Peoples Republic of China's belief that it is immune from judicial proceedings, including any obligation to appear and argue that immunity, is strongly held as a matter of principle,'' said the Justice Department in its filing.
As a practical matter, China has a lot to lose if it does appear in court. 
There are many other issues of bearer bonds floating around, some of which have already given rise to litigation in New York and Pittsburgh. 
So if China defends itself in the Birmingham case but loses, it would likely face a flood of legal claims in this nation, and fighting these would require considerable resources.
On the other hand, if China does not get the railway bond case dismissed, lawyers for the bondholders have said they will try to collect on the default judgment by attaching Chinese bank accounts and assets in this country.
The railway case could have ramifications well beyond the bond claims, too.
As Chinese exports to this country increase, so do product liability claims against the Chinese Government. 
So far, the Chinese have not been defending themselves in such actions. 
In the most publicized case, a 17-year-old boy whose right eye was injured by defective Chinese fireworks sued. 
The Chinese never appeared in court to defend the case, but the claim was apparently dropped after a secret out-of-court settlement.
Still, as China does more business in the United States and as such suits proliferate, most observers believe that China will have to come to grips with the American judicial system.
''As the Chinese come into this world and work with us, they ought to recognize their contractual obligations,'' said Edward Sills, the lawyer who filed the New York bond litigation against China. 
''Under international law, there is sovereign immunity for acts of state, but there is a very clear limitation on sovereign immunity when it comes to commercial transactions. 
The Chinese are really hung up more on the political question than the legal one. 
The Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act clearly indicates that the raising of money through a bond issue is a commercial transaction.''
As his court filings point out, however, the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act was passed in 1976, long after the bonds had been issued.

file: C.I.A. STUDY FINDS CHINESE ARMY STILL OUT OF DATE.txt
text:

China's military modernization program is making ''limited progress'' but still has far to go before Peking attains fully modernized armed forces, according to Central Intelligence Agency analysts.
Their report was part of a compendium of papers issued today by the Congressional Joint Economic Committee, assessing China's drive to upgrade its industry, agriculture, military forces and science and technology.
Represenative Henry S. Reuss, Democrat of Wisconsin, chairman of the committee, noted that despite advances since the death of Mao in 1976, ''China faces serious economic problems.''
WASHINGTON, Aug. 
25 (AP) -China's military modernization program is making ''limited progress'' but still has far to go before Peking attains fully modernized armed forces, according to Central Intelligence Agency analysts.
He added: ''Agricultural production is barely keeping up with the population. 
Oil production peaked in 1979 and has been declining, and energy can be expected to be a constraint on growth for the next few years.
''The defense burden has been rather moderate, outlays having been reduced or kept level in the past several years. 
But there are pressures to increase defense allocations. 
Such a change in policy could have serious consequences for the economy.''
The question of Chinese military modernization has emerged as a particularly sensitive issue in the past few years, since the United States moved to establish full diplomatic relations with Peking and restrict official ties with Taiwan.
Under the terms of a joint United States-Chinese communique issued on Aug. 
17, the Reagan Administration agreed to limit American arms sales to Taiwan but set no date for a full cutoff.
John C. Holdridge, Assistant Secretary of State for East Asian and Pacific affairs, subsequently went before a House subcommittee to offer assurances that the United States could move ''quite rapidly'' to assist Taiwan in case it was threatened by an attack from the mainland.
In the Joint Economic Committee publication, two C.I.A. analysts, Sydney H. Jammes and G. Lawrence Lamborn, wrote that ''although China's defense modernization is still in an early stage and undoubtedly faces severe tests, the program is making limited progress.''
But they said the program would be successful ''only if the nation enjoys prolonged political stabilityI, retains access to foreign capital and technology, avoids costly foreign military campaigns and moves forward in higher priority efforts to modernize agriculture, industry and science and technology.''
Peking's drive to upgrade its military forces has been spurred by strong apprehension over Soviet military intentions in Asia. 
However, Mr. Jammes and Mr. Lamborn noted that ''China evidently views the Soviet Union as a long-term rather than as an immediate danger, and defense modernization probably will continue to hold the lowest priority among the 'Four Modernizations.'
''
While Chinese armed forces should achieve ''limited gains'' by 1985, the analysts said, ''weaknesses in China's electronics industry will prevent the widescale introduction of new radars, sonars and other electronic equipment.''
They added: ''Tactical mobility and logistical support will continue to be hampered by shortages of vehicles and by limited capacity for repair and maintenance. 
And although new ground force equipment such as air defense and antitank missiles will appear in limited numbers, their production will fall far short of P.L.A. needs.''
The P.L.A. is the Chinese Army.
Another specialist on the Chinese military, Thomas W. Robinson of Georgetown University, wrote that the Peking leadership has apparently decided to ''persevere along traditional lines, making internal improvements only when it can be demonstrated that total costs will not rise drastically.''

file: CAPITALISM KEEPS A TOEHOLD IN CHINA.txt
text:
ï»¿
HE BIN rarely leaves home without his Great Wall credit card. 
One of this city's most successful entrepreneurs, Mr. He uses China's latest status symbol with a casual confidence that belies the long hours and political uncertainties he faces.
Five years ago, he was a disgruntled worker in a state shoe factory. 
''I had a skill to make shoes and run a shop,'' he said. 
''The factory 'big bowl' system was not for me.''
The ''daguofan,'' or big bowl, refers to the system of paying workers in state-owned factories a fixed salary regardless of ability or ambition. 
Although the overwhelming number of Chinese still work for the state, Mr. He and hundreds of thousands of others struck out on their own in the early 1980's when the political climate changed under Deng Xiaoping.
The entrepreneurs now hope their careers are not short-lived. 
As hard-line Communist Party leaders reassert rigorous adherence to socialism, the fate of private business in Canton and elsewhere in the country will be the ultimate measure of China's commitment to economic reform.
Mr. He suffered in a previous era of dogmatic socialism. 
''My father began a shoe business in 1921,'' he said. 
''We kept in business until 1958. 
That year, they closed the shop and I went to work in a leather shoe factory.''
In 1958, Mao Zedong launched a three-year effort to accelerate the country's economic growth by creating huge agricultural communes and backyard industries. 
A catastrophic famine resulted in which 30 million people may have died. 
Throughout this period, and the calamitous decade of the Cultural Revolution that ended in 1976, Mr. He and his family lived in the former shoe store on Wanfu, or Ten Thousand Happiness, Street.
In 1982, Mr. He was given the opportunity to begin again. 
He borrowed money from a bank and opened a small shop, which was successful from the start. 
''Before I opened the shop I was worried,'' he said. 
''The first day I sold more than 20 pairs of shoes. 
I didn't expect that at all.''
Unhappy with the quality and styles of state-produced shoes, Mr. He built a factory to make Western-style laced bankers' shoes, slip-ons and women's pumps with delicate leather ribbing. 
$135,000 a Year Today, he said, he and his wife sell about $135,000 worth of shoes a year, an immense sum by Chinese standards. 
''We can turn out a new product in three days,'' he said. 
''It may take the state three months to produce a new shoe.''
There are 50 other independent shoe makers in Canton, he said, and probably 350 private shoe shops.
From the watch repairer's small case on the back of a bicycle to Mr. He's shoe factory, more than 150,000 people work in private businesses in the southern province of Guangdong. 
Private restaurants and clothing stores compete side by side with state-run counterparts. 
Canton's proximity to Hong Kong, which is 85 miles away, and its distance from Beijing, which is 1,200 miles away, have nurtured a self-assured independence in economic life that is unknown in the north.
Cases in Mr. He's shop display the 150 styles of shoes he sells at prices about 10 percent higher than those in state stores. 
There are padded benches - unheard of in state stores - for waiting customers.
''People's living standards are higher,'' Mr. He said. 
''They require quality products.''
Indeed, officials agree that the purchasing power of the Chinese has grown tremendously as a consequence of economic liberalization.
Mr. He's shoes are made in a four-story red brick building that also serves as his home and a dormitory for 18 of his workers. 
He borrowed about $27,000 from a bank to build it and expects to have the loan repaid in three years. 
He said his workers earn about $18 a month, about double what state shoe workers get. 
He also provides housing for his employees and is responsible for their medical fees.
Despite his success, Mr. He admitted that the vagaries of the political climate could affect his and other private concerns here. 
''But so far,'' he said, ''the political changes in Beijing have had no effect.''
A top provincial official said there was no turning back on the economic liberalization. 
''We have been carrying out the correct policy,'' said Xu Zhi, Canton's deputy secretary general. 
''We will not slow down on economic reform.''
In any event, Mr. He said, there was nothing else to do but to work hard. 
''Since 1982 until now, I have been open every day,'' he noted. 
''I am open 13 hours a day. 
I have never closed for even one day.''

China issued new economic regulations today aimed at attracting greater foreign investment by giving more preferential treatment to joint ventures.
Several Western business sources here thought that the new regulations, which were made public by the State Council, contained little that was new because many of the announced changes had already been quietly put into effect.
But the announcement promised to reduce the confusion that has persisted among Western investors about their rights and obligations in joint ventures with Chinese companies controlled by the state.
China issues new economic regulations aimed at attracting greater foreign investment by giving preferential treatment to joint ventures; new rules are aimed at reducing confusion that has persisted among foreign investors about their rights and obligations in joint ventures with Chinese companies controlled by state (M)
''It's comforting that we have it spelled out,'' a United States representative said.
The new regulations, which supplement China's first joint venture law promulgated in July 1979, apply generally to enterprises that combine Western capital and technology with Chinese factories and labor.
Â 
Exemption for Some Imports
Among other changes, the latest regulations exempt certain imported materials from customs duties and industrial and commercial taxes. 
Previously, Western investors were technically liable for duties on what they imported to make a product in China. 
The products made for export are also now formally exempted from the nation's consolidated industrial and commercial tax.
The purpose of the joint ventures has been to generate foreign currency for China by producing quality goods for export, and investors have been prohibited or strongly discouraged from marketing them inside the country. 
Now joint venture products that China urgently needs or would otherwise import can be mainly sold in the domestic market.
The new legislation now authorizes the department responsible for the joint venture to resolve any foreign- exchange imbalance caused by domestic sales, though it does not specify how. 
The new legislation also stipulates that disputes between the foreign and Chinese partners can be arbitrated in the country where the sued party is situated or in a third country if both sides agree. 
While the Chinese may still insist that disagreements be arbitrated in China, this gives an appearance of greater leeway for the foreign investor.
Â 
Directors' Status Recognized
The board of directors of a joint venture is now regarded as its highest authority and is empowered to make all major decisions under the latest regulations. 
Government departments in charge may offer guidance, assistance and supervision but not actual leadership.
''This provision reflects respect for the right of a joint venture to do business independently,'' Yuan Mu, a State Council spokesman, was quoted as saying at a news conference.
A report on the new regulations on joint ventures circulated today by the official New China News Agency did not clarify some problems that have perplexed Western businessmen.
For example, there was no mention of a requirement that Chinese management be paid on a par with Western executives in the joint venture. 
The Government has the habit of siphoning away most of this Western salary, leaving the Chinese manager with little more than the local prevailing salary.
Some Western businessmen said they were waiting to see to what extent the new rules would make it easier to do business in China. 
''The big question still is: How will it work in practice?'' one American said.

The Chinese Government is making more loans to develop a diversified rural economy, according to Li Fei, vice president of the People's Bank of China. 
The New China News Agency today quoted him as saying the funds were supporting light industry and the output of consumer goods, mostly bicycles, sewing machines and watches.
Chinese Government is making more loans to develop diversified rural economy

China, in a step aimed at encouraging imports of foreign products needed for its modernization campaign, today reduced customs duties on 149 categories of industrial equipment and raw materials.
At the same time the State Council, the ruling Government body, raised tariffs on other items of equipment that China already produces.
Import duties were lowered on timber and timber products, rubber, leather, pulp and paper, as well as on raw materials for China's energy industry. 
Tariffs were also reduced on some machinery, parts and accessories used in the textile and other light industries, which the Government is trying to strengthen.
China reduces customs duties on 149 categories of industrial equipment and raw materials
In announcing the adjustments, the official New China News Agency did not disclose the new tariff rates, which it said applied to 16 percent of the total number of items subject to duties.
Â 
A Ban on Exemptions
In a related decisio n likely to affect West ern companies doing business with China, a spokesman for the Gene ral Administration of Customs said that, in general, no customs exe mptions would be granted to foreign companies and that they wo uld not be permitted to write any such exemptions into their contract s with Chinese enterprises.
Today's tariff actions followed a confirmation by a prominent Chinese foreign trade specialist that China would continue to import essential foreign technology and equipment to develop its economy.
Zhou Jiannan, a deputy minister of the Administrative Commission on Import-Export Affairs, said in the latest issue of China's foreign trade magazine that such imports would include equipment for the transportation and energy sectors and the textile and other light industries.
Â 
More Selective About Imports
Officials have said that China will become more selective in buying foreign products, concentrating on advanced technology and machinery that it cannot yet manufacture domestically. 
China will also be more diligent in seeking attractive terms, including lowinterest credits, and joint ventures, they add.
Examples of the kind of imports that China is seeking have included coal-mining equipment from Britain, Japan and West Germany, worth about $800 million altogether, Japanese electronic technology to make color television and sophisticated shipbuilding equipment.
To solicit more investment funds, the People's Bank of China announced earlier this week that it would raise interest paid on deposits to a maximum of 7.92 percent annually for an individual deposit fixed for five years. 
Deposits by overseas Chinese would earn a maximum of 8.28 percent annually for five years. 
The new rates are to take effect April 1.
The bank did not say what its new lending rate would be, but said the rates would be higher for joint ventures with foreign partners than for strictly domestic enterprises.

The Communist Party harshly criticized undisciplined members today and said they were helping to increase inflation and corruption that threaten economic change.
A front-page editorial in the party newspaper, the People's Daily, accused local party organizations of trying to profit illegally from inflation and short supplies and ignoring orders from Beijing to reduce spending.
''Those who don't abide by the party's discipline must be punished,'' the editorial warned. 
The harsh indictment was probably approved by the party's policy-making Central Committee, which began a private, five-day session Monday.
The session is expected to approve a two-year moratorium on a program phasing out price subsidies and to also endorse measures to control inflation and capital construction.
China's Supreme Court, meanwhile, ordered lower courts to punish officials found guilty of profiteering and speculation. 
It ordered an end to fines and said that instead criminal charges should be brought against those found culpable.
Inflation has soared from about 7 percent last year to more than 20 percent this year. 
Overspending by Government offices and state-run factories, and widespread speculation, have been major factors, although the issuing of too much currency and too loose credit are also to blame.
Â 
An Active Black Market
Reports appear in the official media almost daily about local Government officials and factory managers, many of them party members, who bought goods at state-subsidized prices and resold them on the black market for huge profits.
The People's Daily editorial warned party members to put the collective good above individual profit. 
It emphasized that ''the individual must submit to the organization'' and lower-level party organs to higher ones.
''We must enforce party discipline to guarantee the benefit of the whole,'' it said. 
''Strict discipline and unanimous action are good traditions of our party.''

The Chinese Government accused Washington today of delaying approval of the sale of technology products to China and said that, as a result of this policy, the United States was missing out on export opportunities.
An editorial in the official Beijing Review magazine said the United States approved less than two-thirds of the technology exports for which China applied last year.
It added that the United States was maintaining unwarranted restrictions on the transfer of technology.
The editorial appeared on the eve of a visit by Commerce Secretary Malcolm Baldrige, who will be co-chairman of the fifth session of a joint commission on commerce and trade that will review trade relations between the two countries.

But the editorial charged that the United States at times approved technology sales only after learning that other countries were selling the same items to China, or delayed approval until what China finally received ''had become relatively backward.''
The American Embassy declined to comment. 
But a Western diplomat said the editorial voiced concerns that had been expressed by American manufacturers who say they lost business to companies from other industrialized countries with less restrictive export policies.

China today declared its current five-year economic plan to be a success, setting the scene for the introduction of the next five-year plan sometime over the next two weeks.

file: CHINA CAUTIOUSLY INCREASING ITS WORLDWIDE INVESTMENTS.txt
text:
ï»¿
China, on the eve of Premier Zhao Ziyang's first visit to the United States, is testing the waters of international capitalism.
The experiment, which began on a significant scale only last spring, is being conducted worldwide. 
In the United States, for example, the Chinese province of Guangdong has invested in a meatpacking plant in Clive, Iowa. 
The China International Trust and Investment Corporation has taken a 19 percent interest in Santec, a personal computer company based in Amherst, N.H. 
And the China National Metals and Minerals Import and Export Corporation has joined the Wheeling-Pittsburgh Steel Corporation in an international joint venture to trade metals and minerals.
Outside the United States, China is negotiating investments in potash mining in Saskatchewan and wood pulp manufacturing in British Columbia; has bought into a forestry project on the Solomon Islands and has invested in fisheries in Sri Lanka.
According to a State Department estimate, the overall value of such investment abroad by Peking may be as high as $1 billion when Hong Kong real estate is included. 
But analysts say the figure is certain to rise as China becomes more comfortable with the hurly-burly ways of capitalist markets.
Â 
Display of 'Unusual' Confidence
''It shows a confidence by Peking in the international economic system that is certainly unusual for a Communist government,'' said one Administration foreign trade official who asked not to be identified. 
''It also shows a confidence in their own abilities to get out and play with the big boys.''
The issues of bilateral trade and investment are expected to be major topics during the Chinese Prime Minister's visit to the United States and Canada. 
Mr. Zhao, who will be the highest ranking Chinese official to visit Washington since China's leader, Deng Xiaoping, came here in 1979, is expected to sign an agreement on industrial cooperation while in Washington. 
Mr. Zhao left Honolulu today after a day of sightseeing there, and was scheduled to arrive in Williamsburg, Va., early Monday to continue his North American tour. 
He is scheduled to meet with President Reagan on Tuesday.
According to one American official, a nuclear-technology exchange agreement could also be reached during the Chinese Prime Minister's three-day visit to Washington. 
Such a treaty would permit American companies to sell nuclear power reactors to China, which has an ambitious program on the drawing boards to increase electric power generation for several of its major cities.
American analysts say the Chinese have several specific objectives for their investment and trading program: to improve their technical and management skills; raise foreign exchange earnings; get around protectionist barriers that are rising in many of their markets, and secure a stable source of supply of raw materials.
This investment abroad coincides with a rising interest by American companies in joint ventures in China and a new concentration by both Governments on concluding a treaty defining rights and obligations of investors in both countries.
American industrialists see important markets developing in China as it continues with ambitious expansion programs aimed at quadrupling output by the year 2000.
Last year, 20 American companies - including Squibb, Occidental Petroleum, American Motors and Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing - announced expansion moves in China. 
According to the National Council for United States-China Trade, a body with a membership of 500 American companies that facilitates trade with China, the overall stake of the 20 companies is about $100 million.
Along with two-way investment, two-way trade is also picking up. 
According to the council, trade between the two nations could reach a record $5.5 billion to $6 billion this year compared with $4.4 billion last year. 
The rise will be led by growing sales of American capital goods and wheat, the council says.
To date, American companies have been faring well in the China market, Over stiff European, Canadian and even Russian competition, for example, General Electric recently won a contract to provide 200 diesel electric locomotives for Chinese railroads, which will add more than $200 million to the export total this year.
Â 
Big Honeywell Order
And under recently relaxed Washington guidelines for the sale of American high technology goods to China, Honeywell recently won clearance to sell $23 million worth of personal computers.
According to figures filed with the International Monetary Fund, which it joined in 1980, China has accumulated some $20 billion in foreign exchange and gold reserves in recent years. 
But many analysts expect that the reserves may quickly decline as China gets deeper into its domestic industrial expansion programs. 
According to its own estimates, China may be spending as much as $50 billion by the end of the century to expand coal production and $20 billion on offshore oil development.
Some of the expected slack is likely to be taken up through development loans, however. 
With strong American backing after the restoration of full diplomatic ties in December 1978, China became a member of both the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank in 1980 - accepting their disclosure requirements.
Â 
$1 Billion World Bank Loan
China has already received about $1 billion in loans from the World Bank. 
Senior bank officials, such as David W. Berk, acting division chief for China programs, and Edwin R. Lim, senior economist for East Asia and the Pacific region, project that China's borrowing could rise to $2 billion a year in the second half of the 1980's.
Meanwhile, Peking has been putting its huge currency reserves to work in both direct foreign investment and the capital markets.
The China International Trust and Investment Corporation, the vehicle for much of the foreign investment, recently drew $100 million from Tokyo capital markets. 
The Development Corporation of Fujian Province, just across the Formosa Straits from Taiwan, also borrowed around $20 million in Tokyo recently.

text:
ï»¿
China has begun the largest census in history in a meticulous effort to discover just how many people it has. 
The Peking Government claims about a billion citizens out of a total world population of 4.5 billion, though officials concede that no one knows the exact number of Chinese.
The census drive, which started Thursday and was preceded by a publicity campaign with banners, colorful posters and loudspeakers urging cooperation, is ostensibly a response to a 1974 United Nations call for all countries to undertake a new census before 1985.
But with a baby born in China every 2 seconds, articles and speeches here have stressed that the census is crucial to Peking's task of feeding and clothing its population while trying to catch up industrially with the West.
In addition to providing raw statistics needed for a centrally planned economy, the census is expected to indicate how successful China has been in its stringent birth control policies, which are aimed at holding the population down to 1.2 billion by the year 2000.
PEKING, July 5 - China has begun the largest census in history in a meticulous effort to discover just how many people it has.
When Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang went to register his family Thursday, he told the New China News Agency that the census was of great importance for China's modernization program. 
In a televised talk last month, Deputy Prime Minister Yao Yilin described the census as ''a large-scale investigation of national conditions,'' a phrase that has been echoed since by other Chinese officials.
The Communist Government has counted its citizens twice since taking power in 1949. 
Its first census in 1953 revealed 601 million Chinese. 
In the second census in 1964, the population exceeded 723 million.
Both of these figures were tabulated using the abacus, a manual calculator that has been in wide use in China since the Ming Dynasty six centuries ago.
This time, 29 computers are being used to collate the information. 
The computers will be used for final tallies in every province but Tibet. 
The local tabulations will still be done by abacus.
Taiwan is being included in the census, using the Nationalist Government's figure of 18 million inhabitants, in keeping with Peking's claim that the island is its unrecovered province.
Â 
Five Million Census-Takers
On the mainland, the Government has recruited over five million census-takers and supervisors, a contingent larger than the Chinese armed forces. 
Most started today with bundles of questionnaires, traveling by bicycle or foot in the dense eastern cities. 
Other workers set out several weeks ago in sparsely populated regions like the highlands of Tibet and the prairies of Inner Mongolia.
The census-takers and supervisors are instructed to complete their enumerating and checking by mid-July. 
Then over 100,000 data coders and technicians will work for several months feeding the information through the computers.
The preliminary results are to be released next October, with full census data available by the end of 1984. 
China is officially spending $200 million on its census, but that figure must be multiplied several times to give a true picture of the cost.
Â 
21 I.B.M. 
Computers Used
The United Nations fund for population activities also donated $15.6 million for the Chinese to purchase and install 21 new I.B.M. 
4300 computers. 
China is also using eight other Western computers that it purchased earlier.
The computer network will give China the ability to process other economic data that will be needed in its drive for modernization. 
The new census form, which is printed in green ink on paper half as large as a newspaper page, contains 19 questions, as compared with nine questions in the 1964 census. 
In addition to the old categories of name, age, sex, nationality and occupation, the new questionnaire asks women of childbearing age about children they had last year or expect soon. 
Such questions are meant to help evaluate China's birth control program.
Attempts to count the Chinese are hardly new. 
Population surveys have been carried out for thousands of years through successive dynasties. 
By the end of 1981, the State Statistical Bureau reported that China's population reached 996,220,000, an estimate arrived at through the nationwide household registrations checked twice a year.
Â 
Signs of Official Concern
But the Chinese have long been suspicious of the census and once hid for fear that they might be taxed or drafted into the army. 
Last month, Deputy Prime Minister Yao promised that the new census enumeration ''will in no way affect the citizens' rights and interests and obligations.''
Nonetheless, there have been signs of official concern about potential evasiveness, particularly in the countryside where 800 million peasants live. 
Families sometimes do not report a recent death in order to use the extra ration card to get grain or cotton cloth. 
Couples may conceal the fact that they have several children.
In the cities, thousands of Chinese are thought to have drifted back illegally from the countryside, where many were sent during the Cultural Revolution. 
Even some officials may underreport the local population growth rate to meet family planning targets.
People's Daily warned last spring that ''conditions must be reported exactly as they are at the time. 
No hiding the truth or false reporting will be allowed.''
Recently, a Shanghai peddler was fined $6 amid great publicity for having lied about the registration of his children in a trial census last year.
Â 
37,000 Census-Takers in Peking
One census station in the Tianqiao district of southern Peking today offered a glimpse into how the time-consuming enumeration process works. 
Feng Guilan, one of 37,000 census-takers in Peking, sat at a small table checking off responses from Chen @Zhiqing. 
She recorded that Mr. Chen was 52 years old, repaired trucks for a living, had a son and two daughters and that his 46-year-old wife was not pregnant in 1981.
Miss Feng, who is on a two-month leave from her job as a tea salesclerk, filled out the form, read back the responses and then had Mr. Chen sign the form to acknowledge that it was accurate. 
The procedure took about 15 minutes.
The station supervisor, He Qing, acknowledged that the enumeration was starting slowly. 
''We are not so experienced so we are taking only eight households in these first two hours,'' said Miss He, ''but we'll take up to 20 households tomorrow.''
Shen Yiying, a 23-year-old factory worker, came in to register the family for her mother, who she said was illiterate. 
Ma Zhanyu, a 63-year-old retired worker, brought along a paper written by his son to supplement the information in his maroon-bound household registration document.
Mr. Ma, who lives with his grandchildren, said afterward that he had no misgivings about answering so many questions. 
''Our country will have a clearer idea of its population, how many men there are and how many women,'' Mr. Ma said.
Â 
Small Floating Population
Xie Ruibin, who heads the census group of the local Tianqiao street committee, said that his 223 census workers filled out each household's questionnaire themselves to avoid errors and would later take turns checking each other's findings.
He was asked what happened if a census-taker found someone living in Peking without a legal registration or committing some other violation. 
''The main aim of the census is to get a clearer idea of the population, but if irregularities are found out, they will be dealt with by the departments concerned,'' Mr. Xie said.
While the task is likely to be harder in the countryside, Li Chengrui, the director of the census office, said in a recent article that China had one of the world's smallest floating populations, which would facilitate the work.
The Chinese Government seems confident that the careful census procedure and the use of computers will leave negligible room for error. 
A pilot census undertaken two years ago in Wuxi, a small city northwest of Shanghai, produced a discrepancy of only 17 onethousandths of 1 percent from previous estimates, while another study in a remote area of Inner Mongolia found a discrepancy of nine-tenths of 1 percent.

text:
ï»¿
In an unusual alliance of a world power and a university, Chinese officials signed a contract over the weekend that establishes Hofstra University as a deal maker for China.
The agreement calls on Hofstra to form a corporation, headed by its top academic dean, to seek companies who want to market products or enter joint ventures in China. 
Chinese officials, 15 of whom were in New York, said yesterday that they planned to negotiate this week with several companies in the region that could help revitalize China's aging industries.
Hofstra officials likened their role to that of investment brokers, and said the university would receive a commission for each agreement it negotiated between China and a United States business.
Chinese officials sign contract with Hofstra University that calls on Hofstra to form corporation to seek companies that want to market products or enter joint ventures in China; Hofstra officials say university will receive commission for each agreement it negotiates between China and a United States business (M)
''I admit that it sounds like an unusual role for a university,'' said James M. Shuart, president of the university, in Hempstead, L.I. 
''But our academic goal is to make direct contact with the intellectual circles in China, and this facilitates the effort.''
In time, he said, Hofstra's new International Trade Development Corporation, run from the dean's office on campus, ''should also produce us some significant revenues'' that ultimately could total several million dollars.
Â 
Aid to Other Nation Unusual
The agreement appears to add a new, international twist to the growing links between universities and businesses. 
While several major universities have signed agreements with corporations, including foreign concerns, to sponsor campus research, academic officials at several schools said they knew of no other university that was helping a foreign nation import technology.
''It's a very unusual activity, as far as I can see,'' said Gerald Lieberman, vice provost and dean of research at Stanford University, which has had extensive ties with Chinese scholars. 
''All universities are seeking means of finding new sources of funds, but this is an unusual technique.''
The Hofstra agreement was negotiated with the China Association of Science and Technologies, an organization representing hundreds of professional, scientific and engineering groups in each of China's provinces. 
It was the second time in two months that the association had signed agreements with an American university: In September, the group agreed to a joint research-and-development effort with the Georgia Institute of Technology.
Yesterday in New York, the vice chairman of the China Association, Wang Shuntong, said he did not know whether the group would pursue agreements with other universities.
Â 
Two Agreements Reached
''In China, we have a series of interests,'' Mr. Wang said through a translator, ''in electronics, biotechnology, new materials and some conventional technologies. 
We are trying to develop mutually beneficial arrangements that will be helpful in the technological renovation of existing industry in China.''
Mr. Wang would not specify the technologies most sought after by the Chinese Government. 
But Robert C. Vogt, dean of the College of Liberal Arts and Sciences at Hofstra and president of the university's new corporation, said agreements have already been reached with two New York companies. 
One is Vicon Industries Inc., a maker of closed- circuit television surveillance equipment, and the other is Cayron Corporation, a maker of computer equipment used in the broadcasting industry. 
Negotiations are under way with a hearing-aid manufacturer and with numerous electronics and computer technology companies, he said.
''What we have discovered is that a lot of the stuff that China wants is not on the cutting edge of technology,'' Mr. Vogt said. 
But the Chinese, he said, have had difficulty finding and negotiating with the many small and medium-size advanced-technology companies here.
''The large, visible companies like I.B.M. and A.T.&T. have offices in China, and the ties are strong,'' Mr. Vogt said. 
''But the rest of American industry is more of a mystery, and our job is to put people together.''
Hofstra's agreement, signed Saturday before a dinner on the campus for the Chinese delegation and Long Island executives, grew out of a five-year exchange program. 
In addition to traditional exchanges of faculty and students, Hofstra placed several Chinese engineers - all fluent in English and trained before the Cultural Revolution of the 1960's, which destroyed much of China's science training - in Long Island businesses.
''We think it is time to extend our efforts,'' said Yu Qiyu, director of the New Technology Development Center, the arm of the China Association that is acting as the liaison with Hofstra. 
''We have a new policy of openness,'' he said, which has made 14 coastal cities and four economic trade zones accessible to foreign businesses.
Â 
Special Licenses May Be Needed
Â 
Â 
Â 
But that accessibility comes at a time when the Reagan Administration, through export- control legislation, has been cracking down on the shipment of high-technology goods and knowledge to Communist countries. 
Mr. Vogt acknowledged that some of the technology sought by the Chinese, such as earth satellite stations, could require specialized export licenses, but said ''the majority should sail through.''
The Hofstra agreement appears to differ from corporation-university arrangements that have prompted debate about conflict-of- interest problems on other campuses in recent years. 
Neither the Chinese Government nor outside companies are sponsoring research at Hofstra, for example, so there are no fears that scholars concentrating on basic research could face pressure to focus their efforts on the development of products.
At the same time, Hofstra has said that it plans to use some of its own faculty members as paid consultants to the new Hofstra-owned corporation. 
A similar plan, involving faculty specialists in biotechnology, was rejected at Harvard University in 1980. 
Officials on that campus determined, after heated debate, that it would be inappropriate for the university to have a profit-oriented business relationship with faculty members whom it was evaluating for their teaching and research skills.
''I really don't see that as a problem here,'' said Mr. Shuart, the Hofstra president. 
''This is basically an academic enterprise, and I am sure we can control it.''

ï»¿
''We are weeping from too many joys. 
We are rid of the shame of the past. 
Our forefathers can feel at ease in their graves.
O, my Motherland, you are no longer a broken bowl in front of an ancient temple.''
THOSE lines are from a poem that a man named Qing Xian recently sent to a Canton newspaper. 
And, like Mr. Qing, a great many Chinese these days believe that their country's nightmarish past has given way to a new dawn of prosperity and growth beyond their dreams.
Last year the real growth of the Chinese economy - a 13 percent increase in gross agricultural and industrial output, after allowing for inflation - was probably the greatest of any country in the world. 
Nor was that a flash in the pan.
In the past five years since Deng Xioping, the Chinese leader, began his modernization drive and his ''open door'' policy - opening China to the outside world and also opening up the domestic economy increasingly to the gyrations of the marketplace - the nation's total output has grown at an average rate of 10 percent a year.
As a result, economists, foreign businessmen and Chinese officials are coming to believe that China, with its own unique blend of planning and free enterprise, has reached that magic moment in its economic drive - a takeoff into sustained growth. 
So confident are China's new leaders about their nation's forward momentum, that they are even prepared to slow down the pace somewhat, to prevent inflation and an overdependence on imports. 
If China manages to avoid radical political change - and the 81-year-old Mr. Deng has moved to insure continuity by filling key jobs with a group of younger men loyal to him - the strategy, many believe, could succeed.
''They're not yet South Korea or Japan; they're still catching up,'' said Hidetoshi Ukawa, Japan's general consul in New York. 
But concern seems to be growing in Japan and other major Far Eastern exporting nations that the catch-up may come fast, that China may become an awesome economic rival as soon as 20 years from now. 
China, which has relied heavily on imports for consumer and industrial items ranging from refrigerators to trucks, is beginning to churn out its own - for consumption and for export.
And there are ample grounds for expecting China to generate sustained growth. 
On Friday, the World Bank issued a report saying that China's ambitious goal of increasing per capita income to $800, from $450 now, by the turn of the century, stood a good chance of success. 
It said the chances for doing so would be increased if China allowed even more play than it already has for market forces and decentralized decision-making.
There are other signs of optimism. 
Traveling through China this fall, one finds that living standards are rising far faster than anyone had imagined possible and this is itself the strongest reason to believe that the changes inaugurated by Mr. Deng will endure. 
People seem to appreciate what the changes are doing to their lives. 
They are unlikely to give them up.
''We will not get rid of our experiments,'' said Zhang Ge, a young deputy director for the Special Economic Zones at the State Council in Peking. 
''As in the natural sciences, we will learn from them, even when we fail. 
When we get the data, we will go on, we will not stop.''
And Richard Huber, who directs Citibank's operations in Asia, puts it another way: China, he says, is simply ''pretty close to the point of no return'' to the old ways.
But others have their doubts about whether the boom can last - and how much there is in it for foreign businesses and investors, if it does last. 
With several notable exceptions like Citibank, 3M, Exxon, Atlantic Richfield, McDonnell Douglas and I.B.M., American and other foreign companies continue to hold back from major investments in China.
They are concerned that the astonishing reforms that swept this Communist country in the past five years under Mr. Deng could, one day, disappear, propelling China back into an inward-looking and anti-Western stance. 
After all, such xenophobia marked a great deal of Chinese history, and never more so than during Mao Zedong's decade-long Cultural Revolution, which ended in the mid-1970's, shortly before Mr. Deng returned from his second banishment and achieved power in 1978.
Even Chinese peasants seem to fear a return to the older, less capitalistic ways. 
People's Daily, the leading Chinese Communist newspaper, published an article by Zhang Pingli in mid-September, saying that many peasants are so afraid that the Government will change its policy of ''making people wealthy'' that they are hiding their newly earned cash in their homes or putting it in banks far from their home villages.
''Just repeating the words, 'There will be no change,' is not enough to allay the peasants' fear,'' said Mr. Zhang. The peasants, he insisted, ''still need a political and legal guarantee.''
The peasants' concerns have taken on greater significance in Peking because farmers are playing an increasingly important economic role. 
In a land where agriculture accounts for 35 percent of the national income, and 70 percent of the population is rural, Mr. Deng's dissolution of the old system of collectivized agriculture is an important reform. 
Prof. Abram Bergson of Harvard, who recently led a team of Western economists through China, found that the return to China's ancient system of allowing families to farm the land was ''the most far-reaching and dramatic'' of the new developments his team observed in China.
Under the new arrangement, families, free of despotic controls, decide how, when and what crops to produce. 
The families, called ''brigades'' to preserve some flavor of Socialist acceptability, contract with the Government to produce set amounts of particular crops and are free to sell what they produce above those amounts in the open market and retain the cash they earn. 
These strong incentives have produced a surge of farm output. 
Grain production, for instance, has climbed from 305 million tons in 1978 to more than 400 million tons last year.
But China has tackled more than just agricultural problems. 
To foster industrial growth, it has created so-called special economic zones and open cities all around the nation, which Westerners have labeled ''pockets of capitalism.''
The areas, where economic decision-making is decentralized, encourage foreign investment through special tax programs and other incentives. 
''What the Chinese are thinking of is creating a series of Hong Kongs,'' said Mr. Ukawa, the Japanese consul.
As it tries to craft a new and stronger economy, China is determined to make its own rules. 
After witnessing the economic gridlock of Soviet-style Marxism and the failure, during the Mao years, of a rigidly planned economy in China, Peking has forged a sharply different course. 
Out of a poor, backward and Communist nation, it is trying to create a new model for Socialist development - a modern mixed economy where Socialism is coupled with a heavy reliance on market forces.
Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang told last month's Party Congress in Peking that China was already entering a new stage in which the economy would gradually shift from meeting people's basic needs for food and clothing to ''enhancing the quality of their lives.''
By the end of this century, he said, ''the Chinese people will achieve a relatively comfortable standard of living. 
Although this is a gradual process, it is increasingly apparent and we should be fully aware of it.''
One of the keystones of China's plan is to grow by about 7 percent a year for the next five years, a figure that officials are already conceding could be exceeded in practice. 
''A sustained 7 or 8 or even 10 percent growth rate over such a long time is rare in the economic development of any country,'' Prime Minister Zhao said, ''A similar situation has occurred in only a few countries and regions during the 'economic takeoff' stage.''
Only Japan and the ''little tigers'' of the Pacific rim - Singapore, Hong Kong, Taiwan and South Korea - have achieved comparable long-term growth rates, but the mainland Chinese now believe they could do it too.
The goal is to quadruple its gross agricultural and industrial output between 1980 and 2000. 
With its population of one billion growing by just 1.3 percent a year, as China presses its ''one-family-one-child'' policy, annual per capita income is projected to rise to about $800 by the end of the century, a level that would place it among the world's lower-middle-income nations, such as Egypt with $700 in current annual per capita income today and the Philippines with $760. 
China has already moved well ahead of such countries as Pakistan and India, with per capita incomes of $390 and $300, respectively.
And the rise would be striking: Per capita income was only $300 a year in 1980 and is now $450. 
To achieve its quadruple goal for the growth of total national output, China would have to invest an average of 30 percent of its national income each year - an investment rate slightly higher than that of Japan and the ''little tigers.''
The World Bank report released Friday said that if China raised its per capita income to $800, it would be a remarkable achievement almost unparalleled in world history. 
''Only one country - Japan - has indisputably caught up with the developed nations from a position of economic backwardness,'' the report said. 
But, it said China had ''a good chance'' of doing so.
However, the report included some warnings. 
''Unrealistically high growth targets cause fluctuations, shortages and inefficiency, while aiming too low has few adverse consequences,'' it said, offering two other options for more moderate and balanced growth.
The differences among the three options, labeled quadruple, moderate and balance, are in projected overall rates of growth and in their composition and assumptions about efficiency. 
The moderate option, although making most of the same assumptions as the one labeled quadruple, takes a less optimistic view of the future efficiency of China's economy, including slower rates of productivity increase in both agriculture and industry.
In the balance option, the World Bank team proposes giving greater weight to the services sector - especially to commerce and various business and personal services - which would shift the structure of China's economy away from the Soviet pattern and toward the pattern of Japan and other countries at comparable stages of development. 
This would mean improving both the quantity and quality of China's warehouses, shops, vehicles and other equipment and its communications system.
That option would raise employment in services to 25 percent of the labor force by the end of the century, cutting China's capital requirements, allowing a somewhat lower savings rate and permitting a more even growth of consumption and investment.
And, assuming overall national output growing by 6.4 percent instead of 7.3 percent as the quadruple model assumes, following the balance option would raise Chinese living standards just as much, while reducing the strains of forced growth and doing more to improve the quality of life.
China is taking these options seriously. 
''We examined the economic growth rate from various aspects, and calculated it from different points of view,'' Prime Minister Zhao said. 
And he acknowledged that China, with its fast rate of development, has been running into trouble, starting in the fourth quarter of last year and still continuing: ''A number of problems arose, such as an excessive rate of increase in industrial production, excessive investment in fixed assets, overexpansion of credit and consumption funds, sharp increases in some commodity prices and a drop in state foreign currency reserves.''
Already, according to forecasts by Wharton Econometrics, China's growth has slowed, and it will probably go to about 7 percent in 1985 from 13 percent last year. 
Although the 7 percent growth is what China wants for itself in the next five years, the slowdown this year was the result of more than just Government policies: It was also caused by a sharp foreign exchange shortfall and a slowdown in the rate of investment. 
Foreign exchange reserves, for example, which were at a peak of $17.1 billion in the second quarter of 1984, according to the International Monetary Fund, fell to $11.6 billion in June 1985 and reportedly declined further in the third quarter of this year.
Allen S. Whiting, a professor at the University of Arizona, who is a long-time China-watcher and former foreign service officer, points out other hazards that lie in China's path. 
They include the ups and downs of the world economy, to which China is now more exposed, with exports vulnerable to protectionism and imports to price fluctuations; exaggerated hopes of continuous progress that could be disappointed - and exploited by an opportunistic opposition; and natural disasters, such as floods, earthquakes and famines that have plagued China through its history. 
And given the scale of the population and the territory, there are sure to be other setbacks along the way.
But for now, the Chinese are committed to their plan of at least 7 percent sustained growth. 
''If the rate were too high,'' Mr. Deng told last month's Party Congress in Peking, ''that would create many problems that would have a negative effect on the reform and on social conduct. 
It is better to be prudent. 
We must control the scale of investment in fixed assets and see that capital construction is not overextended.''
He said it was important to manage production efficiently, insure quality and seek economic and social returns. 
The contrast with traditional Communist planning, aimed at ''overfulfillment of production norms,'' is striking.
The threat of inflation has alarmed the Government. 
Although official statistics put the rate of consumer price increase at just 6 percent during the past 12 months, unofficial estimates of foreign economists based in China put it much higher - at 10 to 15 percent, with Shanghai calculated at 17 percent.
The decline in foreign exchange reserves has also been worrisome. 
China, remembering its own earlier dependency on foreign capital and observing the development problems facing today's debtor countries in Latin America and Africa, would rather slow its rate of growth than pile up foreign debts. 
And when they decide to crack down on borrowing, they don't waste time: They turn it off. 
Mr. Huber of Citibank says: ''Their financial control system is pretty primitive - it's as though it has just one on/off switch, and either it's on or off.''
Besides concerns about inflation and the loss of foreign currency reserves, another recent development alarmed the Chinese Government and caused it to blow the whistle on breakneck development: evidence of corruption in industry.
The most notorious scandal was on Hainan Island, a designated ''open'' area where local officials were involved in a scheme that used up a lot of foreign exchange for cars and other consumer durables rather than using it for more productive purposes, such as purchases of capital equipment and machinery. 
Hainan is far from being an isolated case. 
The Government recently announced that it was investigating 200,000 ''business companies'' and ''trade centers,'' clamping down on ''unscrupulous profiteering, tax evasion and violation of business regulations.''
The Chinese continue to worry about the moral - or rather immoral - consequences of a freer economic system. 
At the recent Party Congress Chairman Deng warned that ''only Socialism can eliminate the greediness, corruption and injustice which are inherent in capitalism.''
But he did not try to deny the vulnerability of the Chinese. 
''In recent years,'' he said, ''production has gone up, but the pernicious influence of capitalism and feudalism has not been reduced to a minimum. 
Instead, evils that had long been extinct after liberation have come to life again.''
Nevertheless, neither Mr. Deng nor other high officials indicate any intention of reversing course as they try to achieve a more open economy. 
Last week the Shanghai-based World Economic Herald stated that Hainan Island was undergoing ''massive growth'' and that the car-importing scandal would not affect the ''open'' designation nurturing that growth. 
In Peking and in the Special Economic Zones of Shenzhen and Xiamen, officials took a common line in saying that they despised corruption and would do everything to stop it. 
But they denounced party opponents who would use corruption as an argument for trying to reverse Deng Xioping's open-door policy and economic reforms.
Chinese officials, especially in urging foreign corporations to invest in their country, insist that there will never be a change in their openness to foreign investment and the safeguarding of foreign property and rights to repatriate capital and earnings.
Yet some American and other foreign businessmen interviewed in Shanghai insist that serious problems exist for foreign investors, mainly involving the fact that the Chinese Government sometimes breaks a contract it doesn't like. 
The foreign businessmen call for stricter enforcement of Chinese laws protecting foreign investors, and improvement of the laws themselves.
The Chinese are sensitive to the complaints and say ''issues not covered by present laws and regulations may be incorporated into economic contracts stipulating in explicit terms the rights and obligations of both parties.''
The contracts, they insist, once approved by the Chinese Government, ''have full legal effect.''
But bureaucratic snarls or other tie-ups, say the foreign businessmen, sometimes prevent what they thought was a valid contract from getting the approval of the Chinese Government.
The legal situation, according to diplomatic sources in China, is getting better. 
Cyrus Vance, the former United States Secretary of State and now a lawyer in private practice, said at meetings in Shanghai and Dalian that China's legal system was improving, facilitating economic and technical exchanges. 
And Phillipe de Smedt of the Brussels Bar Association told a law seminar in Peking, ''European investors have become more eager to investigate opportunities in China as the Chinese framework of legal and tax regulations has developed more fully.''
But Chinese officials acknowledge that there is still room for improvement.
With an improving legal environment, a growing number of American businesses see enormous market opportunities in China. 
As one cigar-smoking businessman said to another in a recent New Yorker cartoon: ''There's a billion people in China. 
At some point, some of them are going to need agents.''

file: CHINA LAGS ON BUYING U.S. GRAIN.txt
text:
ï»¿
China appears likely to default for a second year running on its commitment to buy at least six million tons of American grain under a 1980 agreement, according to Western diplomats here.
As it did last year, China is blaming United States textile policies that it contends are discriminatory, though the 1980 treaty contains no linkage between grain and other products.
This time, the Chinese Government is angry about new United States regulations that textile imports must come under the quota of the country where they originate and not an intermediate country where the imports are processed. 
It has demanded compensation for losses incurred by not being able to have Chinese-made apparel finished in Hong Kong.
The United States Government has agreed to consult with China on its complaint after the November elections, according to the Western diplomats, who declined to be further identified. 
The new rules, which were sought by United States manufacturers, have drawn protests from other exporters besides China, as well as American retailers.
(In Washington, an Administration trade official confirmed that discussions with the Chinese were planned.)
Â 
No Sanctions in Treaty
So far this year, China has bought only half as much United States grain as it promised to purchase and has shipped even less. 
The Chinese-American agreement, which was signed in October 1980, commits the United States to sell, and China to buy, six to eight million tons of wheat and corn annually through 1984. 
It does not, however, provide for sanctions in case of violations.
China bought only 3.8 million tons of grain last year, but promised to make up the shortfall this year. 
This adds up to an obligation to buy and ship more than eight million tons of grain in 1984.
According to United States Department of Agriculture statistics, China had bought 4,196,700 tons of wheat as of Sept. 
20 and shipped only 3.16 million tons. 
To meet its pledge, the Chinese Government would have to ship nearly five million tons more within the next three months.
It has shown no sign of doing so and economic analysts here believe such a task would now be impossible.
Â 
Different Motives Seen
Some diplomats in Peking are skeptical about China's declarations that its purchases of United States grain are being reduced to retaliate against the textile import policies.
They believe that China has cut down its purchases at least in part because recent bumper harvests, caused by rural reforms that reward peasant productivity, are meeting more of its domestic needs.
''It has nothing to do with textiles,'' one Western diplomat insisted. 
''The Chinese don't shoot themselves in the foot if they can help it.''
A front page article in the People's Daily newspaper today reported that the harvest of summer grain, mainly wheat, would rise by four million tons in 1984 because of good conditions.
This tallies with Western estimates that China's wheat production would increase from 81.4 million tons last year to about 85 million this year.
China has also diversified its imports by buying cheaper grain from Australia, Argentina and Canada. 
Western diplomats say that the Chinese have ignored a provision of the Chinese-American grain treaty obligating them to scale down purchases proportionately from other countries if they buy less American grain.
A Host of ComplaintsChina has regularly faulted United States trade restrictions for its failure to buy all the grain that it promised. 
Last year, it held back until the two had reached a new treaty on textile quotas more favorable to Peking.
Earlier this year, Chinese officials attributed the slow rate of grain purchases to the lack of a new maritime agreement giving Chinese ships greater access to American ports. 
In fact, vessels under third-country flags have carried much of the grain.
The Chinese also complained about reports that United States grain was tainted with harmful pesticides. 
American officials visited Peking to assure the Government that none of the grain being sent was infected.
Most recently, China protested about the country-of-origin regulations, which went into effect earlier this month. 
They would prevent Chinese factories from sending half-finished apparel to Hong Kong for completion so that it could enter the United States under Hong Kong's textile quotas.
Â 
No New Negotiations
The United States is not in a position to retaliate against the Chinese shortfall in purchases because the grain agreement contains no sanctions to punish violations by either side. 
Nor can Washington threaten to hold back future deliveries, because there is a glut of grain on the world market.
(Grain trade analysts in Washington said that the drop in China's purchases of American grain would probably be offset somewhat by an increase in grain sales to the Soviet Union, which has maintained an unusually strong buying pace in the last three months. 
But with large supplies of wheat already in storage in this country and another large corn crop expected, any decline in foreign purchases will be felt in this country's grain markets, they said.)
The Western diplomats said that no efforts had been made to negotiate another Chinese-American grain pact after the current one expires at the end of December.
China has canceled orders for 675,000 tons of United States grain in the last four months, according to the Agriculture Department figures. 
It has further canceled orders for 150,000 tons of American grain to be shipped in 1985, after the current four-year treaty expires.
Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang told American correspondents here before he visited the United States last January that China was willing to buy six million tons of grain this year if no other problems arose in the future. 
Chen Muhua, China's Minister for Foreign Trade and Economic Relations, reportedly gave similar assurances when she went to Washington in May.
As a result of China's failure to buy American grain, estimates of the trade turnover this year between the two nations may be revised downward from $5.5 billion to $5 billion. 
In 1983, such trade amounted to $4.4 billion.
U.S. Agrees to Talks
WASHINGTON, Sept. 
28 - The Reagan Administration has agreed to sit down with the Chinese and listen to their complaints about American restrictions on imports of textiles sometime after the elections, a trade official said today.

Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang will disclose a new five-year economic plan Tuesday that is intended to increase efficiency in China's outmoded industries at least partly by increasing management initiative.

PEKING, Nov. 
29 (Reuters) -Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang will disclose a new five-year economic plan Tuesday that is intended to increase efficiency in China's outmoded industries at least partly by increasing management initiative.
Mr. Zhao will describe the plan, aimed at quadrupling China's output by the turn of the century, in an oral report to the National People's Congress, China's parliament, which began its current annual session last Friday.
Prof. Xiang Qiyuan, deputy chief of a Government economic group, said most of China's enterprises were not run properly, largely because the management system had been borrowed wholesale from the Soviet Union.
''We are now discovering more and more that this kind of management system is not suited in many ways to our country's special conditions,'' he said in an interview. 
''This shows most clearly in the biggest sickness of our enterprises - they have no managerial initiative.''
Professor Xiang said that under the old system, successful enterprises turned all profits over to the state, receiving no direct benefit. 
This stifled management efforts to improve performance.
More than 6,000 state-run companies are now allowed to keep some profits for their own development. 
The official New China News Agency said about 3,100 delegates to the congress continued group discussions today on a new draft constitution, expected to be adopted Saturday.
The new draft reinstates clauses of a constitution promulgated in 1954 but later scrapped, saying all citizens are equal before the law. 
It guarantees religious freedom and the right to criticize Government officials or organizations.

China's oil industry is expected to surpass its production quotas of 130 million tons of crude oil and 13 billion cubic meters of natural gas this year, the official China Daily said today.

Chinese officials have formally opened a $100 million glass factory here, praising the American-Chinese project as an example of their nation's success in opening its doors.
The Guangdong Float Glass Company, featuring technology by Pittsburgh-based PPG Industries, is one of the largest and most sophisticated foreign projects that China has attracted since it began to modernize its economy in 1979.
PPG Industries owns 35 percent of the factory.
The general manager, Robert Niederberger, said, ''The investment has gone generally very well, much better than we expected.''

The factory's 350 Chinese employees work under American managers and advisers, but Mr. Niederberger said that management eventually would be entirely Chinese.

China has decided to link production and possibly prices of a wide range of goods to market demand in a major capitalistic reform that will partially dismantle its system of centralized planning, reports said today.
The state-run China Daily said state production quotas will be removed next year for more than half of the nation's agricultural and industrial goods, and instead production would be determined wholly or partially by market demand.
''Industrial products under centralized state planning will be reduced from 120 to 60 and agricultural and sideline products from 29 to 10,'' the English-language newspaper said.
''The freed enterprises will set production according to general guidelines or market demand instead of state quotas as at present,'' the article said. 
China Daily said the measures were announced during the weekend.
It said those products which remained under centralized state control would be sold at prices fixed by the Government.
Chinese officials have hinted that this month's Communist Party Central Committee plenum is likely to approve a major overhaul of the pricing system to ease the heavy burden of state subsidies.
Western diplomats said the announcement represented a major capitalistic shift.
''When they start talking about relying on market forces, they're talking about price reform,'' one Western diplomat said. 
''But what we don't know is how much they will allow prices to rise. 
I don't think they would allow more than a 10 percent hike.''
He said allowing individual enterprises to set production totals was something of a gamble in a country where all such policy decisions have been made by the state.
''Most of these factories haven't got a clue about what the market will bear,'' he said. 
''Maybe five percent of the people in this country have even a rudimentary knowledge of market research. 
It's going to be hit and miss for awhile, that's for sure.''
China Daily said the state would continue to set production quotas for several industrial items, including coal, oil, rolled steel, non-ferrous metals, timber, cement, chemical fertilizers, synthetic fibers and cigarettes. 
In agriculture, the state would continue to set quotas for cereals, cotton, edible oils, tobacco, jute, pigs and some aquatic products.
