Communist Party leaders have agreed on a five-year draft plan to revise China's system of prices and wages, the official New China News Agency said today.
In a report, the agency said the three-day meeting of the party Politburo, chaired by the party leader, Zhao Ziyang, ended in the coastal town of Beidaihe on Wednesday.
Details of the plan, spanning 1989 to 1993, were not disclosed but the press agency said that ''the price and wage reforms mean an all-around deepening of China's reforms.''
The agency said that inflation, which hit an annual rate of 13 percent in the first half of 1988, would be brought under control by ''effective, comprehensive measures,'' including cutting back on construction projects.
The state would continue to control prices of a few major commodities while allowing market forces to set the rest.
Changes in state enterprises would be speeded up so that company managers would begin to take full responsibility for profits and losses, the agency said.
Diplomats said they doubted this would mean layoffs in the near future although 30 million urban workers are officially said to have jobs in which they do nothing.
Politburo members noted ''the immense significance of such reforms to the endeavor to establish a new, socialist economic order in China.''
Diplomats said China was anxious to dismiss speculation that the country's 10-year-old reform program had ground to a halt because of widespread discontent with record inflation.
The party's Central Committee will meet next month to discuss the draft five-year plan, the agency added.

file: CHINA SEES NO ADDED GRAIN NEED.txt
text:
ï»¿
With a good harvest in sight, China does not expect to buy any more American grain this year beyond the six million to nine million metric tons already agreed upon for the year, Agriculture Secretary John R. Block said today.
Encouraging the Chinese to purchase more of this year's American crop had been one of the aims of Mr. Block when he arrived Friday for a visit that included talks with China's Agricultural Minister, Lin Hujia, and the Minister of Light Industry, Song Jiwen.
Speaking with reporters before his departure today, Mr. Block said that, ''at each of the meetings with each of the officials that we talked to, I did bring up that we have a large crop in the United States of very high quality at very attractive prices and would encourage the Chinese to look toward additional purchases if they have any needs.''
But he added that the Chinese had said that there was no indication that they would need more than the agreed-upon amount.
Agriculture Secretary John Block reports China is unlikely to make additional grain purchases from US in 1981Four-Year Pact Signed in 1980
China signed a four-year agreement with the United States in 1980 in which it agreed to buy a minimum of six million to eight million metric tons of wheat and corn annually through 1984. 
A metric ton is about 2,205 pounds and is equal to 36.7 bushels of wheat or 39.4 bushels of corn.
With the improvement in relations between the two countries, China has already become the fourth-largest foreign market for American agricultural products, and the largest purchaser of American wheat and cotton. 
American farm sales to China grew fourfold, to $2.2 billion last year from $573 million in 1978, according to Department of Agriculture figures.
To insure satisfactory grain quality, Mr. Block said, the Federal Grain Inspection Service will send a team here to investigate complaints that some grain deliveries have had insects and other foreign matter. 
The Secretary insisted that the problem was not serious. 
''It's just that this is such an important market to us that we're going to service it, as we would with any other important market,'' Mr. Block said.
Â 
Private Groups Plan Offices
To further develop the Chinese market, negotiations are under way for private organizations representing American growers of wheat, soybeans and feed grains to open their own offices in Peking.
The United States Feed Grains Council expects to have an office open here next January. 
United States Wheat Associates, the foreignmarket promotion arm of the American wheat industry, and the American Soybean Association also want to open China offices next year.
Robert M. Book of the United States Food Grain Council, who was traveling with Mr. Block's party, said that ''we would probably like to co-locate with agricultural trade offices; this is what we have done in other places.''
Â 
New $1.5 Million Bakery
This morning in Peking, Secretary Block visited a new $1.5 million bakery that has been built to use United States mechanized bakery equipment and American flour. 
Because Chinese traditionally have eaten rice rather than bread, it is one of the few major bakeries in China.
After it opens later this year, the bakery will be used to train Chinese bakers and as a model for baking technology. 
Its production capacity of 1,500 pounds of bread an hour will be sufficient to provide bread for a population of 50,000.
United States Wheat Associates bought the machinery for the bakery and is also working to help set up a similar model 150-ton flour mill in Peking and a plant making instant noodles in Shanghai.
''China already is our biggest wheat customer in the world so I think they will be using a lot of our wheat,'' Mr. Block said.
Â 
Scientific and Technical Program
The Secretary added that he had also encountered strong interest among the Chinese in more scientific and technical exchanges. 
Under the scientific and technical program begun in 1979, he said, 53 teams will have been exchanged by the end of 1981 and another 75 or 80 are planned.
Mr. Block said that the Chinese had also shown an interest in buying American forestry products and would be discussing this later. 
During the current visit, it was agreed to have teams examine quarantine policies so that some American swine could be sent to China for breeding purposes.
The Secretary had initially planned to stay in China until Wednesday, but dropped the Shanghai part of his visit and left today to assist with the Reagan Administration's new farm bill, which is now being considered by Congress. 
The other members of the trade mission are continuing to Hong Kong, Indonesia, Singapore and India.

file: CHINA SHARPLY WARNS U.S. ON TEXTILE CURBS.txt
text:

China today made its strongest threat yet of retaliation against American farmers if the United States imposes new restrictions on textile imports announced on Aug. 
3.
''Americans will be forced to swallow their own bitter pill,'' said the authoritative Chinese-language People's Daily in a commentary in today's issue.
A State Department official, analyzing the commentary, called it a ''clear indication that the Chinese are establishing a rationale for retaliation.''
An Agriculture Department official speculated that China, which has had bumper grain crops for two years, was looking for an excuse to curb its purchases of American grain.
China, through commentary in authoritative People's Daily, makes its strongest threat yet of retaliation if US imposes new restrictions on textile imports announced Aug 3, saying 'Americans will be forced to swallow their own bitter pill'; State Department official says commentary indicates that Chinese are establishing rationale for retaliation (M)
A senior trade official said the situation was ''disturbingly reminiscent of what happened last year when we froze imports of Chinese textiles,'' adding, ''U.S. trade to China fell by $1 billion.''
Both the American officials spoke on condition they not be identified.
Â 
Could Embarrass Reagan
A new suspension of wheat purchases could embarrass President Reagan in the farm belt, where he has been attacking former Vice President Walter F. Mondale, the Democratic contender, for supporting the curtailment of grain shipments to the Soviet Union in 1980 after the Soviet intervention in Afghanistan.
The Peking newspaper charged that the United States ''doesn't care about violating bilateral agreements with other countries,'' and said that many legislators, retailers, importers and farmers are concerned about the consequences of the new regulations for United States trade.
These concerns are well founded, the commentary said, because ''there is no reason to believe that only the U.S. can take unilateral action to violate international agreements and to restrict and harm others, and that others will not adopt corresponding measures.''
''Any attempt to impose one's own will on others can only harm trade between countries,'' it warned.
The executive order tightening so- called rules of origin governing imports of apparel goes into effect today for goods ordered after Aug. 
3, the date the order was published in the Federal Register. 
For goods ordered before that date, the old rules apply for shipments through Oct. 
31, That exemption, affecting about $500 million of merchandise that had been ordered for store shelves this Christmas, came in response to protests from retailers, farmers, third world countries and others.
The new rules are intended to prevent what Customs officials say is widespread ''circumvention'' of American textile import quotas. 
This occurs when goods are cut in one country and sewn in another, then enter the United States under the second country's usually more liberal quota.
Industry sources in Hong Kong have estimated that more than $100 million in semifinished Chinese textile products are shipped to Hong Kong alone each year for finishing and re-export to the United States.
Under the new rules, fabric made in China and turned into clothing elsewhere will be counted against China's quotas for shipment to the United States. 
China's quotas are not as liberal as Hong Kong's.
Â 
Outlook for Wheat Purchases
During an altercation over textiles last year China suspended purchases of American wheat.
Agriculture Department officials said that China may not renew a four- year wheat purchase agreement that expires at year-end, and that Peking furthermore may not meet its commitments in the current agreement.
But one Agricultural official noted that because of bumper crops in China ''it was very unlikely that China would fill its commitments in any case.''
China last year produced a record 387 million tons of grain, against 354 million in 1982 and 325 million in 1981. 
This year is expected to produce another record.
The current agreement calls for China to purchase 6 million metric tons of American grain a year over four years. 
Last year China bought 3.8 million tons - 2.2 million short of its purchase commitment. 
It stopped buying United States wheat during the earlier textile dispute.
So far this year China has bought 4.5 million tons - just over half of what it needs to purchase by the end of the year to meet its annual commitment plus last year's shortfall.

ï»¿
China said today that two or three more years of measures to curb excessive investment were needed to bring capital spending under control. 
The China Daily quoted Zhou Daojiong, president of the People's Construction Bank of China, as saying unauthorized spending by local governments or enterprises of more than 20 billion yuan, $5.4 billion at current exchange rates, was partly responsible for an overheated rate of investment.

ï»¿
A group of scientists has recommended that China establish a body to oversee technology imports and control the approval of key state projects involving imports, the official New China News Agency reported.
The scientists made the proposal today to the science and technology section of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, an advisory body. 
Sometimes the same type of equipment has been imported by several plants simultaneously, the report said. 
It said the problems had occurred because of lack of overall state control and neglect of experts' opinions.

Senator Ernest F. Hollings, a South Carolina Democrat, warned Chinese leaders Friday that China's soaring textile exports to the United States might provoke protectionist legislation from the new Democratic-controlled Congress. 
South Carolina, a major textile-producing state, has been hard hit by imports.

file: CHINA TO GET AID OF GEORGIA TECH.txt
text:
ï»¿
The Georgia Institute of Technology will become the first American university to enter into joint ventures to help develop industries in China for the manufacture of advanced-technology products.
The agreement was signed in Peking last weekend by officials of Georgia Tech and the China Association for Science and Technology, an umbrella organization representing hundreds of Chinese professional scientific and engineering groups. 
It will cover products ranging from ultralight aircraft to optical fibers.
According to the terms of the agreement, Georgia Tech will enter into collaborative efforts with the Chinese in the development of small to medium- size technology-based industries in Shenzhen City, near Hong Kong; Tianjin, which is about 70 miles southeast of Peking, and Nantong, about 65 miles northwest of Shanghai.
Georgia Institute of Technology and China Association for Science and Technology sign agreement under which Georgia Tech will help develop small to medium-size technology-based industries in Shenzhen City, Tianjin and Nantong; Chinese are initially expected to put up $500,000 in seed money toward agreement; Reagan Administration backs agreement (M)
As part of the agreement, Georgia Tech is studying the possibility of opening an office in China to coordinate its work. 
In addition, representatives of Chinese industries may be based in Atlanta at the university's Advanced Technology Development Center, a nonprofit organization set up by state and university officials to assist in the development of high technology industries.
Â 
$500,000 From China
A spokesman for Georgia Tech said the Chinese were expected to initially put up about $500,000 in seed money toward the agreement.
By participating in joint venture contracts that could eventually lead to the development, licensing and exporting of specific industrial applications, Georgia Tech has gone well beyond previous arrangements that American universities have had in China.
For the most part, these have been confined to scholarly exchanges that involve representatives of Chinese scientific or academic institutions.
Officials at Georgia Tech said their agreement had the backing of the Reagan Administration, which has relaxed trade restrictions with China. 
Among the members of the Georgia delegation who went to China to sign the agreement was George Busbee, a former Governor of Georgia who is a member of President Reagan's Export Council.
The products identified by the Chinese that could be covered by specific contracts include a variety of technical and consumer items, such as solar energy cells, hearing aids, air-conditioners, high speed elevators, radiophones, electrical circuit boards, woven fabrics, polyester filament and telephone equipment.
Â 
Potential Military Uses
According to the Commerce Department, most of the products on the Chinese list include components or technology that are subject to Government export controls because they have potential military applications. 
As a result, an export license will be required before the products or particular technology can be transferred overseas.
Henry Bourne, vice president for academic affairs at Georgia Tech, said the agreement marked part of what he called a larger trend, in which Chinese scientists will continue to reach out to research laboratories at American universities for help in developing science and engineering technology.
''I don't think we'll occupy a unique position for very long,'' said Dr. Bourne, adding that Georgia Tech ''has very little to lose and a lot to gain for the country as a whole by building these kinds of bridges with the China.''
But a variety of experts on trade and technology with China said they could not say for certain that this agreement would lead to similar relationships with research facilities at other American universities.
''I would be surprised to see a large number of such agreements,'' said Pierre Perrolle, an official with the National Science Foundation in Washington. 
He said what was significant about the agreement was that it reflected ''the loosening that has been going on in the Chinese system that allows a section of industry or a group of academics to experiment with such an approach.''
Â 
Accord With Japanese
The agreement not only reflects the growing Chinese appetite for American technology, but increasing aggressiveness on the part of American universities in seeking research support abroad. 
Last year, for example, Georgia Tech entered into an agreement with Nissho Iwai, a Japanese trading company, to market its technology and inventions in Japan.
In the last five years, financing of university research in this country by Japanese industry has increased dramatically.
Over all, Georgia Tech ranks third in the nation in the amount of public and private support it receives for engineering research and development.

Inflation at Double-Digit Rate

With inflation running into double digits - the official estimate is 5.8 percent a year but officials concede that rates are three times that high in some urban areas - the 4 percent bonds are no bargain.

file: CHINA, TO RELIEVE UNEMPLOYMENT, GIVES PRIVATE SECTOR MORE LEEWAY.txt
text:
ï»¿
China today moved closer to becoming a mixed economy by formally acknowledging a need for more private enterprise to alleviate its chronic unemployment problem.
The country's two top policy-making bodies, the Communist Party Central Committee and the Government, proposed in a joint decision that new jobs be created increasingly by private businesses as well as by collective, or cooperative, enterprises.
The decision, reached Oct. 
17 but made public only today, signaled a change in the Communist Chinese position of the last three decades that the state owes every able-bodied adult a job.
''Under the state's overall planning and guidance,'' the joint decision said, ''people get jobs arranged by labor departments or get organized on a voluntary basis or find jobs themselves.''
China's Communist Party Central Committee and Government acknowledges need for more private enterprise to relieve nation's unemployment problemsDetails of New Program
In the decision, China's leadership asserted that the state-run and cooperative sectors would still constitute the basic form of economic activity in the nation but said they needed to be supplemented by self-employment ''within a certain limit.''
To encourage private enterprise, every self-employed person in China will now be permitted to have two helpers and five apprentices, according to today's announcement.
Originally, upon the Communists' takeover of China in 1949, private enterprise was permitted on a very small scale. 
An entrepreneur was allowed to employ only members of his family. 
About a year and a half ago, an entrepreneur was permitted to add two apprentices and later five apprentices in certain trades. 
The new decision, by allowing a total of seven employees, will help Chinese to set up larger retail businesses.
''Private business has resumed and expanded, but it still does not meet the needs of the country's national economy,'' said the decision, which was circulated today by The People's Daily and the New China News Agency.
Â 
Extent of Unemployment
Although the precise extent of urban unemployment is unclear, previous articles in the ideological journal Red Flag and elsewhere have suggested that about 10 million Chinese were unemployed at the end of last year, out of an urban work force of approximately 115 million.
The Chinese authorities had hoped to find 10 million new jobs this year, which would still leave about 4 million unemployed because that many people are expected to finish school and seek jobs. 
But indications are that there will be no more than 7 million new jobs.
Only 10 of China's 29 provinces, municipalities and autonomous regions have managed to find jobs for all those who left high school before 1979. 
Of the remaining 19, there are 14 that hope to reach that target by the end of the year, according to a report last month.
Facing a wait of several years for jobs, some young people have started devising their own work, initially by repairing bicycles, tailoring, taking photographs and other relatively simple neighborhood trades.
Â 
Preference for State Jobs
At the end of last March, more than 1.26 million Chinese had registered as self-employed, according to the General Administration for Industry and Commerce. 
Just over half of these were in the major cities. 
Canton, for example, has reported having 14,000 self-employed persons, 48 percent of them youths.
But more young Chinese seem to prefer jobs in the state sector, where they are guaranteed a job for life without having to work very hard. 
Recognizing this preference for what is nicknamed the ''iron rice bowl,'' the decision that was announced today urged that the new approval of private enterprise be widely publicized ''to allay people's misgivings.''
Private businesses have proved useful for China's leaders because they not only reduce the pool of unemployed but also provide services that state-owned businesses have been too inept or unwilling to provide.
The new decision also envisions a ''significant expansion'' in the number of cooperatives, in which workers form an enterprise and split the profits. 
These function much like cooperatives in freeenterprise countries. 
But young Chinese have sometimes been wary of joining cooperatives because their job tenure and pension benefits are not assured.
Â 
Helping People Find Work
According to the State Bureau of Labor, there are now 2,300 labor service companies helping young people in China to find temporary jobs in state factories or to set up their own cooperative enterprises. 
The new decision today proposes that more of these offices be encouraged.
A Chinese labor specialist, Kang Yonghe, reported last month that the labor service companies had found jobs for 2.35 million Chinese in more than 32,000 cooperatives.
In the joint decision, the Government and Communist Party leadership said that restrictions on private and cooperative enterprise should be changed and that self-employed people should be treated with as much political respect as workers in state enterprises.
But the decision added that self-employed and cooperative workers should accept state supervision and abide by the state's policies and laws. 
There was no mention of whether such workers would be included in the social welfare benefits that state-employed workers enjoy.
Â 
Peasants' Separate Status
The announcement does not appear to affect China's 800 million peasants, who live on communes and state farms, although Peking has also encouraged them to take more responsibility in the last few years.
China's leadership has attributed the unemployment problem to the radical leftist rule of the Cultural Revolution. 
During this period, from 1966 to 1976, schools were closed and millions of young people were sent off to work in rural areas. 
This created a tremendous labor surplus when they later returned home to the cities, and some have been sent back to the countryside.
In the last three years, Peking says it has found jobs for 20 million people.

file: CHINA_S BIRTH GOALS MEET REGIONAL RESISTANCE.txt
text:
ï»¿
A Communist Party official in Guangdong Province was dismissed from his job at a petroleum plant and expelled from the party recently for ''feudal thinking'' after he and his wife - they already had six daughters -tried once more to produce a son.
Elsewhere in this coastal province, two women were locked up for 15 days as ''sorceresses'' for inciting pregnant women at their farm commune to flee from family-planning workers. 
All but 9 of the 325 women with unauthorized pregnancies were later given abortions and intrauterine devices.
Those incidents, reported by the Canton radio, are but two skirmishes in a desperate battle that the provincial authorities have been waging over birth control. 
Harsher reports reaching Hong Kong last summer charged that thousands of pregnant women in eastern Guangdong were rounded up and forced to have abortions.
China's birth control goals are meeting stubborn regional resistance
Family planning officials deny that such Draconian tactics are being used. 
But they acknowledge that there is stubborn resistance among Guangdong's 58.8 million inhabitants to the national goal of a one-child family.
An expanding population is the biggest obstacle that China confronts in its push to modernize itself. 
With close to one billion people, China accounts for 23 percent of the world's population but has only 7 percent of its arable land. 
It is estimated that 30 percent of China's national income has been spent raising those born since the Communist takeover in 1949. 
China has adopted a stringent birth control policy. 
Yet a baby is born in China every two seconds.
With half of the population still under 21 years old, a worrisome new baby boom looms as more Chinese approach marriageable age. 
China hopes to hold its population to 1.2 billion by the year 2000, but national family planning officials like Chen Muhua have expressed apprehension over whether this target can be met.
Graced with a lush terrain and warm climate, Guangdong Province is one of China's three most densely populated provinces. 
Its population exceeds that of France, though it is little more than a third as large.
After Mao Zedong's assurance that a large population was ''a good thing,'' Guangdong reached a staggering 4.4 percent annual growth in 1962. 
This has since been brought down, but it still failed to hold to last year's goal of 1.3 percent, instead exceeding 1.5 percent.
Compared with a growth of 1.4 percent in all of China last year, the population of the United States rose by less than 1 percent and that of the Soviet Union by eight-tenths of 1 percent. 
The populations of all three countries have roughly doubled over the last 60 years, but only in China, because of the large number of people involved, has birth control been adopted as an official policy.
The population of China grew from an estimated 476 million in 1920 to 971 million in 1980, in an area of 3.8 million square miles. 
In comparison, the United States, with an area of 3.02 million square miles, had a population of 227 million in 1980. 
The Soviet Union, with an area of 8.6 million square miles, had a population of 265 million that year.
Â 
Incentives and Penalties
Discussing the continuing increase in population in China, Li Hanbo, the deputy director of Guangdong's family planning program, said:
''One of the reasons for a high growth rate is that we have too many families having three or more children.''
Last year, he said, only 27 percent of families took the pledge to have just one child, while 24 percent already had three children or more.
Local legislation augmenting the national family planning directives has given Guangdong some of the strongest incentives and penalties in China. 
Late marriages are encouraged, for example, and students who marry face expulsion from school.
Counties and municipalities set annual quotas for the number of babies who may be born. 
A couple wanting a child must apply for an allotment, with women who marry late getting first priority.
Couples taking the pledge to have just one child are issued pocket-size plastic-bound certificates entitling them to priority for housing and medical care and their child to free kindergarten, schooling and health care. 
If they have a second child, they must reimburse the Government for all the benefits and bonuses.
The system works best in the overcrowded city of Canton, where, Mr. Li said, ''90 percent of families have just one child and very few have three children.''
Â 
Mobilizing the Whole Family
In Canton's downtown district of Yuexiu, Huang Pei, the local family planning director, said that nearly 94 percent of the women of childbearing age were limiting themselves to one child. 
Consulting her small blue notebook, she noted that her district recorded 951 abortions last year, of which at least 80 were beyond the fourth month of pregnancy. 
Asked whether abortions were allowed even in the final month of pregnancy, she said, ''It happens.''
Miss Huang said her teams ''conduct painstaking and careful ideological work 10 or even 20 times on a person'' to dissuade a mother from having another child. 
''We mobilize everyone in the family, not just mothers and fathers but also brothers, sisters and so forth,'' the district director said.
Zhang Zhi, director of the Wuyang Electric Fan Factory, said his 263 employees of childbearing age had been allocated the right to have 18 babies this year. 
''We've had two so far, and five more women are pregnant,'' Mr. Zhang said. 
Among its other incentives, he said, the factory rewarded single children of employees with cash presents on holidays.
''In the countryside, the situation is just the other way around,'' sighed Mr. Li. Peasants have clung to a tradition of having large families to help them in the fields and to support them in old age. 
''The biggest problem is the old habits and customs of 7,000 years,'' explained Miss Huang. 
''They put too much emphasis on having sons.''
Â 
Undercut by Recent Policies
Mr. Li conceded that family planning had been undercut by recent changes in agricultural policy that paid farmers more if they produced more. 
In Guangdong, as elsewhere in China, this has made having children profitable again. 
Without the former policy of work points, Mr. Li said, ''production brigades and teams have no way to punish them if they have more children.''
He added, ''Farmers feel that the land belongs to them and children belong to them too, so they can have as many as they want.''
Peasants are tacitly allowed to have two children but not three. 
''Many families in the countryside want a second child if the first is a girl,'' Mr. Li explained. 
''Our provincial office shows great sympathy because they do have a practical problem. 
It is difficult for the family to manage if there is only one girl. 
We have not proclaimed this as a policy, but if it happens in the grass roots, we would not object. 
But if the second child is also a girl, they have to accept it.''
Mr. Li said family planning workers commonly spent three or four months persuading a couple not to have more children. 
''On the average, each person takes 10 times to be persuaded,'' Mr. Li said. 
''The most difficult person can take up to 100 times.''
On their visits, he said, some workers were cursed or even beaten up by peasants.
The authorities have been accused of playing rough in return. 
Last July, Zhengming, a Hong Kong publication sympathetic to the Peking Government, gave what it said were details of a ''ruthless struggle'' under way in Guangdong's Huiyang prefecture to cut the number of expected babies by 47,000.
Â 
Zeal of Local Officials
A reporter from Zhengming who visited eastern Guangdong reported how vigilantes abducted pregnant women on the streets and hauled them off, sometimes handcuffed or trussed, to abortion clinics. 
Other women, he said, were locked in detention cells or hauled before mass rallies and harangued into consenting to abortions. 
The reporter referred to ''aborted babies which were actually crying when they were born.''
Zhengming attributed such coercion to the zeal of local officials pushing to meet their quotas rather than to explicit directives from above. 
It noted that the ''desired results'' of achieving 47,000 fewer births went conspicuously unreported by Southern Daily, Canton's party newspaper.
Mr. Li said enemies of family planning had exaggerated or distorted the facts. 
He cited a case in Enping county in which two policemen hitched a ride with a truck carrying women off to a clinic to get contraceptives and this was ''misunderstood'' by spectators. 
In Dongguan county, he said, a young man, seeing pregnant women going off for abortions, had tugged at the arm of a plump friend, though she wasn't pregnant, and this joke started ''rumors.''
''There is no question of forcing pregnant women to have an abortion,'' Mr. Li said. 
''We first persuade them to take contraceptive measures so they will not produce more children. 
If they have just one child after marriage, it's reasonable. 
We deal mostly with couples having two children. 
After three children, we demand that they take sterilization measures. 
If they refuse, we must devote more time and more people to come to them.''
Â 
'A Few Stubborn People'
Mr. Li referred to ''a few stubborn people refusing to do what should be done, adding, ''If we don't take harsh measures, the majority would not be happy about it.''
Those with one or two children can have their wages cut 10 percent or more if they keep having children. 
There have been reports of recalcitrant couples having their electricity and water cut off. 
The authorities are even empowered to seize the family television set, bicycle or sewing machine.
''We set a time limit,'' Mr. Li said. 
''If they fail, the punishment will be upgraded. 
If some families can't afford cash, we will take away their property, because if we are not severe on these people, the majority will not be satisfied.''
Even so, he said, some peasants feel that the potential earning power of sons could offset any financial penalties.
Of some 7 million women of childbearing age in Guangdong, 600,000 had reported abortions last year. 
Unofficial estimates indicate that abortions exceeded the number of live births. 
A Canton physician told a foreigner of abortions being performed on the delivery table.
But a single or double intrauterine coil of stainless steel wire is the most prevalent birth control device. 
After being fitted at local clinics, some women have tried to take the coils out. 
In Longchuan county, Mr. Li said, one woman's husband tried to remove the device, and she began hemorrhaging so badly that she had to be rushed to the hospital. 
''We deliberately publicized the incident to warn other people,'' he said.
Â 
Sterilization Is Promoted
Attempts to promote sterilization have been more successful with women than with men. 
At the Daxin Handicrafts Factory in Canton, Zhang Yunfang, head of the local women's organization, said the factory director and the party secretary, both women, ''set a very fine example'' for the employees by undergoing sterilization. 
They were followed by 29 other women and one man.
''In the feudal system of imperial China, they had eunuchs in the courts,'' Mr. Li said. 
''So some men feel that sterilization will affect their sex life. 
The women also worry that their man's physical health will be affected.''
This year, the growth target for Guangdong is again 1.3 percent, slightly higher than the 1.2 percent national rate, and officials will feel even more pressure to meet it by whatever means. 
The alternative, officials like Li Hanbo point out, is a runaway population subsisting on resources insufficient to maintain, let alone improve, the living standard.
Mr. Li observed that it cost more to prevent a birth in Guangdong than to raise a rural child to the age of 15, an expense reckoned at about $865. 
The hope in the countryside, he said, is to get half of the families to have only one child and the rest not to have three or more.
''Though that's the case, the ideological work is still hard,'' Mr. Li said. 
''There are still cases of some families having four, five, six children and even more.''
Some party workers, he reported, ''say that we have had many difficult things since liberation, but this is the most difficult.''

file: China_s Economy Takes Small Leap Backward.txt
text:
ï»¿
China's Communist Party Central Committee meets Monday to deal with economic problems that have grown increasingly serious since the country embarked on an ambitious program of restructuring its economy nearly a decade ago.
In the last year, as China has moved farther away from the Soviet model of socialism, the country has been racked by soaring inflation, bank runs by panicky depositors, corruption within the bureaucracy and a rising tide of worker unrest.
China's financial system is in disarray with an uncontrolled growth of the money supply, its currency is sinking rapidly in value against the dollar and a patchwork of free and controlled prices has created gluts in some areas and shortages in others for everything from industrial raw materials to daily consumer goods.
Salt, the most basic seasoning in Chinese food, is now being rationed in Beijing. 
Pork, sugar, eggs and cooking oil have been rationed for six months now and people in the capital are beginning to voice doubts about the benefits of the country's economic direction.
'There Are Problems'
''Of course there are problems,'' a Chinese economist said recently. 
''But to change from the old way to the new way has never been done. 
We are exploring a direction that nobody else has.''
These problems, however, have severely shaken China's leaders, according to Chinese academics who are familiar with policyy discussions, and the Communist Party chief, Zhao Ziyang, has lost some of his authority. 
Already, hints that the leadership will dramatically scale back various forms of economic experimentation and restructuring have appeared in China's press. 
The 175 members of the Central Committee who will meet Monday are to ratify this slowdown in reordering the country's economy.
Deng Xiaoping, the country's senior leader, told a group of Japanese economists this weekend that China's policies would be modified to cope with these concerns. 
''The difficulties we are facing now concern development and are different from those we had before,'' Mr. Deng was quoted by the official New China News Agency as saying. 
''The readjustment we are going through now is not a change of policy. 
Neither is it a change of development strategy. 
We are working out methods and measures for future progress after summing up our experiences and we are capable of overcoming the present difficulties, including combating inflation. 
The rate of development is now too fast.''
Â 
'The New Economic Order'
''The transition from the old economic order to a new economic order is now generally blamed to be responsible for most of the irregularities of Chinese society,'' China Economic News, a weekly review of economic and financial issues, said recently.
This new economic order, what China's newspapers are calling ''the new order of socialist commodity economy,'' has achieved much, particularly in recent years. 
The country's farmers, almost all of whom till their own land, are thriving. 
For the first time in Chinese history, farmers are benefiting from substantial economic growth. 
They are building new homes, buying consumer goods common in urban areas and are educating their children.
In urban areas, department stores are jammed with consumer goods, from televisions to refrigerators to cosmetics. 
Vegetables are available in the winter in the north and fish are sold at many inland markets.
What has invigorated agriculture is now being tried in other segments of the economy. 
But transforming the industrial, power, housing and service sectors of the economy into a system propelled not by planners but the efficiencies of the market has proved far more difficult than most Chinese economists had envisioned.
For the first time since China began this process, the difficulties of erecting a new structure while slowly dismantling the old are becoming manifest.
Â 
Industrial Growth Put at 17%
Industrial growth is continuing to roar along, with the rate of increase for the first six months of this year at about 17 percent, according to the State Statistical Bureau. 
But this growth, a level many Chinese economists believe is excessive, has fueled inflation and unhinged efforts by the central bank, the People's Bank of China, to impose discipline on the financial system.
Thirty-six percent more money was put in circulation in the first six months of this year than during the same period last year, a trend the bank hopes to end.
''With more currency in circulation, bank loans increased rapidly,'' the press agency reported. 
And, as inflation picked up, it said, ''people panicked.''
Much of the panic stemmed from the widespread belief that prices would, and indeed did, begin a steep climb for most consumer goods. 
Accustomed to relatively stable prices, China's urban consumers for the first time faced official inflation rates of 24 percent and widely acknowledged, but unofficial, rates closer to 50 percent.
Retail sales in many cities jumped 50 percent over those of a year ago. 
''As a result, the supply chain of goods began to falter and the amount of goods in stock became 'weak,' according to the statistics bureau,'' China Daily reported over the weekend.
Many economists, both Chinese and foreign, argue that a major element in any structural reform of the country's economy is the freeing of prices from centralized control so that goods and services are distributed by market forces. 
Mr. Zhao, the party leader, has pushed aggressively for what he calls ''price reform,'' regardless of the short-term pain it would bring.
But other members of the leadership have decided that uncontrolled inflation and the potential for urban discontent are problems too severe to continue with price reform at the moment.
Â 
Putting Off Price Reform
In a meeting this weekend with Valentin L. Pavlov, the chairman of the Soviet Union's State Committee for Prices, Yao Yilin, one of the five members of the Standing Committee of the Politburo said that any further freeing of prices would be put off for two years.
The prices of half of the raw materials, industrial and consumer goods and food - including grains, cotton and edible oils - are still subject to control, Mr. Yao said, according to the New China News Agency.
''China is not prepared to free the prices of these commodities, nor is it ready to restore the prices of those commodities that have already been freed from Government controls, because this is conducive to production and consumption,'' the agency quoted Mr. Yao as saying.
At the same time, China's currency, the yuan, has begun sinking in value on the black market. 
Last year, one dollar fetched about five yuan. 
Today, the same dollar is worth between eight and nine yuan.
Although the official rate of exchange, 3.7 yuan to the dollar, is fixed, the growing disparity between the official and black market rates has raised the concern of foreign investors, who are burdened with the artifical rate in computing their transactions with the Government. 
Effectively, foreign investors and traders who are bound to the official rates are paying double for Chinese goods.
Of growing concern to China's leaders as well is the mounting level of industrial unrest. 
Chen Ji, a senior official of the All China Federation of Trade Unions, said that there have been 49 strikes reported throughout the country in the first six months of this year with many more strikes probably going unreported.
''Since we have begun reforms,'' he said in an interview, ''we have new contradictions between prices and wages. 
Now factory directors earn more than workers, and some workers earn more than other workers. 
There are new problems we never met in the past.''

China's gross national product will exceed $270 billion this year, up 9 percent from 1986, the official New China News Agency said. 
Zheng Jiaheng, deputy director of the State Statistical Bureau, said in an interview earlier this week that industrial output increased 14.5 percent while agricultural output was up 4 percent. 
China's G.N.P. 
- a broad measure of the value of all goods and services produced in the country - is the eighth largest in the world, although the country remains one of the world's poorest nations because of its population of more than one billion people.

file: CHINESE FARMER FINDS HIS PROFIT IS A PROBLEM.txt
text:
ï»¿
Yang Xiaoyun, an industrious young peasant in Hubei Province, turned a sizable profit last summer by selling more than five tons of grain to the state. 
But when he set out to treat himself to a new bicycle, he could not find one.
The 25-year-old farmer received some front-page sympathy in the official party newspaper, People's Daily, which noted that he was typical of peasants who have begun to prosper under the agricultural policies of Deng Xiaoping, the Chinese leader.
Such tales do not appear in the Chinese press by accident. 
With a good autumn harvest expected, the newspaper was warning both factories and local officials to do more to meet rising consumer demand from farms.
Chinese farmers begin profiting from agricultural policies of Deng Ziaoping but find spending the money difficult due to shortage of goods
The agricultural policies begun nearly three years ago have made it worthwhile for the Chinese peasant to work harder. 
Instead of earning work points for time on the job, most peasants are now being paid for what they produce.
Â 
Other New Rules
About four-fifths of China's 800 million peasants are said to be tilling the land of their communes under the latest system of greater responsibility. 
More than a fourth of the country's farmers, generally in the poorer regions, have returned to working like tenant farmers under a system in which they are allowed to keep whatever they earn above their quota.
Other measures have included increasing private plots to a maximum of 15 percent of a farm's cultivated land and encouraging individual farmers' markets, which now account for a quarter of the poultry, eggs and fish bought in the cities. 
As a consequence, by one official reckoning, incomes rose 81 percent in rural areas from 1977 to 1980 as against 38.5 percent in urban areas. 
The Government has had problems filling the demand for consumer goods that the rise in incomes has created.
Two years ago, the new policies were adopted at the Yanghe commune in Yingcheng County, where Mr. Yang was a production team leader. 
His family of six set to work raising grain, rice, pigs, chicken and fish. 
The five tons of grain he sold to the Government last summer provided enough to feed 50 people for a year, People's Daily said.
The family received 4,600 yuan, about $2,800, which made their per-capita income more than four times the national average.
Â 
No Bicycles Found
But a bicycle was not to be found at the local stores. 
The newspaper said that at least 110 bicycles were to be sent from Shanghai to Yingcheng County every year but in fact most if not all were sold before ever reaching the county.
In response, local authorities in Yingcheng County have promised that any peasant who exceeds a quota for produce - for example, twoand-a-half tons of grain or four pigs - will be entitled to buy a rationed item, such as a Shanghai bicycle or a sewing machine or building lumber and tiles. 
The press is encouraging other local governments to make similar offers.
In the meantime, many farmers will have to be content with saving their money. 
The Agricultural Bank of China disclosed in June that total savings on communes had risen to 14.4 billion yuan, about $8.6 billion.
Â 
A Shift in Emphasis
The shortage of goods seems unlikely to be resolved soon. 
Red Flag, the Peking party journal, reported last spring: ''There is such a great demand among the 800 million peasants for light industrial products that it is far from being satisfied. 
It is obvious that the development of light industry is not good enough; what is more, it is far from being good.''
Peking has tried to emphasize the production of consumer and light industrial goods over heavy industrial products such as steel. 
As a result, production in heavy industry this year is running behind last year's rate, while light industrial production has increased 12 percent in the first eight months over the same period in 1980.
In the end, Mr. Yang got a bicycle. 
A factory in Shanghai was alerted to the problem and sent him one.

text:
ï»¿
With what appears to be a sense of discovery, officials and industrial and farming-commune managers here laud the virtues of a market-oriented economy and of private agriculture. 
At the same time, they denounce the restrictiveness of the highly centralized and planned economy that prevailed in China through the first three decades of Communism.
The officials interviewed in and around this capital of Sichuan Province defend central planning when asked to do so. 
But they preferred to concentrate in long discussions on what they described as the important place being given to individual initiative and the need to expand it.
Chinese authorities use incentives to spur production of factory and farm workers
In 1979, this province, then led by the present Prime Minister, Zhao Ziyang, as chief of the provincial Communist Party, sought to revitalize its sluggish agriculture and industry by giving enterprises a measure of autonomy in production and marketing, increasing the scope of private plots on collective farms and providing material incentives to workers and communal farmers.
Many Chinese provinces have been undertaking experimental programs since the party's Central Committee called for such moves in December 1978. 
But Sichuan, the native province of the principal Communist leader, Deng Xiaoping, began earlier and made the boldest advances under Mr. Zhao's leadership. 
These advances are continuing.
As a result of the changes, said Deputy Governor Mou Haixiu in an interview, agricultural production and farmers' income have risen dramatically, and industrial output has doubled since 1977.
At the Tian Yuan People's Commune, an hour's drive from here, the first secretary of the party organization, Dai Suihua, said the collective of 21,200 members, growing mainly rice and wheat, had raised its grain output from 8,500 tons in 1977 to 9,800 tons last year. 
This has raised each member's ration from 448 pounds a year to 616 and his money income from 110 yuan ($68) to 142 ($88).
But, the party official said, this is only from the grain derived from the collective enterprise; it does not include the sizable profits from the increase in private plots, first authorized in 1976, to 7 percent of the commune's total area of almost 3,000 acres.
Not only are private plots bigger, Mr. Dai said, but members are free to grow what they want and market it freely. 
''In the slack season, when state stores often run out of fresh vegetables, the private market supplies them,'' said Mr. Dai. Officials interviewed often remarked that present policies represent a rejection of the Soviet model China adopted at the outset. 
They appear unaware that Soviet agriculture many years ago adopted similar changes and greatly increased the availability of produce.
''Before, there were no private plots; that was considered capitalism,'' said the party leader. 
''This was wrong. 
There should be private plots. 
There are two different economies in China, state and private. 
The private is supplementary. 
It is better to have two.''
The change in collective farming is based on setting production quotas not for the commune as a whole but for separate work brigades and sub-units and allowing the commune to retain a significant share of the value of production above the quota. 
Since the shift, Mr. Dai said, every house on the commune has received electric power. 
The number of bicycles, sewing machines, radios and even television sets has increased and the commune now has 11 trucks, where it had none before.
The changes in the industrial sphere have given enterprises autonomy to produce, beyond the centrally set quota, goods of their choice and market them where they can find a market.

file: CHINESE STUDENTS LEARN WESTERN-STYLE MANAGEMENT IN BUFFALO.txt
text:
ï»¿
About 100 Chinese students at the State University campus here are learning accounting, organizational behavior and the intricacies of the free market system in a new experiment in the compatibility of Marxist economics and Western-style management.
The performers in this delicate balancing act are participants in a program that last December graduated China's first 39 American-accredited M.B.A.'s. 
The intent, its founders say, is not to preach capitalist ideology, but to improve Chinese management skills and, in the process, make China more productive.
''We are not teaching capitalism,'' said Frank C. Jen, a management professor at Buffalo who was born in China and is a founder of the program, part of the science and technology exchange that began in 1980. 
''We are teaching them a series of management techniques that will help them raise their standard of living.''
The idea for the Buffalo program, with courses in English and similar to most M.B.A. programs, grew out of shorter courses offered by a joint United States-China project, the National Center for Industrial Science and Technology Management in Dalian, a major seaport on the Bay of Korea.
Â 
Conflict in China Noted
Previously the Chinese had offered their students short courses in the Western style of management. 
But under the new program - three semesters in China and an intensive final semester of study here - the students return to their homeland with the equivalent of two years of Western training and extensive knowledge of the free market system. 
Awaiting them is an industrial system that is largely state-owned and that, despite some reforms, remains closely tied to the Communist Party.
University officials acknowledge the push and pull between reformists and hard-liners in China. 
Last year's pro-democracy demonstrations there and the Government's ensuing campaign against capitalism were ample evidence of the political conflicts.
''We want to allow the students to function as China exists today,'' said Joseph A. Alutto, dean of the university's School of Management. 
''We also want them to be able to adjust as China changes.''
Mr. Alutto said the Chinese Government had given every indication that it was happy with the M.B.A. program and that it intended to renew its contract with the university. 
Two more classes of students are expected to graduate before the current contract expires in 1989.
Â 
Western Techniques in China
From the outset, the primary concern among program supporters has been the sharing of power. 
They question the willingness of Chinese leaders to institute Western management techniques, even when they proved effective.
But Mr. Alutto, citing the advancement of earlier Dalian graduates, expects success from the M.B.A. program. 
In the short term, he said, graduates should advance rapidly as managers. 
The long-term outcome, he said, should be an increase in Chinese-American joint business ventures and greater interest in trade between the two countries.
Eager to capitalize on the potential for additional trade, the university has established a China Trade Center. 
Raymond G. Hunt, director of the center and associate director of the China M.B.A. program, said the center relied on the growing trust between the university and China and served as a conduit for companies that want to trade with China, and Chinese enterprises anxious to enter the United States market.
Â 
Obstacles and Frustration
''By providing China with proper management, we will help them to re-industrialize and in the long run promote bilateral trade,'' said Richard W. H. Lee, the United States Commerce Department's director of science and technology for East Asia and the Pacific.
The program has not been without obstacles and frustration. 
In addition to the loss of a student who chose to remain in the United States, there has been political resistance in China.
Mr. Alutto said the economic reforms adopted by the Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping had been supported by top managers and younger workers. 
The resistance has come from middle managers, the sector of management most heavily infiltrated with untrained people, many of whom are rewarded for service to the Communist Party.
Mr. Jen said he had told the Chinese at the program's outset: ''You can run a very good economic system. 
But if you want to reward Communist Party members who fought the long war, send them to management school.''
Mr. Jen and Mr. Alutto both agree that Marxism and Western management are not totally incompatible.
''China has to find her own destiny,'' Mr. Alutto said. 
''All we can do is provide the technology.''

file: CHINESE THREATEN TRADE REPRISALS IF U.S. CURBS IMPORTS OF TEXTILES.txt
text:

China said today that it would retaliate economically against the United States if the Reagan Administration carried out a threat to curb imports of Chinese textiles unilaterally later this month.
The Administration announced last Tuesday that it would act to curb Chinese textile imports on Jan. 
15 if the two sides could not resolve the dispute in negotiations that are expected to resume here later this week.
The New China News Agency today quoted an official of the Ministry of Foreign Economic Relations and Trade as saying that China ''cannot but respond strongly in order to safeguard our own interests'' if the Reagan Administration carried out its threat.
Should the trade skirmish escalate, the unidentified official added, ''the U.S. side would bear all the consequences.''
PEKING, Jan. 
2 - China said today that it would retaliate economically against the United States if the Reagan Administration carried out a threat to curb imports of Chinese textiles unilaterally later this month.Talks Under Way Since August
At issue is a new agreement, under negotiation since August, to limit the quantity of clothing and other textiles that China may export to the United States. 
The current agreement expired on New Year's Eve, but the United States allowed that deadline to pass in hopes of giving negotiators a last chance to solve the dispute before Secretary of State George Shultz's scheduled visit to China on Feb. 
2.
The official did not say how China would respond to any curbs, but the Chinese have hinted in past talks with some businessmen that they might cut back on imports of American corn and wood products. 
American cotton sales to China have already dropped sharply, partly because of three successive record crops in China.
According to United States figures, China bought $2.57 billion worth of American goods in the first 10 months of 1982 and sold about $1.92 billion worth in the United States. 
The resulting trade deficit of $655.6 million is about half the imbalance that China incurred in the same period of 1981.
Textiles, however, accounted for $750.5 million, or 39 percent, of total Chinese sales to the United States in the 10-month period, up from $590 million in all of 1981. 
Overall, textile exports account for a reported 25 percent of China's foreign-exchange earnings.
The person quoted by the official news agency was not identified, but China's chief negotiator on the textile question, Li Dengshan, is a prominent official of that ministry. 
The American side has been led by Peter Murphy, an assistant United States Trade Representative. 
He is expected to return here for new talks that begin Thursday.
The previous three-year textile agreement expired last Thursday after the two sides failed to get closer to an agreement in three rounds of talks last year. 
The American side then extended the accord for 15 days to permit a new round of negotiations to begin.
The Chinese news agency quoted the unnamed official as saying that the Reagan Administration had ignored a Chinese offer to reach an interim arrangement through consultations and had set its own terms.
''This is an evident violation of the principle of negotiation on the basis of equality,'' the official was quoted as saying. 
''We are resolutely against it.''
In 1979, the Carter Administration also imposed textile quotas unilaterally after failing to reach an agreement. 
The Chinese side then returned to the negotiating table and worked out the treaty that is expiring.
Â 
Biggest Textiles Producer
Although China is the world's biggest textiles producer, it now accounts for just 10 percent of United States imports, which ranks it behind Taiwan, Hong Kong and South Korea, the three largest suppliers.
But the trade figures for the first 10 months of 1982 show that Chinese textile sales to the United States increased by 32 percent from a year earlier, with clothing and accessories jumping by 53 percent over the similar period in 1981.
The United States, meanwhile, has already negotiated new agreements with the three largest suppliers that allows them to increase exports at a rate of less than 1 percent a year from the year-earlier total. 
American producers want President Reagan to peg overall imports to the growth of the domestic market, which now runs about 1.5 percent annually.
Â 
Seeking 6% Growth Rate
China, however, does not want to accept the growth rate imposed on other Asian producers and argues that its share should be larger to compensate for the overall trade deficit that it runs with the United States. 
Its target is thought to be closer to the 6 percent growth rate allowed for secondary foreign shippers.
The differences between the two sides encompass more than the growth rate, however. 
They also include the basic quotas that would apply when a new agreement goes into effect, the categories of textiles to be controlled and the methods of future consultation.
The current consultation mechanisms give the United States the right to call for talks with China when it feels that too much of a given type of textile is being imported. 
It is one of the touchiest points for the Chinese, who want a more flexible system.
The previous agreement regulated 14 categories of textiles out of a possible 110, but the United States added another 14 categories to the regulated list last year. 
The American side reportedly wants about 30 categories included in the new agreement, while China wants only about 20.

Hopes for Accord

THE president of the Farmstead Telephone Group might be based in Glastonbury, but he is doing a lot of business in Beijing.
The Farmstead president, David M. Jastrembski, is overseeing the fulfillment of a telecommunications contract that is expected to bring his company $100 million. 
No one is more surprised by all this than Mr. Jastrembski, who a few years ago did not expect to be doing business in China at all.
Mr. Jastrembski is one of a growing number of Connecticut business executives who find that their overseas itineraries include China.
For years, major Connecticut companies like the United Technologies Corporation have had their own business dealings with China, but over the last few years, smaller companies have been getting involved, many through the efforts of the State Economic Development Department, which has made trade with China a priority.
There are about 200 Connecticut companies doing business with China, and about 20 of those in Shandong Province, with which Connecticut has a sister-city relationship. 
It is estimated that business with China represents about $150 million of the $6 billion that Connecticut does in export business annually, said the director of marketing for the State Department of Economic Development, David C. Driver.
The state's role in fostering such relationships dates back to 1980, after the normalization of trade relationships between the United States and China. 
State Economic Development Commissioner John J. Carson was the deputy commissioner then, and he recalls being skeptical when his boss, Edward J. Stockton, went to China and returned brimming with enthuasiasm. 
Since then, Mr. Carson has become a believer.
''The China relationship nicely combines two strategic market segments that Governor O'Neill has encouraged us to be involved with: small business and exporting,'' Commissioner Carson said. 
''That's one of the fundamental reasons why we are both excited about it and fairly active in the China trade business right now.''
He acknowledged that not all Connecticut businesses could benefit. 
The Chinese know precisely what they are looking for, he said, and are most keenly interested in companies that combine high techology with such industries as transportation equipment, including aviation; electronics; machine tooling, and instrumentation.
Until recently, the Economic Development Department functioned as a matchmaker, providing Connecticut companies with free consulting services to help them find the right market for their goods. 
But in the last legislative session, the General Assembly passed the Financial Capital Act, which will provide companies doing business overseas with low-interest loans, said Mr. Driver.
China is not the only country with which Connecticut deals. 
The Economic Development Department also oversees offices in Japan to aid Connecticut companies doing business in the Far East, as well as in West Germany, for European trade. 
The legislature has also passed a bill to establish the Connecticut Israel Exchange Commission, to encourage more commercial and cultural exchange with that country, he said.
In doing business with China, personal contact is key. 
To this end, the department has organized several trips to China, including an important mission last September led by Governor O'Neill. 
This was the first official visit by a Connecticut governor to the Far East, and in a country like China where government is all important, Mr. Driver said, his presence lent an invaluable stamp of prestige.
But, even when businesses cannot visit China directly, state officials take along brochures from Connecticut companies. 
This led to the $100 million contract for the Farmstead Telephone Group.
Mr. Jastrembski laughed when he recalled rebuffing repeated assertions by state economic development officials that the Chinese were very interested in buying the refurbished telecommunications equipment his company specializes in. 
In fact, it was not until he learned that the Chinese were ready to sign a contract that he became interested at all. 
Now, he plans to spend about 11 months a year in China.
Farmstead will be in charge of modernizing China's telephone system, a system that ''is about what ours was like in the 1930's and 40's,'' Mr. Jastrembski said. 
The agreement with China is expected to bring Farmstead, a company with fewer than 50 employees, about $100 million over the next decade. 
Also, through a joint corporation set up with China, Farmstead expects to do business with other countries as well, such as Australia and India.
''If it all comes to fruition, this will overshadow our operation here,'' said Mr. Jastrembski, conservatively enough, Farmstead had about $3.5 million in sales last year.
When he thinks about it all, Mr. Jastrembski still marvels.
''I think we've moved so fast not because of any brilliance on our part but because we happen to deal with a product China is interested in,'' he said. 
''China is trying to develop its infrastructure and a key element is telecommunications, so they are buying it now. 
We have the right product at the right price. 
That's the key to our success.''
Usually, Connecticut businesses dealing in China have to be prepared for delays that drag on for months, or even years.
The president of Bauer Aerospace Inc. in Farmington, Louis J. Auletta Sr., is optimistic that his current negotiations with the Chinese will lead to some lucrative contracts, but he expects it to take a while, he said.
His company, which has about $5 million in sales annually, manufactures test and ground-support equipment for the aircraft industry, and exports account for about 60 percent of its business.
Mr. Auletta is working with members of China's Civil Aviation Authority, which, he said, has a very modern fleet of aircraft, and is now seeking to begin servicing them independently, which is where his company would come in.
''As a result of my trip in September, we've had communications back and forth,'' he said. 
''I do foresee visiting China again in 1989 and '90. 
It is absolutely a long process. 
You have to establish trust and credibility early on. 
Visiting the country, your presence there is important. 
You also need to do good planning, and have patience and persistance to go along with it.''
But doing business with the Chinese is not for everyone. 
Just ask Anne Evans, owner of JAR Trading in Hebron, a tire business.
Ms. Evans, whose company expects to export about $39 million worth of tires this year to Europe, Africa, South America and the Far East, also went along on the Economic Development Department's trip. 
She discovered, though, that adding China to her export business would probably be impractical for a business her size, which has two full-time employees.
A potential for business with China exists if Mrs. Evans wants to become involved in having rubber companies manufacture tires to Chinese specifications. 
That, she said, ''could be enormously profitable if I can be very patient and want to spend an enormous amount of money to make it work.''
''The Chinese, who are so used to working with big companies, think it's easy for you to spend $10,000 to get on a plane and go there,'' she said, ''but I'd have to hire interpreters, technical people. 
And when I look at my time and resources, even though I could do a lot in China in two years, do I stop what I'm doing here?''
Personal preferences play a role too. 
While Mr. Jastrembski found the Chinese people warm and friendly, Ms. Evans said she ''never felt so alone,'' as during some of the time she spent there.
Still, China represents a huge market, and Ms. Evans is trying to see if someone she knows in the tire business, and who is interested in living in China, wants to join her company. 
That, she said, appears to be the only way doing business in China would work for her.

Thousands of parents are likely to pay more for diaper services as a result of import quotas the United States has quietly imposed on plain cotton diapers from China.
The quotas, which were fixed after a textile trade pact signed with Beijing on Dec. 
20, illustrate the complexity of trade issues and the trade-off involved in using protection as an instrument to preserve jobs.
The action was taken to placate the domestic textile industry, which has long complained about the job-destroying effects of imports. 
The industry is pushing legislation to set quotas on all textile and apparel products entering the United States.
Â 
Only 60 Jobs Involved
Only 60 jobs at diaper plants in South Carolina are involved. 
But the action seems likely to raise prices charged by diaper services around the country, as they face higher prices for diapers. 
It has also prompted criticism on environmental grounds because it may encourage more use of disposable diapers.
If use of disposable diapers increases, layoffs at diaper services may outstrip the number of jobs the cloth-diaper quotas are meant to preserve. 
At the same time, of course, the number of jobs at companies that make disposable diapers would presumably increase.
Environmental, consumer and free-trade advocates are the leading critics of the curbs. 
''They will mean higher prices, a switch to disposables and more environmental problems,'' said Mark Silbergeld, director of the Consumers Union's Washington office. 
''I'm not sure how much they can really help the domestic industry.''
Â 
'Destroys Their Credibility'
Representative Ron Wyden, Democrat of Oregon, criticized the Administration's trade policy as inconsistent. 
''For guys like me, fighting in the trenches for free trade,'' he said, ''this sort of protectionist action to help a grand total of one company destroys their credibility.''
The Reagan Administration says the curbs are necessary. 
Gary Holmes, a spokesman at the Office of the United States Trade Representative, said the domestic industry ''told us they were being killed by imports.''
Only one company in this country makes the thick-ply diapers that compete with Chinese diapers as the mainstay for hundreds of services. 
The Gerber Products Company of Fremont, Mich., a $1 billion-a-year baby-products concern with a small plant in Pelzer, S.C., makes Curity brand diapers as part of its Soft Care Apparel division.
Sixty of the 400 jobs at the plant are related to production of the heavy Curity diapers used by diaper services, said a company spokeswoman.
About a year ago the Government imposed temporary quotas, following a surge in imports in 1986. 
Meanwhile, Gerber raised prices twice -12 percent effective Oct. 
15 and 15 percent May 1 - increasing prices to around $9 a dozen. 
Diapers from China now cost roughly the same.
For many diaper services, the cost of diapers is about one-fifth the cost of doing business.
With Chinese diapers limited and prices higher for domestic diapers, some services now plan to increase their rates. 
''Within two months we will raise prices 6 percent, our first increase in two and one-half years,'' said Brian Smithson, president of Baby Diaper Service of Seattle, which calls itself the largest service in the country. 
That increase would work out to 50 cents on top of the $9 it now costs to provide the 80 diapers an average baby uses in a week.
Paul J. Anderson, president of Babyland Diaper Service of Portland, Ore., said that over the next two years diaper prices could go up by an additional 25 percent. 
''When you have only one supplier, you're at their mercy,'' he said.
Although shipments of diapers are normally measured in dozens, the quotas are fixed by weight. 
China this year is barred from sending the United States more than 1.27 million pounds of diapers, of which 270,000 pounds will go to Pro Diaper. 
A dozen diapers weigh approximately three and a half pounds.
Â 
Many More Jobs at Stake
Mr. Anderson maintained that many more American jobs are at stake than the 60 in South Carolina to be protected under the quota policy.
At least 40,000 people are employed by diaper services, including drivers, office and sales personnel and people who launder and package diapers for customers.
According to importers, the Chinese diapers, made in Nanjing, Shanghai and Beijing, are thicker, more durable and more absorbent than the South Carolina diapers.
A Gerber official who asked not to be identified acknowledged that the Chinese diapers were thicker, but added that Gerber was working on a comparable product. 
90% Come From China Diapers are also imported from South Korea and Mexico, but far more come from China. 
In 1986 diapers from China totaled 894,000 dozen, up from 45,000 dozen in 1985, according to Knox H. White, an associate of the Greenville, S.C., law firm of Haynsworth, Marion, McKay & Guerard, who sought the quotas in representations before the Office of the United States Trade Representative and the Commerce Department. 
The Chinese sales accounted for 90 percent of the one million dozen diapers taken by diaper services in 1986.
''This was a classic case of an import surge,'' said Mr. White, who represents a number of textile companies. 
Mr. White has some powerful allies in Washington, including Senator Strom Thurmond, the ranking Republican on the Judiciary Committee, and Representative Butler Derrick, a Democrat on the Rules Committee. 
Both are South Carolinians. 
The quotas have become all the more controversial because of the timing. 
Only recently have analysts begun to see at least a tentative consumer shift away from disposable diapers back to cloth diapers.
Â 
'Worst of All Worlds'
So trade policy, as public policy experts note, appears to be undercutting environmental policy. 
''We try to solve our trade problems only on a political basis,'' said Clyde V. Prestowitz Jr., a former counselor to the Commerce Secretary. 
''The result is that we get the worst of all possible worlds. 
We pay the cost of protection and get no benefits from it.''
Establishment of the first new diaper services in years - Diaper Fresh in Las Vegas, Nev., and KC Diaper Service in Baton Rouge, La. 
- is cited as one illustration of the revival of cloth diapers.
Because Beijing was a party to the restraints, it has not protested. 
Chen Ming Hui, commercial attache at the Chinese Embassy here, said, ''We will abide by the agreement, but of course we are opposed to any more restrictions.''
Â 
Visions of 'Mount Diaper'
Long before the Chinese came to the scene, the domestic industry had been hurt because of the popularity of the disposables, made chiefly by Procter & Gamble, Kimberly-Clark and Weyerhaeuser. 
Today this product, made of plastic, bleached paper and chemicals, accounts for about 85 percent of the country's diaper changes and racks up annual sales of $3.5 billion.
Nearly 18 billion disposable diapers were dumped into trash cans last year, accounting for 3 percent to 4 percent of all the waste going into the nation's landfills, according to Carl Lehrburger, manager of recycling programs for the Energy Answers Corporation, an Albany resource recovery concern.
A Washington State legislator, Georgette Valle, who has introduced a bill that would require that disposable diapers be biodegradable by 1990, said, ''Someday I will look out my window at Mount Rainier and there will be another mountain - of disposable diapers.''
