THE decision of the Central Committee of the
Communist Party of China to give greater
freedom to capitalist-style market forces and independence to a million state-owned enterprises may be the most damning indictment thus far of the failures of central planning and rigid controls of Communist states.
The Chinese, under Deng Xiaoping, are moving further along the capitalist road, without calling it that. 
The announcement said China would continue to adhere to Communist principles. 
Deng, unlike his predecessor, Mao Zedong, does not believe in great leaps forward or cultural revolutions; even after the reforms, some central planning will remain for key industries, such as steel, coal, cement and fertilizers, and there will be a mixture of collectively and privately controlled enterprises.
Leonard Silk (Economic Scene) column on move by China to give greater freedom to capitalist-style market forces and independence to many state-owned enterprises; says action may be most damning indictment thus far of failures of central planning and rigid controls of Communist states; sketch (M)
Yet a genuine overhaul of the centrally controlled system seems to be in the works. 
Strikingly, the Chinese declaration said the most crucial change would be in the price system, switching from fixed to flexible prices, responsive to changes in supply and demand. 
And the Chinese stress their determination to promote competition and provide greater economic incentives to producers to meet the needs of consumers, to increase productivity and to innovate.
The changes in China's economic system could have a far more powerful effect on the Soviet Union than earlier experiments in Hungary, Yugoslavia and other Communist countries because of China's huge population and the strategic threat Peking represents to Moscow.
For what the proposed changes in the Chinese system imply is acceptance by a group of top Communist leaders that the complexity of developing and operating a modern economy is incompatible with the methods of central planning and control practiced in the Soviet Union, and still preached as orthodoxy through much of the Communist world.
A new book, ''The Idea of Economic Complexity,'' by David Warsh, a reporter on The Boston Globe, serves to demonstrate that economic development involves not just greater wealth or new technology but a higher degree of complexity, with economies consisting of a greater and greater number of ''separable, analyzable parts.''
Growing complexity, in economic terms, means an increasing number of different jobs, different businesses, different machinery, different goods and services; it also means, with greater and greater division of labor, greater interdependence, nationally and internationally.
On the surface, it might seem that greater complexity would require greater control for an economy to work efficiently. 
But the reverse is true, as the experience of capitalist and Communist countries demonstrates. 
The gap between living standards in Western and Communist economies, as Mr. Warsh notes, grows greater every day. 
There are 26 centrally planned economies that, with nearly 40 percent of the world's population, produce slightly less than 20 percent of the world's goods.
But the Communist countries account for nearly 40 percent of the world's military spending. 
This huge outlay on arms helps to retard the Communists' economic development and exacerbates tensions among themselves and with the West.
''The prospect for the knitting together of these two blocs through extensive foreign trade is not bright,'' Mr. Warsh says. 
He doubts that two such different systems can really coexist peacefully when the gap between them - material and technical - keeps widening. 
''Given the exceedingly precarious balance of the arms race,'' he says, ''it seems to me that all the questions really worth worrying about grow out of this great inequality.''
China's decision to try a new route to narrow the gap in income and living standards is thus important not only for its own development, and possibly that of the entire Eastern and world economy, but also for international peace. 
That would be particularly important if China should succeed in moving forward in industry, as it has in agriculture, and establish a model for the Soviet Union.
But resistance to capitalist-style economic change is strong in the upper reaches of the Soviet political ruling class, the bureaucracy and the military. 
Partly. this resistance seems rooted in the habits of the oldest Communist regime in the world, partly in fear of the political consequences of the lifting of repression. 
Yet the Soviet system may be mired in endless stagnation if its leaders continue to resist the lessons that the Chinese - and many Soviet economists - have been learning about the complexities of modern economic systems and how to deal with them.
''The chief advantage of time,'' said Henri Bergson, the French philosopher, ''is that it prevents everything from happening at once.''
To this, the economist Jagdish Bhagwati of Columbia University adds, ''The chief advantage of economic theory is that it prevents us from considering everything at the same time.''
There's a second corollary, which Mr. Warsh's book inspires: Growing complexity requires greater simplicity, independence of decision-making, and interdependence within and among nations. 
There remain problems, including air and water pollution, congestion, crime, disease and the arms race, which require cooperation and control. 
Capitalists as well as Communists still have things to learn.

A Chinese boycott of American agricultural products last year cut American exports to China by more than a third, according to preliminary Government figures released today.
Huang Wenjun, a spokesman for the Ministry of Foreign Economics and Trade, also said at a news conference that China's total foreign trade reached $40.14 billion in 1983, up 2.2 percent from 1982, despite what he called a sluggishness in demand.
China's exports last year were $22 billion and its imports $18.14 billion, leaving a trade surplus of $3.86 billion. 
This is less than the $4.7 billion surplus in 1982.
China says its total foreign trade reached $40.14 billion in '83, up 2.2% from '82 despite sluggishness in demand; puts exports in '83 at $22 billion, imports at $18.14 billion, leaving trade surplus of $3.86 billion; says boycott of American agricultural products last year cut American exports to China by more than third (M)
Mr. Huang said China's exports to the United States had remained at the 1982 level, while its imports from the United States dropped 38.3 percent. 
He gave no specific statistics, but there have been estimates that total Chinese-American trade dropped to less than $4.3 billion last year, from nearly $5.2 billion in 1982.
Â 
Curbs on Farm Products
The sharp drop in China's imports came after China refused to purchase United States grain and other agricultural commodities in retaliation for American quotas placed on the purchase of Chinese textiles. 
A new textile agreement was reached last August, but China failed to meet its commitment to buy a minimum of 6 million tons of grain annually under a long-term purchasing agreement extending through 1984.
Last month, the Chinese Embassy in Washington told the United States Government that China would make up its obligation by buying the remaining 2 million tons of grain for delivery in 1984. 
It bought only 4 million tons last year.
The United States Embassy here said Friday that China imported $1.8 billion worth of American goods in the first 11 months of 1983, while exporting $2.1 billion in Chinese products. 
If this trend continues, it would give China its first trade surplus with the United States since relations were normalized between the two countries.
Â 
Textile Exports to U.S. 
Climb
Despite Washington's imposition of controls on Chinese textiles, sales of Chinese clothing and accessories to the American market climbed 25 percent in the first 11 months of last year, to $713.9 million.
Chinese-American trade has declined from its high point of $5.5 billion in 1981. 
The Washington-based National Council for United States- China Trade predicted earlier this month that commerce between the two countries could bounce back to a record $5.5 billion to $6 billion this year, because of the Reagan Administration's move to loosen restrictions on the sale of advanced technology to China.
Mr. Huang told reporters today that Hong Kong remained the leading market for China's exports. 
Hong Kong bought $5.3 billion worth of Chinese goods last year, a 6.6 percent increase over 1982.

text:

BY the end of its first year in business, Sun Associates Inc. in Elmsford, an international trading and consultant company, had one customer but nevertheless managed to gross $7.5 million. 
Four years later, Sun Associates, still with the same single customer, has quadrupled sales to post figures of $28 million gross this year.
''It helps when your customer is the People's Republic of China, with one-quarter of the world's population,'' said Robert C. Sun, the company's founder and president. 
Mr. Sun, an electrical engineer, spent 16 years in International Business Machine's development laboratory in Poughkeepsie as a computer designer and engineer of future systems before starting Sun Associates in 1982.
''The development lab was an exciting place to work,'' he recalled. 
''We started working on the design of the I.B.M. model 3081, the big computer, in 1970 and it was not until 1980 that the first one was shipped. 
All our projects were 5 or 10 years down the road. 
I liked my job very much but when I saw that a new era was beginning for China, I felt strongly that I was in exactly the right spot to take advantage of it. 
China wanted modernization, I knew they would need high-tech computers, my specialty, so I decided to start a business directed to the China market.''
Mr. Sun, who is 51, was born in Zhejiang, China, but moved to Taiwan with his family in 1949 when the Communists came into power in China. 
Two years after he graduated from Chengkung University in Taiwan, he won a scholarship for graduate study at the Steven's Institute of Technoloy in Hoboken and set out for New Jersey.
''My father, who is also an engineer, encouraged me to come to the United States,'' he said. 
''I found the teaching here very different from Taiwan. 
The atmosphere was much more stimulating. 
Professors encouraged creative, original thinking.''
Before being recruited by I.B.M., Mr. Sun worked for Western Union, and later for CDS Communications. 
''My wife and I liked it so much here that we became American citizens as soon as we could,'' he said.
However, when Mr. Sun was invited to visit China in 1972 by Premier Zhou Enlai, he accepted with alacrity.
''I was part of a group of 28 overseas Chinese who made the first return into Communist China,'' he said. 
''I was very anxious to see my former home and my grandmothers, who were still living there. 
We were all also very anxious to see what was going on in China first-hand.''
Soon after he returned to the United States, he took part in a seminar at the State University of New York at New Paltz, on trade with China. 
''I was very impressed with the predictions made concerning the increase of trade with China,'' he said. 
''Here is a brand new opportunity, I thought. 
It is my time to try it. 
I have been very lucky in choosing the right field and the right time.''
Capitalizing the company start-up himself, Mr. Sun, drawing on his knowledge of computer technology for the power industry, put together a sophisticated package including hardware, software, training and maintenance of equipment for Chinese power stations. 
He won his first contract for 11 systems from the Ministry of Water Resources and Electric Power in the People's Republic of China.
''Vast problems occur in China when the power fails,'' he said. 
''If electicity is kept constant, productivity is increased; on the other hand, when it is disrupted, productivity dips considerably. 
The Chinese Government's emerging power industry is anxious to expand its power networks throughout the country.''
Mr. Sun strengthened the capabilities of his company with the addition of Robert S. Lin. Mr. Lin, who is 47 and Sun Associates vice president, comes from a background similar to Mr. Sun's.
''I was born in Fujian, in the south of China,'' he said. 
''My father was a businessman. 
When I was 9 years old, the Communists took over. 
We went to live in Taiwan, where I went to school and eventually studied engineering. 
I had a scholarship for graduate work at McGill University in Canada and stayed there for one year before transferring to the University of West Virginia, where I finished my master's degree. 
I became involved with nuclear power and it became my specialty.''
For a decade, Mr. Lin worked on the design of the Clinch River nuclear power plant in Tennessee, only to see the project terminated by Congress.
''One billion dollars and 10 years' work went down the drain,'' he recalled. 
''It was very frustrating. 
When friends introduced me to Mr. Sun and he described his company to me, I joined the company happily. 
I wanted to have some control over my own destiny.''
Using first-hand knowledge of current technology in the power industry, Sun Associates delivered 11 of what is known in the industry as SCADA/AGC systems based on a DEC Super-Mini processor to ten regional power stations in China in the fall of 1985.
''We had to develop a special Chinese character set for the display-generation equipment,'' said Mr. Lin. ''It was an expensive project that we financed ourselves. 
The Chinese character terminals and printers were integrated into the system to meet the requirements of the Chinese end-user. 
It was a complex task.''
The contract that sent the special VAX computer system to China also brought 50 Chinese engineers to the United States for training by Sun Associates.
''Training the engineers in the use of the VAX computer system was part of the package deal we made with our customer, the Chinese Government,'' said Mr. Sun. ''In China, computers are installed in various regional power bureaus and will be operated by the people we train here. 
We built classrooms and a computer laboratory here in Elmsford to give the engineers hands-on experience. 
The courses are conducted in Mandarin by our in-house engineers, who are Mandarin-speaking specialists in communications, hardware maintenance, software programming and other areas of computer science. 
It is not a simple business staffing such a school.''
Sun's training program must also prepare students to perform substantial portions of the maintenance and troubleshootings on their machines in China; students must also have the ability to diagnose problems that demand the attention of Sun's maintenance staff.
''We keep a maintenance staff and a huge inventory of spare parts in China,'' said Mr. Sun. ''As part of our agreement, we supply free maintenance service for all the systems for a full year.''
Two groups of students have already completed the 12-week training course in Elmsford. 
A third group has just begun the same intensive course.
''The training program has received high praise from the top officials of the Ministry of Water Resources and Power,'' said Mr. Sun. ''I believe it is what gives us the edge over our competitors - training engineers on the spot. 
We are competing with the Japanese, the French and the English for a share of the huge China market.''
Sun also serves as China representative to Westinghouse Systems Ltd. of the United Kingdom. 
''We helped Westinghouse win one of China's largest contractor awards for 1986-1987,'' said Mr. Sun. ''It calls for Westinghouse to supply energy management systems to four power centers and development systems to two energy research institutes in China. 
We provided Westinghouse with a formal introduction to the Ministry of Water Resources and Electric Power and we negotiated on their behalf at numerous liaison meetings in Beijing, the United States and the United Kingdom.''
Sun is supplying equipment, training and maintenance for the project and as the sub-contractor will supply a large portion of the hardware and integration for Westinghouse Energy Management Systems. 
Wen Xinguang, one of the engineers now being trained for the Westinghouse project, will go to England for additional training before going back to China.
''I find this course very interesting and very challenging,'' he said. 
''In two or three years, China will be very different. 
Since the People's Republic was founded, the Government has placed great importance on developing its power industry in the entire country.''
Mr. Wen and his group are billeted at the Elmsford Motel, where arrangements have been made to allow them to cook their own meals. 
Weekends are spent sightseeing. 
''We work them very hard from Monday to Friday,'' said Mr. Sun. ''On the weekend, they need a change of pace. 
We show them whatever we can of the United States. 
We have been on numerous trips to places like Niagara Falls, to museums, to Washington, and we have even had a tour of a supermarket. 
Local people have been very generous in inviting our students to dinner in American homes. 
Cultural exchanges, we feel, are very important.''
Mr. Sun, a charter member of President Reagan's Republican Presidential Task Force, has served as host to many official Chinese delegations visiting the United States.
''I am very happy to be an American citizen,'' he said. 
''But I have a very personal interest in the modernization of the land of my birth.''

text:
ï»¿
Put simply, the city was broke.
Year after year for decades, the bulk of Fuxin's 1,300 businesses and factories, all ponderously run by the city government, lost money, lots of money. 
Food was short in the winter. 
The water works managed to pump water only three hours a day.
Like the rest of China, the city just shuffled along, subsidizing and absorbing losses and tolerating inconveniences in the spirit of socialism. 
Wang Yachen has changed all that. 
''Like a seriously sick patient, Fuxin is at a critical state,'' Mr. Wang told the official New China News Agency shortly after becoming the city's mayor last year. 
''If we don't perform major surgery, it will never recover.''
Mr. Wang's brand of surgery amounted to putting the city on the auction block - leasing out virtually every grocery store, department store, movie house and factory in town in what is still a radical step in this country where government is only reluctantly extracting itself from control of economic life.
Â 
City of 700,000
Like much of China's northeast, especially here where the vast plains that stretch into Mongolia begin, life is hard and the people are poor. 
Single-story dun-colored houses, their barreled roofs rolling through the city like furrows in a newly plowed field, crowd together as if afraid of getting lost in the wilds beyond.
At the heart of this city of 700,000, a soaring stone statue of Mao, an increasingly rare sight in this country, points his hand down the nearly deserted main shopping street. 
The broad boulevards that dissect Fuxin, unlike the gridlocked streets of southern cities, are often deserted even in midday, emptying into dirt roads that wind off into the suburbs where coal miners labor in the huge mines that circle the city.
''Compared with other cities in this province, people's income is among the lowest,'' said Dai Mingxun, the Deputy Mayor of Fuxin. 
''We have even a wider income gap with the cities in southern parts of China and in coastal areas.''
''Many, many enterprises were losing money,'' Mr. Dai said.
Typical was the state of Fuxin's No. 2 Knitting Factory. 
Perenially in debt since it was founded in 1966, the factory, which primarily makes nylon socks, lost $118,000 in the two years before Chen Zhiqin, a factory employee, decided she could make money if she could run it. 
The city agreed to lease the plant to her for a deposit of $3,000, which she paid from savings.
Â 
Reward Hard Workers
''Before I leased this factory,'' the 43-year-old Mrs. Chen said, ''it was on the verge of bankruptcy.''
But Mrs. Chen turned the place upside down. 
''I gave 2,000 pairs of socks to each worker to sell,'' she said. 
''If they sold them they got paid. 
If they didn't, then they got nothing. 
We began to reward those who worked hard and punished those who were lazy.''
''Last year,'' she said, flashing a grin of success, ''we turned those losses into profits.''
There is no rent as such to be paid beyond the deposit, but she is responsible for paying taxes on the profits. 
Last year the taxes came to about $28,000.
While in much of China things tend to happen at molasses speed, here Mayor Wang, whose previous management experience consisted only in running a machine-tools factory, bulldozed his way through the sclerotic city administrative apparatus.
''I am for the saying 'a new broom sweeps clean,' '' the Mayor said. 
''The citizens will judge whether you are an effective and competent broom by how you sweep.''
In little more than nine months, Mayor Wang had nearly everything auctioned off.
Â 
City Agencies Not Immune
Even city agencies were not immune. 
Mayor Wang stormed into the city water department shortly after taking office and announced that if water was not running 24 hours a day they would all be out on the streets looking for work. 
Twenty days later the water was flowing.
City officials admit that opposition to the Mayor was substantial.
''Some cadres,'' said the Deputy Mayor, using the Chinese lexicon for a government functionary, ''doubted whether leasing out factories was socialist or not. 
Some of the workers and staff felt that leasing would give directors much higher wages. 
And many department heads felt that leasing would mean that they would lose control of enterprises.''
''Well, the fact is that it is all right for directors to have higher wages,'' Mr. Dai said. 
''The directors have to work harder and have greater responsibilities. 
They're the ones running the risks.''
Â 
Halved Administrative Staff
At the sock factory Mrs. Chen is acutely aware of the risks. 
''The city has set a profit quota for me of 100,000 yuan,'' or $27,000, she said. 
''Even if I make that, I still get nothing. 
Only over that figure do I begin to make money. 
And if I don't make it, I lose my leasing deposit.''
Where once a city agency had approved every minuscule decision about how the factory was run, Mrs. Chen became solely responsible for management. 
By halving the size of the company's administrative staff, reorganizing the shop floor and paying attention to her market, Mrs. Chen turned a profit of about $220,000 last year, eight times what she was required to make.
''We've been successful so far,'' said Li Jiaoyi, the head of the city's economic restructuring agency. 
''Production and profits are up. 
The city is booming.''
Last year, because of the leasing alone, profits jumped 50 percent for the town's enterprises, making Fuxin the most rapidly developing urban economy in the country.

text:
ï»¿
PEKING CHINA, a land where almost no natural resource goes overlooked, has mounted the world's largest and most determined effort to generate substantial quantities of methane gas for rural household use by fermenting human and animal wastes.
The program has advanced well beyond the experimental stage, and millions of backyard fermentation tanks on communes and farms are supplying up to 35 million peasants with fuel for cooking, lighting and heating that would be otherwise difficult to obtain.
China's experience in producing ''zhaoqi,'' or marsh gas, was described by Zhang Jigao, a prominent agricultural engineer, at a recent seminar in Peking entitled ''The Changing Rural Habitat.''
The seminar, sponsored by the Aga Khan Foundation, brought experts from nine countries together to share locally developed technologies.
Christopher Wren describes program in China which uses human and animal wastes to generate methane gas for fuel
''We now have built seven million tanks, which we call digesters. 
Their main use is for living - cooking three meals a day and heating hot water,'' explained Mr. Zhang, who is affiliated with the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences.
The notion of extracting energy from human and animal wastes may strike Americans and Europeans as bizarre, but the Chinese cannot afford to overlook any potential fuel source. 
A recent survey on the use of energy in rural China, where more than 800 million peasants live, found that about 70 percent of the households lack enough fuel.
The gleaning of firewood, straw and weeds, which account for threequarters of the energy consumed in the countryside, is not only a time-consuming chore but has also contributed to soil erosion in many regions.
Recognizing that China does not have sufficient conventional fuel for its needs, Yu Qiuli, a Deputy Prime Minister, told a session of the State Energy Commission in Peking last month that the energy shortage in rural areas should be met by building more methaneproducing digesters, as well as by reforestation.
Chinese studies on producing methane gas from wastes contend that the fermentation system also improves rural sanitation and produces an organic fertilizer rich in nitrogen, potassium and phosphates. 
The New China News Agency reported last week that the digesters were providing 40 million tons of fertilizer matter as a byproduct.
Nightsoil, as human wastes used to fertilize crops are euphemistically called, has often been used in poorer countries, but it also poses a health hazard for both farmers and consumers. 
In an interview, a Chinese public health specialist here said that with proper fermentation in the digesters, bacteria and parasites were killed, making nightsoil safe.
The conversion idea is not new in China. 
In 1936 Zhou Peiyuan, a well-known Chinese scientist, constructed an underground hydraulic pressure tank in Jiangsu Province for cooking and lighting. 
An indoor tank in Hebei Province, built a year later, is still reportedly in operation. 
Similar digesters have been tried in other countries, notably India, with less success.
The technology has been widely introduced in China only within the last decade and has been kept intentionally simple. 
The peasants dig a pit in the backyard and construct a fermentation well of concrete blocks or rocks and cement. 
The tank is then buried, except for a removable concrete cap tightly fitted on top.
A feedstock pipe slants down into the tank from the nearby latrine and pigsty. 
On the opposite side is a storage chamber into which fertilizer is pushed under gas pressure. 
Mr. Zhang said that the feedstock often consisted entirely of human wastes, though straw and other crop stalks might be added.
Once the cap is closed, the contents are left to ferment under pressure for a month to 40 days. 
Because gas pressure building within the fermentation tank could be unstable, the process requires careful tending, though Mr. Zhang insisted that ''acidity and temperature control has been well mastered in China.''
Â 
Temperature Is Important
The methane gas produced by the fermentation is later drawn through a hose into the farm kitchen for cooking with stove rings adapted to function at low pressure. 
After the gas is spent, the remaining waste is pumped out and carted to the fields for fertilizer. 
Then the process is started again.
The system's efficiency depends heavily on the climate because fermentation will not take place in the tank below 50 degrees Fahrenheit. 
Not surprisingly, most of the digesters -about five million - have been built in Sichuan, a southern province with a generally mild winter.
Mr. Zhang also said that digesters were operating nearly year-round in Guangdong, another southern province. 
The current cost of building a medium-size digester of eight cubic meters, to provide fuel for a family of four or five, is about $56, with communes and farm households generally sharing the cost.
Â 
Zhaoqi Is 'Easier to Manage'
The New China News Agency estimated that 68.3 billion cubic meters of methane gas could be generated annually if just half of the human and animal waste in rural China were put to use. 
Larger digesters have been tried in some urban areas, particularly Shanghai. 
But Mr. Zhang noted, ''The main purpose of zhaoqi is for the farmer. 
It is easier to manage there and we save on pipes and accessories.''
As energy costs rise, the digester has become more attractive to the third world as an alternate fuel source. 
A Western economist familiar with process estimated that China's digesters were already supplying the energy equivalent of 4 million tons of oil.
The Chinese experience has caught the attention of some officials in the United Nations Development Program. 
And Roger Carmignani, an energy specialist from the World Bank who attended the seminar in Peking, remarked, ''It is apparent that developing methane production is one of the most efficient ways of solving the problem of rural energy resources.''

text:

A hand-cranked telephone still stands between Ma Tianying and his hopes of becoming the richest peasant in his village in Sichuan Province.
Mr. Ma runs his own small sawmill, repairs trucks and tractors and makes prefabricated housing slabs. 
Last year he and his family earned the equivalent of about $6,000, making him the second wealthiest resident of the village of Chengbei.
But Mr. Ma, a stocky man whose business attire is a T-shirt and baggy blue trousers held up by an old army belt, has yet to catch up with Zhang Daishen. 
She got a head start in turning out the prefabricated concrete that is in demand because of the housing boom touched off by recent changes in agricultural policy.
Agricultural specialist in China has estimated that as many as 70% of China's peasants are economically superfluous and Chinese Government, hoping to better utilize peasants, is encouraging them to stop tilling soil and set up small workshops, service trades and specialized occupations that will keep them gainfully employed; photos; map (M)
Miss Zhang earned about $6,800 last year and installed the village's first and only private telephone.
Â 
Rivalry Is Encouraged
Miss Zhang and Mr. Ma personify the kind of rivalry that the Chinese Government likes to encourage. 
The country's agricultural output has soared since 1979, when a new policy let farmers keep whatever they could grow beyond a quota set by the state. 
But the new productivity has revealed the extent of underemployment that long existed among China's 800 million peasants.
Because China has too many farmers and too little arable land for them to cultivate, the Government wants more peasants to stop tilling the soil and set up small workshops, service trades and specialized occupations like raising livestock that will keep them gainfully employed in the countryside.
Du Runsheng, a leading agricultural specialist, estimated three months ago that as many as 70 percent of China's peasants were economically superfluous. 
The cities could not afford to absorb them, he said, so new jobs must be created for them in rural areas.
Mr. Du, who heads the Rural Policy Research Center of the Communist Party's Central Committee, said at a news conference that he envisioned a strategy of shifting 30 to 40 percent of China's rural labor force out of traditional farm work and into sideline occupations and small industries.
Â 
A Policy for Development
''In a situation of surplus rural labor,'' Mr. Du said, ''this may be a proper way to increase employment and people's incomes, to raise their cultural level and to speed up rural development. 
In short, this is a policy for comprehensive development of the countryside.''
A directive since issued by the Cabinet-level State Council and the party's Central Committee has made clear that Mr. Du's views are more than academic. 
It urged that by the end of the century 40 percent of the rural labor force, or about 200 million peasants, should be performing jobs not in the fields.
The directive noted that 31 million peasants already worked in commune- run enterprises and that two million others had set up their own businesses.
Chengbei village, set in the rolling hills and bright green rice paddies of Ziyang County in Sichuan, has benefited from the changes. 
The village head, Zhang Chenming, said that his community had 395 households with 1,584 people, but only 61 acres of farmland, which is a fraction of the meager national average of a quarter acre per person.
Â 
No More Handouts
Before the 1979 changes, Mr. Zhang said, the village was crippled by leftist egalitarianism and so poor that it relied on annual state subsidies of grain and money. 
After the land was contracted out to individual households, the peasants began working harder and the handouts stopped. 
Last year Chengbei's annual per capita income reached about $230, which is nearly three times the income in 1979.
''The responsibility system is like an elixir for the people,'' Mr. Zhang said. 
''In the past, we all ate from the same big pot. 
Now we have broken the iron rice bowl.''
Mr. Ma, who is 45 years old, earned 55 cents a day under the old commune system. 
When the new policies let him stop, he set to work for himself repairing tractors and machinery, then took up making concrete housing slabs. 
He borrowed about $3,000 from the state bank and later invested $4,000 that he had saved. 
Recently, he built a large new three-story house with his workshops on the ground floor and two rooms for each family member on the upper floors.
Â 
Success Is Not Resented
Now that peasants are allowed to go into long-distance hauling, Mr. Ma bought a secondhand truck and plans to buy a couple more so that he can compete with the state-run transportation companies.
Asked if the neighbors resented his success, Mr. Ma said, ''No, because all of us are trying to become well-off.''
Mr. Ma said he also wanted to get a telephone, to let him compete better with Miss Zhang. 
She insisted her rival was actually her brother-in-law, Liu Zifu, who broke away from her business to set up a workshop of his own.
''At the beginning, our family was the only one making building materials here,'' she said. 
''Later on, some people learned from our example. 
Now more than 20 households are doing the same job.''
Miss Zhang, who is 36, started out as a fieldhand, earning only work points from the commune. 
She also pulled a handcart carrying charcoal and coal. 
Now, she said, she employs 10 other villagers in her enterprise, which makes asbestos tiles as well as concrete slabs, and raises poultry on the side. 
She has not hired her husband, Lu Ziling, who works as a purchasing agent for the local marketing cooperative and earns far less than she does.
Â 
Phone a Status Symbol
''We have very serious competition now,'' said Miss Zhang. 
''I try to offer lower prices and better quality.''
To solicit orders from the provincial capital of Chengdu, 50 miles away, Miss Zhang bought a black telephone with a hand crank. 
The installation cost about $140, nearly as much as an average Chinese peasant earns in a year.
The telephone is a status symbol in Chengbei, where there is no one else to call. 
But Miss Zhang explained that ''it does provide a lot of convenience for business.''

An oil discovery off China this year by a Japanese drilling company, part of the first major foreign oil exploration in Chinese territorial waters since the Communist revolution, appears likely to galvanize trade between the two nations, trade officials said here.
The discovery, announced by the state-owned Japan National Oil Corporation, which has been drilling under a joint-production agreement with China, offers the prospect of the first significant Japanese production of Chinese oil since World War II.
The oil strike comes at a critical time for China, which is beset by inflation for the first time since the Communist revolution in 1949. 
China, under the leadership of Deng Xiaoping, is also troubled by shortfalls in onshore oil production that threaten to undermine plans for industrial expansion and are also causing a serious lack of foreign exchange.

Oil is the key to Chinese-Japanese trade, which has nearly tripled to more than $9 billion a year in the three years since China and Japan concluded a long-term, $20 billion trade agreement in early 1978.
China exports its oil primarily to Japan; it shipped eight million tons here last year. 
These exports help pay for imports of vital Japanese industrial plant and equipment. 
China's long-term development plans appear to hinge on oil production, which totaled 106 million tons last year.
''Oil and the foreign exchange that China obtains abroad, mostly from Japan, are the keys to Deng's plans,'' said a trading house executive.

Â 
Also Crucial to Japanese
Industry executives here say that the oil is also crucial to Japan in the long run.

Japanese planners have sought for 20 years to diversify supply sources away from the Middle East, which still supplies threequarters of all oil consumed by Japan. 
Japan has virtually no domestic oil, and nearby Pohai offers a secure source of the type that Japan has so far lacked.
The Japanese Government, which finances the national oil company, and about four dozen Japanese concerns that are minority partners with the state company in the Pohai Bay exploration stress security of supply, not profit, and are offering China attractive terms.
Â 
Seismic Surveys Completed
The discovery came just after dozens of Western companies had completed seismic surveys in the South China Sea at their own expense. 
They are expected to tender bids for the first joint production opportunities that China will offer in that part of its 2,800-mile coastline, and the Atlantic Richfield Company and the Philips Petroleum Corporation have already reported such an agreement.
Japanese and French concerns, led by the Compagnie Fran,caise de Petroles, went ahead with China faster in Pohai Bay than private Western companies elsewhere along the coast. 
Their rapid success in finding oil suggests that Western estimates in the 1970's of offshore Chinese reserves of close to four billion tons may be conservative.
Oil is not expected to flow from Pohai Bay until about 1984. 
But Japan National Oil is scheduled to sink five wells in Pohai Bay this year, and some unofficial Japanese estimates put reserves there as high as 10 billion tons.
Â 
Hopes May Be Too High
Press reports here have put the likely yield from the field found by the Japanese at 300,000 to 400,000 barrels a day, or between 15 million and 20 million tons a year, with Japan to pay all costs and receive 42.5 percent of the oil. 
But one Japanese executive described the forecasts as ''perhaps wishful thinking - it's just too early to tell.''
American geologists in Peking believe that Pohai Bay's oil is scattered in rich but small pockets and that the oil-bearing strata have been disrupted -and made hard to tap - by earthquakes in the region. 
If the warnings are justified, then Japanese hopes may be pitched too high.
Reports from Peking say that Deputy Prime Minister Gu Mu has forecast that China's onshore production may drop by 10 million to 20 million tons a year by the mid-1980's. 
Tokyo executives said that the new finds offshore were timely, to make up for this possible decline, and because of the tentative shelving by China of $1.5 billion worth of contracts for industrial plants from Japan.

The American Motors Corporation expects to sign an agreement later this week with China to jointly produce Jeeps in Peking and export some of them to other nations in the Far East.
The four-wheel-drive vehicles are to be produced by the Peking Jeep Company, a joint venture of Peking Auto Works and A.M.C., which is the smallest of the American automobile companies and the only manufacturer of Jeeps. 
Production is expected to reach 40,000 vehicles a year, which are to be sold in China and other Asian countries.
''This is probably the largest individual joint venture in China,'' said A.M.C.'s chairman, W. Paul Tippett, at a briefing last week before he left for China for the scheduled signing. 
He added that negotiations for the project had been in progress for more than four years and had been initiated by A.M.C., which sought access to the potentially huge Chinese market. 
It also wanted a low-wage area to manufacture vehicles to compete with Japanese companies in overseas markets.
SOUTHFIELD, Mich., May 2 - The American Motors Corporation expects to sign an agreement later this week with China to jointly produce Jeeps in Peking and export some of them to other nations in the Far East.
A.M.C. executives had hoped to withhold public announcement of the agreement until the actual signing, they said, to avoid angering Chinese officials and possibly endangering the accord. 
They declined, in fact, to comment today on reports appearing in Ward's Auto World, a trade publication, that said the formal announcement of the agreement was due shortly. 
However, last week, company officials, in advance briefings for reporters, said the signing was planned for Thursday in Peking.
The Chinese-made vehicles are not intended to be sold in the United States, Mr. Tippett said. 
The A.M.C. agreement, if it is signed, will be the first joint production agreement in China by an American auto manufacturer, an agreement that could result in the start of actual production this year or next.
Nevertheless, Volkswagen of West Germany has a preliminary contract to start making a new-model car in 1988 in a joint venture at a plant in Shanghai, where Chinese auto production is centered. 
The Ford Motor Company has been attempting to set up a joint venture to produce trucks and tractors.
A number of other American companies have established themselves in China, including the R.J. 
Reynolds Tobacco Company, which has been producing cigarettes there, and Avon Products Inc., which is marketing cosmetics. 
The largest single-project agreement apparently is a $230 million coal-mining development to be undertaken by the Occidential Petroleum Corporation.
Peking Jeep will be in a factory owned by Peking Auto Works, which now produces about 20,000 units a year of an older-design, fourwheel-drive vehicle based on a 1954 Soviet design for a Soviet Army jeep. 
A.M.C. will invest $8 million in cash and $8 million in technology for a 31.4 percent share of the $51 million joint venture. 
A.M.C.'s share could rise to as high as 49 percent under the terms of the agreement.
The initial plan for the joint venture, Mr. Tippett said, is for A.M.C. to update the existing Chinese 212 model with A.M.C.'s new four-cylinder engine and other engineering improvements intended to make the vehicles more fuel-efficient and to increase their carrying capacity. 
The engine is to be manufactured largely in China.
Within a few years, Mr. Tippett said, the objective is to develop a new vehicle, based in large part on A.M.C.'s CJ7 Jeep, the company's basic model.
''This is important to the Chinese and to us,'' Mr. Tippett said. 
He noted that, in China, autos are largely confined to urban areas while four-wheel-drive vehicles are necessary for the primitive rural road system. 
''The Chinese view transportation as one of their top five priorities in terms of economic development,'' Mr. Tippett added.
For A.M.C., he said, the venture gives the company an inside position in what could develop into a vast market for utility vehicles for all types of use in rural areas. 
It also gives the company a pool of 4,000 factory workers at the Peking plant whose pay averages 60 cents an hour, compared with about $12 an hour in labor costs in Japan and more than $20 an hour in the United States.
The average-equipped Jeep manufactured by American Motors in the United States sells for $11,500. 
Mr. Tippett did not indicate what the price of the vehicle built in China will be.
Â 
President to Be From A.M.C.
The president and chief operating officer of Peking Jeep will be an A.M.C. executive, although the chairman will be Chinese. 
''Basically, we plan to run it,'' said Mr. Tippett, who added that 8 to 10 A.M.C. executives would be permanently assigned to Peking with others visiting as needed. 
None of the American executives of the venture have yet been named, he added.
Mr. Tippett also said that officials of Renault, the French auto company that controls 46.4 percent of A.M.C.'s stock, had not been involved in the Chinese negotiations, other than to approve the transaction at the board level.
The agreement was initialed about a month ago, while a delegation from China was visiting here, he said. 
The formal signing was put off so that it could be done in the Great Hall of the People in Peking and publicized from there, Mr. Tippett said.
(In Peking, reports had circulated that a deal with American Motors was near for the venture, but there had been no official comment.)
Â 
Long-Term Strategic Move
The joint venture, Mr. Tippett said, will permit competition with Japanese companies that now sell 97 percent of all the 100,000 fourwheel-drive vehicles purchased in Pacific basin countries each year. 
A.M.C. now sells 2,000 to 3,000 of its Jeeps in the Pacific area, out of a total of 91,000 jeep-type vehicles sold in this country and abroad last year. 
''This is a long-term strategic move by A.M.C.,'' he said. 
''It will be a long time before there is much in the way of profit, but the opportunities seem very great to us in the long run.''
Mr. Tippett said Chinese officials would handle distribution and sales within the country while A.M.C. would use its own marketing channels for export.
Mr. Tippett said the only restriction on bringing profits back to the United States was that they not represent a drain of hard currency on China. 
Sufficient export sales of the vehicles should satisfy that requirement, he added.

text:

A year ago Feng Lanxiu seemed a discouraging prospect for marriage. 
She was totally deaf and unable to speak even in sign language, and she was still being cared for by her parents.
Now Miss Feng, who is 34 years old, has a doting husband who kids her gently about not yet producing their first child. 
Her husband, Liu Jinli, 32, also cannot hear or speak. 
He met Miss Feng and married her last July through an unusual matchmaking service.
Profile of matchmaking of handicapped people in China
In this Manchurian city, an agency run by amateur marriage brokers tries to find spouses for physically handicapped people who in traditional Chinese society were long considered unmarriageable.
Hong Zhiguo, director of the city's Society for the Disabled, said regular employment had been found for 92 percent of Harbin's 6,000 handicapped adults. 
Their disabilities have been turned to advantage sometimes. 
Many of those who are deaf work in a local truck assembly plant where the noise does not disturb them.
Â 
46 Have Registered
This reduces the burden on their families, Mr. Hong said, but does not guarantee the disabled an independent life. 
So early last year his society set up its marriage service.
About 100 people have visited the bureau so far and 46 have registered. 
Two couples got married last July, and a third couple is preparing for marriage. 
Three other couples are courting and expect to wed, Mr. Hong said, ''so basically we have a success rate of 25 percent.''
The introductions are arranged by Li Shuqing, a staff member, every Monday and Wednesday morning in her small office, which is over a bottlecap factory. 
''The job of matchmaking is new to us; we have no experience at all,'' Miss Li acknowledged.
With the decline of traditional family-arranged marriages, Chinese cities have enjoyed a boom in matchmaking centers. 
But Miss Li said her responsibilities went well beyond the simpler task of bringing ordinary people together.
Â 
'This Job Is Delicate'
''Because marriage is a major event in the life of young people, it is concerned with their happiness or bitterness,'' she said. 
''So I know that this job is delicate. 
They are disabled physically but not mentally, and they have this desire for marriage and happiness.''
Miss Li said her handicapped clients made good marriage partners because ''they may be more considerate and careful than normal people.''
But because they are self-conscious about asking for a spouse, the first tense visit to the matchmaking office often includes anxious relatives and even translators for sign language.
''They fear that it will be difficult to find a partner or that they won't find someone, so they come together with their parents,'' Miss Li said. 
''We tell them that is it normal and natural for young people to marry and there should be no problems.''
''They are very shy at the first meeting,'' she said. 
''They don't talk much. 
They may arrange the next meeting by themselves, at a park or movie theater, and then report back to us.''
Â 
Handicaps Are Also Paired
In addition to trying to match hobbies, interests and family backgrounds, Miss Li said she also usually paired physical handicaps, reasoning that those sharing the same problems would be more sympathetic to a partner's needs.
But sometimes weeks of effort by Miss Li end in failure. 
She recalled introducing a 25-year-old man, ''crippled in both arms but good-looking,'' to a 25-year-old woman who could not walk and got about with a hand-cranked tricycle. 
Both were working hard to become foreign language translators, he in Japanese and she in English, so Miss Li decided that ''in my opinion, they were a very good match.''
But she could not negotiate the stairs to his second-floor apartment, and she worried that he would not be able to carry a child. 
''So they didn't make it,'' Miss Li said with a sigh.
On another occasion Miss Li introduced two deaf people who were each married before and had a child. 
''At their first meeting they got along very well, but then it broke down,'' Miss Li said. 
The two people worried that if their children quarreled, they could not hear it and family harmony would be upset.
Â 
Problems After Marriage
''Sometimes we feel discouraged, but the difficulties of the disabled are bigger than ours,'' Miss Li said. 
''So we try to persuade ourselves to be patient and to keep working.''
While the office is also prepared to mediate problems that may develop after marriage, the couples so far seem to have made their own adjustment. 
Shao Kuihe, a husky 30-year-old, is proud of saving $750 in preparation for his marriage to Sheng Lijuan, who is 28. 
Neither can hear nor speak. 
Mr. Shao explained in sign language through an interpreter that he and Miss Sheng communicated by writing messages and watching the shape of each other's mouth.
Once a couple decides to marry, the office refers them to specialists at a Harbin medical college to determine whether they should have a child. 
Mr. Hong said heredity was not involved in the disabilities of the couples matched so far.
The matchmaking service is open to those who are blind as well as to those who are deaf and mute or handicapped in some other way. 
It has not turned down anyone for being too disabled.
''We do have some severe physical cases, but if the problem lies within the bounds of the marriage law, we will try our best to make it possible,'' Mr. Hong said. 
''For some people, we have to tell them in advance that their case will be difficult, so they must be patient.''

Critics are seeking to delay a regulation that the Reagan Administration says would improve its ability to monitor imports of textiles and apparel.
The critics claim that the regulation - which the Government issued Aug. 
3 and is to take effect Sept. 
7 - would strand $500 million worth of foreign-made textiles and apparel that American companies have already ordered.
They say that would cause substantial financial difficulties for retailers and other businesses, as well as apparel shortages and price increases of up to 20 percent for consumers. 
It also could cause China to take retaliatory trade measures, they say.
US textile and apparel importers seek delay in Federal regulation--announced on Aug 3 to take effect Sept 7--changing Customs Service's country-of-origin rule as it applies to textile import quotas established through bilateral agreements; say it would strand $500 million worth of foreign-made textiles and apparel that American companies have already ordered and cause substantial financial difficulties for retailers and other businesses, as well as apparel shortage and price increases of up to 20 percent; say China might also retaliate (M)
The proposed measure would change the Customs Service's country-of-origin rule. 
It applies to textile import quotas established through bilateral agreements.
Under current regulations, if parts of a garment are made in one country and shipped to another for assembling and then shipped to the United States, they are counted against the import quotas of the second country.
For example, if sleeves or other parts of sweaters are made in China, but sewn together in Hong Kong, they have been counted against the textile import quotas of Hong Kong rather than China.
The Administration proposal would apply the country-of-origin designation to the country where the fabric originated - in the example above, China rather than Hong Kong. 
That could reduce the amount of Chinese textiles that ultimately find their way into this country, since China has a smaller quota than Hong Kong, which has been trading longer with the United States.
Â 
Varied Group of Opponents
The measure's opponents include retail industry groups, textile importers, agricultural interests and members of Congress who contend that the proposal is ill-conceived and motivated largely by the re-election concerns of the President and two of his Senate allies, Senator Jesse Helms, Republican of North Carolina, and Senator Strom Thurmond, Republican of South Carolina.
But Federal officials, along with some members of Congress and domestic textile manufacturers, offer two reasons for the regulation. 
One is to prevent fraud and evasion of textile quotas established by bilateral trade agreements. 
The other is to protect American textile manufacturers and workers against a burgeoning volume of less-expensive imports.
Although the proposed change would apply to each of the 36 nations with which the United States has bilateral textile trade agreements. it would most sharply affect those in the Far East.
According to Government and industry figures, four countries - Taiwan, Korea, Japan and China - and the colony of Hong Kong together supply nearly 60 percent of the textiles and apparel imported by the United States. 
The proposed regulation would also require inspection of shipments of textile imports at their United States port of entry rather than at their destination.
Rules now allow textile shipments that enter the country through one port but are bound for another location to be sealed, bonded and shipped to their destination before the Customs Service makes its inspection.
Walter C. Lenahan, Deputy Assistant Secretary of Commerce, who directed the Government group that drafted the rule, said Government statistics show that in 1983 the Customs Service seized about $5 million worth of textiles that were imported fraudulently.
By contrast, the estimated value of illegal goods seized so far this year is close to $28 million. 
This year, special textile squads were assigned to the ports of New York and Los Angeles, where 75 percent of the imported textiles enter the country.
The proposed rule was praised by James H. Martin Jr., president of the American Textile Manufacturers Institute. 
Mr. Martin is also vice chairman of Ti-Caro Inc., a Gastonia, N.C., company that manufactures yarn and industrial sewing thread.
''It clarifies the fact that the intent of the bilaterals have been stretched, even to the point of fraud in some instances,'' he said. 
''We're not against imports, but we feel that trade should be orderly, above-board, and fair.''
Â 
Called 'Administrative Overkill'
However, critics such as Sim Gluckson, chairman of the textile and apparel group of the American Association of Exporters and Importers, contend that as a fraud-fighting device, the new policy ''amounts to administrative overkill.''
He said: ''It's a very bad regulation that will be extremely disruptive to the fall and winter retail season.''
Mr. Gluckson, president of a New York-based knitwear company, said that because textiles and apparel are bought six to nine months in advance, the proposed rule would likely mean that shipments already ordered by companies would not arrive in time. 
''Contracts have been signed. 
Letters of credit have gone out, dates of shipment have been arranged,'' he said. 
''And now this. 
It's thrown the whole industry into confusion.''
At least a score of senators and representatives have complained in letters to President Reagan that the regulation ''would suddenly make illegal widespread methods of textile and apparel production which are absolutely legal under present U.S. law and which have been legal for many decades.''
Â 
Concern About China
Others, including Senator Bob Dole, Republican of Kansas, expressed concern that the measure would sour the United States-China trade relationship. 
About 11 percent of the textiles imported by the United States last year came from China.
The official New China News Agency has said that the proposed regulation would ''adversely affect the textile exports of the Chinese mainland for Hong Kong.''
The comments by the news agency have raised concern among agricultural interests that China might limit or ban imports of American grain or other commodities in retaliation.
Last year, China banned purchases of several United States exports, including wheat and cotton, when the two countries could not agree on ceilings for textile and apparel imports.
Finally, several critics assert that the rule change was pushed primarily to help the re-election chances of the Carolinas' Senators and the President's own re-election campaign.
The charges of political motivation were denied by Mr. Lenahan and by Senators Helms and Thurmond.
The textile industry nationwide employs about 2.4 million people, according to the industry, with North Carolina, New York and South Carolina, respectively, the top three states in textile-related employment.

text:

Lines formed in Peking today as the city's 9.5 million people stocked up on meat, fish and poultry a day before the steepest food price increases here since the Communists took power in 1949 were to take effect.
At every work unit, announcements from the city authorities were read out during the week detailing the increases, which will add an average of 50 percent to the prices of 1,800 ''nonstaple'' food items.
The price increases are up to 70 percent for pork, 130 percent for beef, 18 percent for eggs and 340 percent for yellow croaker, a popular fish.
At the same time, residents were promised a monthly per capita grant of 7.50 yuan - the equivalent of $2.62 - to help meet the higher costs.
Peking's 9.5 million residents stock up on meat, fish and poultry on day before steepest food price increases since Communists took control in 1949 are to take effect; increases, part of Goverment effort to introduce market mechanisms into economy, will add average of 50 percent to such 'non-staple' food items as pork, beef, eggs and some fish; residents are promised small monthly per capita grant to help meet higher costs, but increases are still expected to force shift in diets; photo (M)
With the average annual income among urban Chinese last year falling at 608 yuan ($207), and beef rising to the equivalent of 2 yuan a pound, it seemed plain that the increases would force a shift in diets, at least in the short run. 
Economists here have argued that over the longer term the increased returns to producers from the higher prices will stimulate higher output and lower prices in the marketplace. 
But for those worrying about the immediate future, this was scant consolation.
One young man with a wife and child said he would have to choose between shifting a much higher proportion of his monthly pay into buying food, or cutting down sharply on his family's consumption of meat and chicken. 
''Until now, people have been very happy with Deng Xiaoping,'' the man said, speaking of changes instituted by China's supreme leader. 
''But now we can see there is another side to the changes. 
It is going to be hard.''
Â 
Following a Set Pattern
The pattern in Peking has been the same as one followed earlier in 22 other cities, including Canton, Shanghai and Wuhan. 
And as in those cities, consumers flooded stores and markets to stock up on the affected items.
By the last days of the week, places like the Chongwenmen Market in central Peking had little left but fatty scraps of pork and low-grade samples of dried fish. 
A rush on canned foods left shelves similarly bare.
The move is part of a drive by the Government to introduce market mechanisms into the economy. 
After years of prices that remained the same or rose hardly at all, millions of people across urban China are encountering steep increases in food costs.
How fraught with difficulties the process will be can be gauged from the care that party leaders have taken to prepare the public. 
For months before the current round of increases officials were putting consumers on notice that strains lay ahead.
Usually, the warnings were accompanied by pledges that the Government would do everything it could to ease the transition, but there have been periodic bouts of ''panic buying'' as shoppers sought to protect themselves.
Â 
Calculated Political Risks
When Chiang Kai-shek was in power before 1949 few things eroded confidence as fast as the spiraling inflation that gave rise to banknotes denominated in millions of yuan. 
Now, the Communists who supplanted the Chiang Government and virtually abolished inflation are deliberately pushing up prices on a wide range of consumer goods, food in particular.
The increases involve calculated political and economic risks. 
From the outset of the program in 1979, officials putting into effect Mr. Deng's policies have been determined to replace what they refer to as the irrational pricing system established under Mao Zedong with something much closer to the Western model, with the market place replacing the bureaucracy as the chief arbiter of value.
Men like Tian Jiyun, the Deputy Prime Minister who has principal responsibility for price changes, believe that unleashing the power of supply and demand is the key to the entire modernization program set forth by Mr. Deng.
It is an article of faith among those involved in the program that only by allowing prices to rise and fall in response to market conditions can the country free itself from the burdens of scarcity and oversupply, shoddy quality and the other problems that beset the typical Communist economy.
Â 
Market Principle Referees
No other nation that is formally wedded to the doctrines of Karl Marx, not even Hungary, the most economically adventurous member of the Soviet bloc, has attempted anything so far-reaching.
Although Mr. Deng and his associates insist that the state will be on hand as a referee, they are convinced that prosperity will come only through the fullest possible application of market principles that most Communist countries, China included, have spent decades suppressing.
The problem lies in the transition from an economy in which the Government has manipulated prices to keep some items - not only food, but also rent, electricity, children's toys and tens of thousands of other goods - unrealistically cheap. 
At both ends of the economic chain, producers and consumers must be weaned from a system of large state subsidies that has entrenched inefficiencies and drained at least 20 percent of all revenues - some Western economists say the real figure may be closer to 40 percent - from the Government treasury.
The Government has so far excluded food grains, edible oils and basic vegetables like cabbage from the price changes.

Could Soon Reach 1.3 Billion

file: THE COLD GIVES A LIFT TO DOWN PRODUCTS.txt
text:
ï»¿
The down business is up. 
Thanks to the bitter Canadian winter weather blowing south to the United States, Canada's makers of down winterwear, major suppliers for the American market, are reporting surprisingly good sales despite the recession and record high world prices for the little puffs of feathers.
''Given inflation, people are looking for real value at today's high prices,'' said Russill H. Morin, president of the Canadian Down and Feather Products Association. 
''And they are finding it in down.''
Andrew Malcolm comment discusses how cold weather conditions have helped sales of down products
They are also finding a radically different, more fashionable and costlier product than consumers knew not so many years back when down was something worn only by geese, ducks and a few hunters in reversible red and green vests.
Now it has become a $100 million-a-year industry in Canada alone, has started a lucrative surge in international sales and has seen several Asian countries begin their own down industries to serve the exploding market in North America and Japan.
Â 
2 Million to the Ounce
Down, whose tiny resilient filaments number 2 million to the ounce, has long been popular as a pillow-filler and, in Europe, for bed comforters. 
It was warm and lightweight. 
But its bulk and perceived image as masculine, ''outdoorsy'' and unfashionable confined sales to the sporting goods sections of most North American stores.
There is considerable dispute about which one of Canada's many private clothing companies first combined new colors, better design and a stylish stitching pattern to make the first women's down coat. 
But there is no dispute that it happened about five years ago here in Winnipeg, the old prairie riverboat town that has the lowest mean temperature of any Canadian city.
''You don't care what you look like in Winnipeg in the winter,'' said Mr. Morin, who lives in Toronto, ''you just want to be warm.''
Consumers can now buy a complete line of down-filled products, from coats, mittens and parkas to comforters, sleeping bags, lounging slippers and the high-priced down skiwear made by Mr. Morin's company, Russill H. Morin Ltd.
Winnipeg's down manufacturers, such as Victoria Squire and Miami Fashions, cite many reasons for down's sudden success without largescale advertising. 
They include inflation, changing tastes toward more outdoor activities, acceptance of more pragmatic clothing, down's impressive insulation power and the strength of a fad that first introduced many to the comfort, practicality, light weight and warmth of some slightly used feathers.
Â 
'It Lasts a Lifetime'
''You use down one time,'' Mr. Morin said, ''you'll never go back to anything else. 
And it lasts a lifetime, too.''
The basic quality of down, however, owes nothing to man. 
Its many water-resistant filaments, naturally arrayed in clusters like a ripe dandelion pod, trap warm air next to the body yet allow the garments to ''breathe.''
The best down comes from the breasts of geese. 
One mature, 10-pound goose might produce eight ounces of feathers. 
But that includes only two ounces of down. 
The down, however, costs $54 a pound in December, which is a lot more than the entire rest of the bird is worth.
The problem is that feathers and down are a byproduct of the meat industry and there has never been that overwhelming a demand for goose and ducks in North America. 
So, according to Mr. Morin, a number of Canadian farmers are raising geese, selling the meat frozen to European outlets at little more than cost, and making money off the byproduct.
Still, the farmers are far from meeting the market's demands. 
For many years, the world's major feather supplier has been the Orient, primarily China, whose birds produce half the world's supply. 
Last year Canada imported some 2 million pounds of feathers, or 80 percent of its needs.
Â 
Prices Have Soared
But three years ago, China realized that it could create some domestic jobs and reap more foreign exchange benefits by founding its own down clothing industry. 
So it slashed down exports by half, sending down's price up. 
In 1970 down cost $4.25 a pound. 
In 1975 it cost $7.10. 
In 1978 the price tripled to $24, and it has doubled again since.
The feathers arrive at Canadian processors in burlap-wrapped bales in 40,000-pound container loads. 
They are washed, blown dry and blown sorted for shipment to Canad ian clothiers, who have been scrambling to provide th e best designed, most fashionable fabrics to wrap aroundthe feathers.
''There is a wider array of colors now than ever before,'' said Jeff Black, vice president of merchandising for Victoria Squire Inc., where 250 workers are already sewing next winter's down jackets. 
''The U.S. demand is growing all the time. 
''We've been increasing our production 25 percent a year since 1977.''
''We're pushing the more tailored look,'' said Murray Waldman of Miami Fashions Ltd., known in New York as the Canadian Garments Company. 
''Down is becoming more fashionable all the time.''
'People Will Remember the Cold'
''We've had two mild winters,'' Mr. Waldman noted, ''and people forget about the cold. 
Then, wham, comes this winter and our sales are way up. 
The boost will carry over to next year, too. 
People will remember the cold.''
The problem for Canadian and American down clothiers is competition from Asia, primarily Korea and China, where wages are but a fraction of North America's.
''I just came back from China,'' Mr. Waldman said. 
''They make a coat for half our costs. 
They're paying about 25 cents an hour. 
We pay $5.''
Thus, a domestic down coat might cost $250 to $300 at retail today, while Chinese coats, he said, might sell for $150 to $180 and cost the stores only $75 wholesale.
''Our challenge is to make our coats look that much more expensive than the imports,'' he said.

''Inside the Guan Guangmei phenomenon,'' promised a headline on page 1 of a national newspaper. 
Boasted another, ''Benxi produces Guan Guangmei!''
In the prestigious and influential Economic Daily, a two-week debate of sorts has raged over whether her success and methods are truly ''socialist'' or are, in fact, blatantly ''capitalist.''
Â 
A Rare Debate on Issues
And although anonymous commentators, editorialists and letter writers who support Miss Guan heavily outnumber her detractors, the extended discussion of the ''Guan Guangmei phenomenon'' is a rare instance of public exchange over issues that are at the very core of China's modernization effort. 
To be sure, the degree of official and public support for Miss Guan suggests strongly that her example is being used not only to champion the need for economic reform but also as a way of smoking out the ideological opposition.
Benxi's Communist Party branch has held a series of meetings over the last year to assess Miss Guan's endeavors. 
Her critics within the party, according to The Economic Daily, have attacked her for a variety of sins.
One party member who has worked for a quarter of a century in one of the stores now leased by Miss Guan accused her of ''disliking the supervision of the party and for being good at dancing.''
Another party member contended that Miss Guan ''plays down the role of political education,'' while a third charged: ''The leasing system of Guan Guangmei takes advantage of the situation to benefit herself. 
It has the character of exploitation.''
Â 
China's Current Dilemma
These criticisms, even the denigration of her ballroom talents, are fundamental to China's current dilemma: how to invigorate an economy that is resisting virtually all stimuli under a blanket of bureaucratic incompetence and corruption, while preserving a necessary patina of socialist ideology. 
That Miss Guan dances well raises the question of whether she is polluted with bourgeois values just as much as her high salary may imply she is a capitalist.
''They're not used to these things, so they oppose us,'' said Miss Guan of her critics. 
''Some workers are used to administration from above and the iron rice bowl. 
They think socialism means everyone should have rice to eat, whether they work or not. 
This kind of thinking is a real problem.''
Miss Guan, whose short black hair is beginning to show the first strands of gray, grew up in a rural area near this grimy town driven by steel mills. 
After graduating from high school in 1968 in the midst of the political hysteria of the Cultural Revolution, she worked on a commune near her home where she was eventually chosen as a production team leader in charge of 340 people. 
In 1971, she was transferred to Benxi, where she sold pork at the Xiaofang grocery store. 
Two and a half years later she was named head of the foodstuffs department and, shortly thereafter, became assistant manager of the entire store.
Â 
Seeks Better Standard of Living
''When we worked in the fields, life was very difficult,'' Miss Guan said, the words tumbling out at a speed rivaling the patter of a disk jockey. 
''So I thought, once we got enterprises going, we could make the country rich. 
I wanted to make it more successful but couldn't. 
Back then, I wanted to make the countryside rich.''
Her biggest disillusionment came, she said, when she was trying to turn the Xiaofang store around. 
''Even if you had talent you couldn't do well because the country didn't give you power,'' she said. 
''As assistant manger, I couldn't do anything because they wouldn't listen to me. 
We had no power.''
In 1984, the city of Benxi announced that private individuals could lease enterprises and run them as they wished. 
That decision, Miss Guan said, changed her life.
''I thought, by using this leasing method I could improve other enterprises,'' she explained. 
''I started looking at losing enterprises. 
I looked at the Guangming food store in 1986, which had consistently lost money for six years.''
Â 
Using Wage Incentives
''It lost money for lots of reasons,'' she said, ''Primarily because the managment was no good.''
In April of that year, Miss Guan leased the Guangming store. 
''The leaders were no good, so I demoted them,'' she said. 
''By the end of the year, the workers had bonuses.''
Her strategy at the Guangming store, she said, was typical of her management techniques at other stores. 
''There was a tremendous amount of waste,'' she said. 
''Internal management was terrible. 
Goods sat around. 
Nobody cared if they were sold or not. 
I set targets for every worker. 
If they didn't meet the target, their wages were cut.''
The combination of rising wages and tough discipline worked wonders on the work force. 
Jiang Xiu-e, a young clerk who confessed she had once had a notorious reputation for a quick tongue and nasty manner with customers, said that after Miss Guan leased the store, she ''told me that if I didn't change my behavior, I would be heavily penalized.''
She added, ''I didn't believe her at all.''
Â 
A Turning Point
But one day, after a raucus argument with a customer, Miss Guan cut 20 yuan, or about $5, from Miss Jiang's salary - about one-quarter of her monthly wage. 
''From that very day, I began to be more cautious with customers,'' Miss Jiang said. 
''Finally, I began to see that customers were actually reasonable. 
It's strange, isn't it?
Now I get the highest monthly bonus of the 220 workers in the store.''
The Economic Daily chronicled the transformation of one of Miss Guan's stores, as described by a frequent customer. 
''I live next to the Guangming grocery store,'' the customer was quoted as saying. 
''The store was dirty and disorderly. 
When you asked for something, no one would answer, and if they did you'd get a very cold response. 
One day, I went to the grocery store and found it had been whitewashed and the floor had been cleaned. 
A salesperson who had always quarreled with me in the past greeted me with a smile, saying, 'We have a new stock of bread, would you like some?'
''
Painfully aware that her success would breed both envy and criticism, Miss Guan canvassed the entire Communist Party hierarchy of Benxi looking for allies. 
In 1985, she stumbled on Li Ming, then the 35-year-old director of the political research office of the city's party branch and a fervent proponent of economic reform and experimentation. 
With the blessing of the city's party secretary, she wooed him away and installed him as the assistant general manager of her operation.
''I was looking at leasing and thought this was the way to promote reforms,'' Mr. Li said. 
''I said, 'If we go according to the Guan Guangmei model, profits will go up dramatically.'
I was interested in going to an enterprise and experimenting in a real environment. 
This was a way for me to be closer to real life.''
Â 
Burgeoning Success
With his help and the party's support, Miss Guan steamed ahead, leasing a total of eight stores and creating a holding company to oversee the venture. 
In two years, she earned more than 44,000 yuan, a sum equivalent to about $12,000 - 50 times what China's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping, earns. 
Much of her earnings she ploughed into Government-required ''risk funds,'' a rainy-day account in case her stores fail, and into extra bonuses and awards for workers. 
Still, she said, she is probably the wealthiest person in Benxi.
Despite her wealth, Miss Guan's achievements have earned her recognition as a national model worker, as well as the ''May 1 Labor Award'' and the ''March 3 National Woman's Award,'' both accolades usually conferred on exemplary factory workers. 
And just last week, she was elected by the Benxi Communist Party as a delegate to the 13th Party Congress to be held in Beijing this October.
''There are many outsiders who object to this,'' Miss Guan said. 
''They think I make too much money. 
Lots of people didn't understand me. 
'Why do you want this trouble?' they said. 
But I said I must do this to make the country better.''
