text:
ï»¿
IF not capitalism, at least a capitalist ethic is seeping into the marrow of China.
Everything Western, everything from the capitalist world outside, is copied, studied and worried about. 
In those areas of Guangdong province near Hong Kong, it is impossible to find a television station tuned to Chinese broadcasts. 
The slam-bang frivolity of Hong Kong TV blares from urban homes and farmers' huts. 
In Beijing, the city seems to lurch to a halt at six o'clock on Sunday night when Mickey Mouse cartoons are shown for 30 minutes. 
''It's done in a way even adults can appreciate,'' an older Chinese man said somewhat solemnly.
Spurring this has been the Government's increasing tolerance of freer economic activity. 
Last week, Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang said that his countrymen would have to embrace even greater economic changes if China's general backwardness was to be overcome. 
Indeed, the China that Prime Minister Zhao described in his opening address to the 13th Communist Party Congress is the China that Mao Zedong loathed and sought to prevent from materializing: a China that permits private enterprise at home, on the farm and in the cities. 
And far from stifling rich peasants, closing down small private industries, suppressing individual entrepreneurs, as Mao deemed essential if China was to truly become a socialist country, Mr. Zhao said they should flourish.
In short, the Prime Minister called for the further introduction and expansion of a vast array of economic practices that smacked more of capitalism than socialism, or at least socialism along the lines practiced in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. 
Across China, farmers, managers of small workshops and factories, restaurant owners, even physicians who have small private practices have eagerly grabbed the chance to improve their lives by making as much money as they possibly can.
Mr. Zhao talked of stocks and bonds, of commercializing the housing market, of stimulating private industry and leasing state enterprises to individuals. 
He urged regulating China's money supply through credit policies in the manner of the Federal Reserve Bank in the United States. 
He called for a sweeping reform of tax policies, piece-rate wages, free market pricing and free competition among enterprises.
But burdened by a legacy of revolution and socialism, Mr. Zhao hastened to disavow the apparently capitalist aura of his program, instead fashioning a schema that sought to preserve ideological rectitude without stifling his policy objectives. 
His solution, widely hailed in the Chinese press, was simply to say that China was in the primary stages of socialism where just about anything in the economic realm is acceptable.
Still, Mr. Zhao's championing of Western economic practices hardly means that China is on the verge of shucking off its socialist manacles in favor of fast, freewheeling capitalism. 
Indeed, the most severe critics of the Chinese regime are inclined to view the economic reform program created by the country's senior leader, Deng Xiaoping, and pursued now by Mr. Zhao, as doomed. 
The core of the problem, these critics contend, is that the Communist Party, which intrudes into virtually every cranny of Chinese life, is unlikely to willingly relinquish its control of society and the economy.
Fang Lizhi, an astrophysicist who headed the country's prestigious University of Science and Technology in Hefei until he was summarily fired last winter for supporting college students' calls for greater democracy, explained the problem in an interview published in the West German news magazine Der Spiegel.
''In China, the party does not want to manage only politics,'' he said. 
''It wants to control everything, including the way of life and the thoughts of the people. 
Today, factories are being managed by managers, but the party cadres keep wielding the power. 
Peasants enjoy the free-market system, but the cadres tell them: 'You still need our rubber stamp, you still have to buy us off!'
There lies the root of the new corruption. 
In order to create a true economic democracy in China, one ought to abolish political controls. 
That is exactly what the party fears most.''
Yet it is far from clear how successful Mr. Zhao will be in encouraging his fellow Communists to extricate themselves from the management of day-to-day affairs in favor of technocratic managers, profit-oriented bankers and bottom-line manufacturers. 
Many western observers believe that the economic reforms of Mr. Deng and Mr. Zhao are at a critical juncture. 
They can move forward, away from socialism and toward a more Western economy, if the party gives up substantial amounts of its power. 
Or, their reforms can flounder in the hands of a party that holds power and refuses to let go.

text:

A ranking United States trade official said today that the Reagan Administration hoped to raise the level of American technology that China was permitted to buy.
The official, Lawrence J. Brady, Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Trade Administration, said that ''we anticipate the technology levels to increase and we're willing to license in a manner that is different from the past.''
The assistant secretary added that the Administration was even willing to permit the export of some items that the Chinese could put to military use.
Â 
80 U.S. 
Companies Represented
Mr. Brady made his remarks at a news conference before he opened an exhibition of American light industry at Peking's exhibition center, where nearly 80 American companies are displaying products worth nearly $4 million.
Christopher Wren comment discusses plan by Reagan Administration to raise level of American technology that China is permitted to purchase
In contrast to the first United States trade exhibition here, which offered an assortment of agricultural and industrial commodities in November 1980, this smaller exhibit is concentrating on what American light industries can offer.
The Chinese Government, which requested the theme, is carrying out a huge restructuring of its economy to provide its nearly 1 billion citizens with more consumer goods and a higher standard of living.
Â 
Trade Could Reach $7.5 Billion
The exhibition, which covers 77,000 square feet, features textileand shoe-manufacturing machinery, cold-storage and refrigeration units, food-processing and packaging machines and printing and photographic equipment. 
But it also includes sophisticated analytical and process-control instruments, including lasers and spectrometers.
Eugene K. Lawson, the Deputy Assistant Secretary for East-West Trade, who also came here for the exhibition, said Chinese-American trade was expected to reach $6.8 billion to $7.5 billion in 1982.
This is well above the $5.5 billion achieved last year and more than six times the $1.1 billion of 1978, just before the United States and China established formal diplomatic relations. 
The United States has become China's third largest trading partner, after Japan and Hong Kong.
The American exports are predominantly agricultural, mostly grain. 
With the Chinese closing their trade gap from $2.7 billion in 1980 to $1.7 billion last year, American companies are anxious to sell more machinery and other industrial products.
There have been complaints that some exports to China have been hampered by United States export-control requirements, which set a limit on the technological sophistication of products that can be sold without Washington's permission.
Mr. Brady, who oversees the export controls, observed today that the Reagan Administration had ''dramatically shortened the time required for the processing of export licenses to China of items not on the export control list'' and had eliminated the backlog of applications.
Chinese Annoyed by Delays
Chinese officials had expressed particular annoyance at the delay they encountered in getting permission to import American computers that they said China needed to conduct its national population census this summer.
Mr. Brady also noted that the Reagan Administration had already raised the level of computer sophistication t hat could be permitted for China, which does not come under the rest rictions imposed on the Soviet bloc nations.
The assistant secretary said the United States was now willing to allow the export of computers with a data processing rate of up to 68 bits, which is more than twice the previous ceiling. 
A bit is a technical standard for measuring a computer's capacity.
Â 
Some Exhibitors Still Concerned
Mr. Brady said Peking's desire to have Washington raise the ceiling on its export controls ''indicates that the Chinese want higher technology from the United States, and if we're prepared to license it, they'll b uy, and that is precisely why this Administration has undertaken th e policy that it has.''
Nonetheless, some of the current American exhibitors expressed concern that the Department of Commerce might not issue licenses in time if the Chinese offered to buy their display models. 
The need has developed because of the widespread utilization of microprocessors, which require export licenses.
Ron Reggev, export sales manager for E.G. and G. Applied Research in Princeton, N.J., said many of his company's analytical instruments for physics and chemistry needed licenses because of technological advances. 
''Several years ago,'' Mr. Reggev said, ''only 5 percent of our products needed export licenses. 
Now it is 50 percent.''
Â 
Holding Seminars for Chinese
In addition to the exhibits, 32 seminars, each lasting a day and a half, are being presented for the Chinese by the representatives of some products being displayed. 
While United States officials concede that the seminars could be used to secure sensitive technical data, Nancy A. Rinehart, the director of China exhibitions for the Department of Commerce, said that ''We've gotten it down to where we can give away sufficient information without giving away the store.''
Not all of the exhibit's participants deal in high technology. 
Paul G. Durmeyer said that his company, Gilson Brothers Company, in Plymouth, Wis., hoped to interest the Chinese in co-producing its lawn tillers and small garden tractors for farm use.
''Our visit here is purely exploratory,'' Mr. Durmeyer said. 
''We don't know if we will be able to sell our equipment here, but we think we can develop contacts for the future.''
Admission to the exhibition is by invitation only, with the China Council for Promotion of International Trade determining which Chinese officials, managers and engineers will be allowed to attend. 
About 80,000 tickets are being given out for the 10-day exhibition.
To alleviate the heavy dose of industrial wares, the United States International Communications Agency has contributed a bright display of telephones, bicycles and even a new Dodge sedan.

Statistics May Help Shultz
The United States, China's third-largest trading partner after Hong Kong and Japan, accounted for 13 percent of Chinese trade volume last year.
The trade figures, which the American Embassy released shortly before the arrival in Peking today of Secretary of State George P. Shultz, seemed likely to help him in his meetings with Chinese officials this week.

Peking had been holding out for a larger share of the American market.

But China evidently expanded its textile exports far more than the previous agreement had envisioned.
Â 
Some U.S. 
Products Banned
China retaliated against the curbs by announcing last month that it would ban future imports of American cotton, soybeans and synthetic fibers. 
But these categories of American exports had already fallen sharply, according to the 1982 trade figures, because the Chinese no longer needed them after several record harvests. 
Thus Peking's ban was mainly a symbolic gesture.
The latest American statistics indicated some shifts in the pattern of China's commerce with the United States, which has climbed sixfold from the $97.5 million level of a decade ago, when the two countries resumed normal trade relations.
With its record harvests, China has cut back on buying some American farm products. 
But China has bought more of the technology that is wanted for its current modernization drive, as well as lumber and fertilizer, which are in limited supply in China.
Agricultural exports to China from the United States declined last year in all categories except corn, which tripled in value, reaching $189.4 million.

Wheat Value Shows Decline
Wheat sales to China, because of depressed prices, dropped by $222.3 million, although the tonnage of shipments increased. 
Wheat remains the largest American commodity sold to the Chinese, with a value last year of $1.05 billion.

Western agricultural experts expect China to buy 9 million more tons during the present fiscal year.

China's sales of other petroleum products rose 36 percent, to nearly $400 million.
Chinese purchases of American coal-cutting, mining and welldrilling machinery jumped more than 53 percent, to $45 million. 
Office machines and computers rose even more sharply, by nearly 64 percent, to account for $36.2 million of China's imports. 
Scientific instruments from the United States also grew 18 percent, reaching $65 million.

WASHINGTON THE Commerce Department and the United
States International Trade Commission are
gearing up for major decisions on low-priced imports from China and the Soviet Union that could set a pattern in trade with centrally planned economies.
The textile industry's politically explosive case against China says that Peking's textile monopoly receives subsidies of more than 40 percent on exports to the United States because of a dual exchange rate benefiting exporters.
The domestic industry, still smarting from recently negotiated import quotas on Chinese textiles that it regards as too liberal, wants countervailing duties imposed by the Commerce Department that would practically halt the imports. 
China is the fourth-largest textile supplier to this country after Hong Kong, South Korea and Taiwan.
The State Department and other agencies fret about the broader political consequences. 
Washington and Peking have taken a number of steps since the late 1970's to improve relations. 
The cutting off of its textile trade would hardly be seen by Peking as a friendly act.
Experts believe that the case, which was prepared for the industry by a former Commerce Department official, John D. Greenwald, now with the Washington law firm of Verner, Liipfert, Bernhard & McPherson, will reach the decisive stage next April at about the time President Reagan is scheduled to visit China. 
That will also be in the heat of a political campaign that promises heavy involvement of the textile lobby, one of the most potent because of the large labor force it represents. 
Employers as well as unions filed the complaint.
Some in the Administration are urging the Commerce Department to dismiss the case, arguing that quotas are the only equitable way of dealing with centrally planned economies.
The ferroalloy industry's case against the Soviet Union involves two sizable shipments into New Orleans this year of a product known as 50 percent ferrosilicon, used in the deoxidation of steel.
The argument is that the 11,000 tons have suddenly raised imports of this sparsely traded product from 5 to 13 percent of the domestic market and are therefore causing ''market disruption.''
The Russians went from zero to 8 percent of the United States market within a three-month period.
At the urging of the National Security Council, the United States trade representative, Bill Brock, asked the trade commission to make a finding on whether the shipments constitute disruption. 
The commission's preliminary ruling may come before the end of the year.
Here, too, the penalty could be higher duties. 
The Russians already pay a 13 percent tariff on the 50 percent ferrosilicon. 
No duty is currently levied on the product if it comes from countries with whom the United States has normal trading relationships.
Competing With Exhibits
''Retaliate,'' came the order from the United States command at the Geneva-based International Labor Organization, and soon officials were wheeling into the assembly models of geothermal power plants, tractors and earth-moving equipment. 
A lightweight firefighter's suit drew cheers.

Washington's decision was in response to a propaganda offensive undertaken by the Russians to try to convince third-world delegates of Moscow's industrial leadership.
''The Soviets would usually give them a couple of glasses of vodka, then show them movies of Soviet industries that were 20 years behind the American industries,'' said Barbara Dunkak, a Labor Department international affairs officer. 
Added her boss, Robert Searby, Deputy Assistant Secretary of Labor for International Labor Affairs, ''We're in a competition.''

Howard, Democrat of New Jersey, to withdraw an amendment that would upset the delicately balanced trucking deregulation package.

Mr. Howard said he could not oblige.

text:

TO many people, the opening of China to foreign investors at the outset of the 1980's seemed like one of the most promising political and economic developments since World War II. 
But now, fresh on the heels of the American Motors Corporation's well-publicized problems with its jeep-making venture here, there is a growing sense among Americans and Chinese alike that the lure of investing in China has dimmed.
In public, at least, the Chinese continue to stress their successes. 
According to Chinese Government statistics, 2,300 joint ventures between foreign companies and Chinese state enterprises had been approved by the end of 1985, drawing $6 billion in foreign equity investment to China. 
Of this, about $1.4 billion was American, including investments by such Fortune 500 corporations as McDonnell-Douglas, A.M.C., Pepsi-Cola, Coca-Cola, Atlantic Richfield and Occidental Petroleum.
But now - despite the Chinese decision to meet A.M.C.'s threat of a pullout with concessions that at least temporarily resolve the problems -there is widespread doubt among foreign investors whether their efforts to establish a foothold here are worthwhile. 
Many are increasingly doubtful that their dream of gaining access to the vast Chinese market will ever materialize. 
All but a handful of them remain plagued with the same foreign exchange problems, disputes over contract interpretation, inflexible bureaucracy and high costs that have shadowed A.M.C.
Currency remains the major sticking point. 
Only a few investors -mainly owners of luxury hotels built to accommodate foreign tourists and business executives, which have guaranteed hard currency earnings - are untouched by the problem. 
The 1,000-room Holiday Inn-Lido Hotel in Peking enjoyed a profit rate of more than 50 percent on revenues last year of nearly $38 million. 
Robert Lo, the Singapore millionaire who is the majority owner, is said to be confident that he can pay off his investment in three and a half years, faster than hotels in Hong Kong. 
BUT most joint ventures have yet to show a profit in anything other than the inconvertible Chinese currency, the renminbi. 
To some executives the compromise with A.M.C., which involved a pledge to resume payments to that company in dollars, represented the first hope that the Chinese, after years of promising investors at least a ''reasonable'' hard-currency profit, might be preparing for more than the half-measures adopted hitherto. 
But to others the deal looked like an exceptional fix, made to avoid the ripple effect of a pullout by A.M.C. 
''A happy ending?
Don't bet on it,'' said one American executive.
The Chinese, clearly worried, have intensified their efforts to reassure investors, particularly Americans. 
Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang, meeting last week with an American business group headed by Robert Strauss, the United States special trade representative in the Carter Administration, acknowledged that there were ''inconveniences'' because of shortcomings in China's legal system, its limited foreign exchange and low industrial efficiency. 
But he said ''the problems will surely be resolved.''
Still, skepticism persists, partly because of a growing awareness that China and its foreign partners are seeking contradictory ends. 
Ever mindful of foreign depradations in the century before Communist power, Chinese leaders have always said that foreign investment is a tool to be used for the shortest time necessary to effect a transfer of technology and managerial skills. 
Their declared purpose is to help China modernize in a manner that ultimately will make it possible to manage without a major foreign investment presence in China.
Until recently, executives making investment decisions, usually far away, have tended to minimize this stated concern for sovereignty and to assume that China - in the manner of many of the non-Communist nations in Asia - is embarking on a path that will make it progressively more receptive to multinational corporations. 
But recent events are forcing a reassessment.
There is concern as well about the future of the ''open door'' policy after Deng Xiaoping, the 81-year-old head of the Communist Party, passes from the scene. 
The past two years have shown more clearly than before that forces are at work inside the party that are a good deal less friendly to foreign influences - and to investments - than Mr. Deng.
For some companies, which cannot afford to take the long view, the question of whether China's markets will open to foreigners is academic. 
Among them, there is growing fractiousness over day-to-day treatment. 
In matters involving labor, taxes, customs duties, and living costs, among others, there is a sense that foreigners have been marked for discriminatory treatment.
Some executives who have had difficulty holding Chinese partners to negotiated terms have concluded that the Western notion of contract, implying a pact between equals, is alien to traditional Chinese concepts of the role of foreigners on Chinese soil, in which the foreigner has no rights, only the privileges the Chinese confer.
This dovetails with another view, which sees the free enterprise ideas of Westerners as the natural enemy of the monopolistic attitude ingrained in a state-owned economy. 
Winston Lord, the United States Ambassador, who is optimistic that investment conditions will improve, puts it politely. 
''The Chinese,'' Mr. Lord said recently, ''are having some difficulty mating Communism and capitalism.''
A West German executive is more blunt: ''Here, you see every evil of textbook monopoly. 
Dealing with a Chinese state enterprise is like bargaining with a pistol at your head.''
Not everyone believes the blame can be easily apportioned. 
Lois Dougan Tretiak, a senior China analyst with Business International Ltd. in Hong Kong who wrote a study of joint ventures, said many problems resulted from poorly negotiated contracts. 
''People come here and they get over-awed,'' she said. 
It is virtually a truism among foreigners who have lived here for some time that an initial acquaintance with China - its lavish banquets, elaborate courtesies, physical beauty and lingering sense of mystery - can cause normally hard-headed people to suspend or relax their judgment.
The A.M.C. experience demonstrated the pitfalls. 
The jeep maker made a deal with the Chinese in 1984 to import kits of the company's Cherokee model for assembly at the Beijing Jeep Corporation. 
But by October 1985, when Vice President Bush drove the first model off the assembly line, the country was in a foreign exchange crisis. 
Abuse of new, decentralized economic powers had drained state reserves, which sank to barely $10 billion, a drop of more than 30 percent in six months. 
All foreign exchange payments to A.M.C. stopped.
The freeze left the company with millions of dollars in uncollected bills for the $12,000 kits, as well as millions of renminbi from its share in the profits from the production of a standard Chinese jeep. 
When the Chinese refused to compromise, the American company halted shipment of Cherokee kits. 
It took months of acrimony and an appeal to Prime Minister Zhao Ziyang to produce the recent pledge to resume dollar payments.
It is a concession that is unlikely to be granted to others. 
Under a recent Chinese directive, most new joint ventures will be expected to export 51 percent of their production and to draw their earnings from the hard- currency receipts. 
But most enterprises face price and quality problems that make exports of that scale an illusion. 
A.M.C., for example, has exported none of the 800 Cherokees it has assembled, and does not expect to until it has sharply reduced production costs, which are higher than in its main Cherokee plant in Toledo, Ohio. 
FOR many, the best that can be expected is an accumulating surplus of renminbi, whose value is questionable. 
At one point last year, for example, Pepsi-Cola Inc.'s bottling plant in the Shenzhen special economic zone near Hong Kong had a surplus of 8 million renminbi, $2.5 million officially. 
The company used several million renminbi in the construction of a second plant, in Canton. 
But Pepsi's efforts to spend the rest faltered when it was unable to buy even simple chemicals in the local market.
On the principle that China will not allow itself to be exploited for ''cheap'' resources, and to help rebuild foreign currency reserves, Western businesses are being subjected to very high costs. 
Mats Engstrom, president of Tsar Nicoulai, a San Francisco-based fine foods company, had to parry Chinese demands that he pay a daily rental of $100 each for two $19,000 Cherokee jeeps that he had bought for his caviar operation here this spring. 
''I told them, 'They're my jeeps,''' Mr. Engstrom recalled. 
''After a while, they got the message.''
One United States company was asked to pay $9,000 a month for a Chinese-trained high-technology specialist, more than 10 times the specialist's take-home pay for a year. 
Many are paying rents of $90,000 a year for three-bedroom apartments, and proportionate amounts for offices. 
And new import duties of up to 275 percent have pushed the cost of a medium-sized Japanese car close to $40,000.
Problems with workers have been another bugbear. 
Peking's Sheraton Great Wall Hotel, dogged by financial troubles for most of its first two years of operation, recently won the right to fire incompetents among its 1,200 Chinese employees. 
But the concession was rare. 
Generally, the work force is supervised by the Chinese partners. 
In many cases, the result has been dismal productivity rates that make it more expensive to produce products here than in Western Europe and the United States.
Confronted with a chronicle of such problems, Chinese officials are inclined to point out that few joint ventures have collapsed, indicating at least minimal satisfaction. 
But many foreign executives say that this is a false standard, since their head offices have made a strategic decision to stick with their investments here for the time being, regardless of cost. 
It is a demoralizing situation, and the turnover among expatriates -A.M.C. had three chief executives in a year - is high.
One source of comfort for American investors is that their complaints have been taken seriously by a succession of senior United States officials visiting here. 
The most recent was the Treasury Secretary, James A. Baker 3d, who raised some of the most pressing problems with senior Chinese officials last month. 
A briefing paper prepared by the American Embassy for the visit put the situation starkly: ''In every case, U.S. partners are paying a very high price to be in China now because their parent corporations have made a strategic decision to enter the China market for the long term. 
They have taken a great commercial and potential political risk, and, for most, the potential payoff is still years away.''

China may eventually rank with India as the World Bank's two largest borrowers, according to a top bank official who has completed talks with the Government here.
''We are still far from reaching our cruising altitude with regard to China,'' said Munir P. Benjenk, the World Bank's vice president of external relations. 
He estimated that China might approach India's level some time in 1985.
PEKING, Oct. 
6 - China may eventually rank with India as the World Bank's two largest borrowers, according to a top bank official who has completed talks with the Government here.
India borrows close to $2 billion a year, Mr. Benjenk said; China has drawn only $260 million so far. 
There have been reports here that the Government is unhappy with the amount of aid that it has got since it joined the World Bank in May 1980. 
China wants foreign capital to help finance its ambitious modernization program.
Â 
Current Talks on Project Loans
But Mr. Benjenk said he saw ''no sign at all'' of such unhappiness. 
He noted that the World Bank was now negotiating four other project loans and working on another 20 potential projects that would qualify for financial assistance in China.
When China joined the bank, a round of loans for the previous members had already been worked out, and special arrangements had to be made to find money for China.
But China will be a party when the seventh replenishment, or allocated capital, is negotiated next month. 
And Mr. Benjenk told Chinese and foreign journalists at a news conference today that China would get more substantial aid then. 
The World Bank arranges its replenishments every three years.
The World Bank offers two kinds of loan to developing countries. 
The first is at near market rates, using a formula of the cost of borrowing for the previous three to six months plus a service charge of one-half of 1 percent; the current interest is 11.43 percent.
The other, more desirable, kind of loan is made through the bank's affiliate, the International Development Association. 
It bears no interest, only a service charge of three-quarters of 1 percent, and is repayable over 50 years, with a 10-year grace period.
Â 
Loans Are Usually 'Blended'
Because funds are insufficient to give every developing country interest-free loans, the World Bank often offers a blend of loans, based on a country's per-capita income and other economic resources.
China's negotiations with the World Bank recently have centered on what share of the development association loans China will get. 
Its gross domestic product was estimated at only $279 per capita last year. 
However, it also ran a foreign trade surplus of $3.8 billion and is now preparing to tap what are thought to be considerable reserves of oil offshore.
Mr. Benjenk said the World Bank, in giving loans, took into account not only a country's income level but also its creditworthiness and potential for repayment. 
''China, as the largest developing country in the world, will have to have a share of I.D.A. funds,'' he said.
He insisted that China's participation in the World Bank would not reduce the money available to poorer countries, including the 31 nations the bank calls the least developed. 
These are mostly in Africa, and qualify for exclusively interest-free loans.
''Everybody would like to borrow more from the I.D.A. than from the World Bank - it's natural,'' Mr. Benjenk said. 
''But there is a scarcity of resources of the I.D.A. 
The rationing process is based on the greatest need, and the greatest need is in Africa.''
